## 1. System Overview — 8-Zone Induction Power Architecture

The Aegis-Forge I induction power electronics subsystem delivers controlled, frequency-agile electromagnetic energy to eight independent coil zones surrounding the ZrB₂-SiC drum. This is the nervous system of the thermal cascade — translating digital setpoints into precisely shaped magnetic fields that selectively heat target materials while leaving dielectric components untouched.

### 1.1 Architecture Summary

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Total Installed Power** | 500 kW (continuous) |
| **Input Supply** | 480 VAC, 3-phase, 60 Hz industrial |
| **Zone Count** | 8 independently controlled resonant inverters |
| **Frequency Range** | 100 kHz → 1 kHz (zone-dependent) |
| **Topology** | Class E resonant inverter with GaN HEMT switches |
| **Control Loop** | PID ±5°C with resonance tracking (1 kHz update) |
| **Sensing** | 384 FBG sensors (PMMA POF, WDM+TDM multiplexed) |
| **Isolation** | All-dielectric control wiring (PMMA optical fiber) |
| **Safety Rating** | SIL-3 + Carrington GIC immunity |

### 1.2 Zone Mapping to Thermal Stages

The eight coil zones correspond directly to the eight thermal processing stages. Each zone heats a 100 mm axial band of the 800 mm drum length.

| Zone | Axial Position | Thermal Stage | Target Temp | Frequency | Power Range | Primary Material |
|------|----------------|---------------|-------------|-----------|-------------|------------------|
| Z1 | 0–100 mm | Stage 1: Drying | 80–150°C | 100 kHz | 0–50 kW | H₂O, volatiles (indirect) |
| Z2 | 100–200 mm | Stage 2: Polymer | 150–450°C | 100 kHz | 0–50 kW | Thermoplastics (indirect) |
| Z3 | 200–300 mm | Stage 3: Pyrolysis | 450–700°C | 50 kHz | 50–80 kW | Zn, Pb, char (onset) |
| Z4 | 300–400 mm | Stage 4: Low-Temp Metals | 420–900°C | 10 kHz | 80–150 kW | Zn, Pb, Sn, In, Al |
| Z5 | 400–500 mm | Stage 5: Aluminum | 660–720°C | 10 kHz | 80–150 kW | Al alloys |
| Z6 | 500–600 mm | Stage 6: Copper | 1085–1200°C | 5 kHz | 100–200 kW | Cu, precious metals |
| Z7 | 600–700 mm | Stage 7: Ferrous | 1200–1600°C | 2 kHz | 150–350 kW | Fe, Ni, Cr, RE magnets |
| Z8 | 700–800 mm | Stage 8: Mineral | 1600–2200°C | 1 kHz | 200–500 kW | Silicates, RE oxides |

### 1.3 Power Distribution Strategy

The 480 VAC 3-phase supply enters a dedicated isolation transformer bank (3 × 200 kVA, delta-wye, BFRP-housed) providing galvanic isolation between the industrial grid and the process electronics. Each inverter module draws from a dedicated 3-phase feed with individual harmonic filtering (LCL, 5th/7th/11th notch). The isolation transformer secondary is floating — no earth reference — eliminating ground fault paths and providing inherent GIC immunity for the process electronics.

---

## 2. Resonant Inverter Design — 8× GS66516T GaN HEMT Class E Topology

Each of the eight zones employs an identical resonant inverter module, differing only in the resonant tank component values (L, C) to achieve the target frequency for that zone. The topology is Class E zero-voltage switching (ZVS), chosen for its simplicity, high efficiency (>97%), and natural suitability for variable-frequency operation.

### 2.1 Class E Resonant Inverter Principles

The Class E topology achieves ZVS by shaping the voltage waveform across the switch such that it reaches zero with zero derivative at the switching instant:

$$v_{DS}(t) = V_{DD} \left[ 1 - \frac{\pi}{2} \sin(\omega t + \phi) \right]$$

The shunt capacitance $C_{shunt}$ (comprising the GaN output capacitance $C_{oss}$ plus external capacitor) and series resonant inductance $L_r$ form the tank:

$$\omega = \frac{1}{\sqrt{L_r C_{shunt}}}$$

At resonance, the switch current is sinusoidal and the voltage is a shaped half-wave, eliminating switching losses. The GaN HEMT's near-zero reverse recovery charge ($Q_{rr} \approx 0$) makes it ideal for Class E — no body diode conduction losses during dead time.

### 2.2 GS66516T GaN HEMT Specifications

| Parameter | Value | Note |
|-----------|-------|------|
| **Device** | GS66516T (GaN Systems) | 650 V, 16 A |
| **Topology** | Half-bridge Class E | Single switch per leg |
| **V<sub>DS</sub> max** | 650 V | Derated to 400 V operating |
| **R<sub>DS(on)</sub>** | 30 mΩ (typ) @ 25°C | Low conduction loss |
| **C<sub>oss</sub>** | 55 pF (typ) @ 400 V | Forms part of resonant tank |
| **Q<sub>g</sub>** | 3.5 nC | Ultra-low gate charge |
| **T<sub>j</sub> max** | 150°C | Junction temperature limit |
| **Thermal resistance R<sub>θJC</sub>** | 0.8 K/W | Junction-to-case |

Each inverter leg uses two GS66516T devices in a half-bridge configuration with bootstrapped high-side drive. The driver IC (LMG1210 or equivalent GaN-specific driver) provides 2.5 A peak gate current for fast switching transitions (<2 ns rise/fall).

### 2.3 Variable Frequency Operation

The resonant frequency is varied by adjusting the effective tank capacitance. A switched capacitor bank (binary-weighted: C, 2C, 4C, 8C, 16C, 32C) allows discrete frequency steps, while a varactor diode array provides fine continuous tuning (±5% range). The control loop measures the actual switch voltage waveform zero-crossing and adjusts the varactor bias to maintain ZVS across the full operating range.

Frequency switching transients are managed by a pre-computed trajectory table — the controller ramps frequency in 100 Hz steps with 10 ms dwell, allowing the tank energy to settle before the next step.

### 2.4 Efficiency Analysis

At nominal operating points:

| Zone | Frequency | Output Power | Switching Loss | Conduction Loss | Total Loss | Efficiency |
|------|-----------|--------------|----------------|-----------------|------------|------------|
| Z1–Z2 | 100 kHz | 50 kW | 0.3 kW | 0.7 kW | 1.0 kW | 98.0% |
| Z3 | 50 kHz | 80 kW | 0.2 kW | 1.2 kW | 1.4 kW | 98.3% |
| Z4–Z5 | 10 kHz | 150 kW | 0.1 kW | 2.0 kW | 2.1 kW | 98.6% |
| Z6 | 5 kHz | 200 kW | 0.08 kW | 2.5 kW | 2.6 kW | 98.7% |
| Z7 | 2 kHz | 350 kW | 0.05 kW | 4.0 kW | 4.1 kW | 98.8% |
| Z8 | 1 kHz | 500 kW | 0.03 kW | 5.5 kW | 5.5 kW | 98.9% |

Losses dominated by GaN conduction (R<sub>DS(on)</sub> × I<sub>rms</sub>²) and inductor ESR at low frequencies. Switching losses become negligible below 10 kHz.

---

## 3. Frequency Ladder & Zone Mapping — Physics-Based Design

The frequency ladder (100 kHz → 1 kHz) is not arbitrary — it is derived from the skin depth equation and the magnetic properties of target materials at each stage temperature.

### 3.1 Skin Depth and Frequency Selection

Skin depth determines how deeply the magnetic field penetrates the material:

$$\delta = \sqrt{\frac{2\rho}{\omega \mu}}$$

Where $\rho$ = electrical resistivity (Ω·m), $\omega = 2\pi f$ = angular frequency, $\mu = \mu_0 \mu_r$ = magnetic permeability.

For uniform heating of a material of thickness $d$, we require $\delta \geq d/2$. For selective surface heating (e.g., thin foils), $\delta \ll d$.

### 3.2 Material Property Tables at Operating Temperatures

#### Electrical Resistivity (ρ) vs Temperature

| Material | ρ @ 20°C (nΩ·m) | ρ @ 500°C (nΩ·m) | ρ @ 1000°C (nΩ·m) | ρ @ 1500°C (nΩ·m) |
|----------|-----------------|------------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| Aluminum | 26.5 | 78 | — (liquid) | — |
| Copper | 16.8 | 45 | 85 | — (liquid) |
| Iron (ferritic) | 97 | 320 | 580 | 920 |
| Nickel | 69 | 210 | 380 | — |
| Zinc | 59 | 120 (liq) | — | — |
| Lead | 208 | 450 (liq) | — | — |
| Tin | 115 | 240 (liq) | — | — |
| Indium | 84 | 180 (liq) | — | — |
| Steel (304 SS) | 720 | 1100 | 1350 | 1500 |

#### Relative Permeability (μ<sub>r</sub>) vs Temperature

| Material | μ<sub>r</sub> @ 20°C | μ<sub>r</sub> @ 500°C | μ<sub>r</sub> @ 770°C (Curie) | μ<sub>r</sub> @ 1000°C |
|----------|---------------------|----------------------|-------------------------------|------------------------|
| Iron (pure) | 5000 | 200 | 1 (paramagnetic) | 1 |
| Nickel | 600 | 50 | 1 (Curie 354°C) | 1 |
| Cobalt | 250 | 20 | 1 (Curie 1115°C) | 1 |
| Ferrite (MnZn) | 2000 | 100 | 1 | 1 |
| Non-ferrous (Al, Cu, Zn, Pb) | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 |

### 3.3 Skin Depth Calculations at Zone Frequencies

| Zone | Freq (kHz) | Material | ρ (nΩ·m) | μ<sub>r</sub> | δ (mm) | Target Thickness |
|------|------------|----------|----------|--------------|--------|------------------|
| Z1–Z2 | 100 | Air/N₂ (indirect) | — | 1 | — | — |
| Z3 | 50 | Zn (liq) | 120 | 1 | 7.8 | 150 mm charge |
| Z3 | 50 | Pb (liq) | 450 | 1 | 15.1 | 150 mm charge |
| Z4 | 10 | Al (solid) | 78 | 1 | 14.0 | 10–50 mm pieces |
| Z5 | 10 | Al (liq) | 280 | 1 | 26.6 | 50 mm pool depth |
| Z6 | 5 | Cu (solid) | 85 | 1 | 20.7 | 20 mm wire bundles |
| Z6 | 5 | Cu (liq) | 220 | 1 | 33.3 | 50 mm pool |
| Z7 | 2 | Fe (solid) | 580 | 1 | 17.1 | 30 mm plate/slab |
| Z7 | 2 | Fe (liq) | 920 | 1 | 21.5 | 50 mm pool |
| Z8 | 1 | Silicates | 10⁹ | 1 | >1000 | Full penetration |

**Key insight:** At Z7 (2 kHz), ferromagnetic materials have lost permeability (above Curie), so heating relies on eddy currents only. The lower frequency ensures deeper penetration into large ferrous pieces. At Z8 (1 kHz), the refractory minerals are essentially insulators — heating is purely by thermal conduction from the drum wall and susceptor materials.

### 3.4 Ampere-Turns and B-Field Requirements

The magnetic field strength $H = N I / l_e$ (ampere-turns per meter) must produce sufficient flux density $B = \mu H$ for the target power. For a 100 mm axial zone with 8-turn coil:

| Zone | Target Power | I<sub>rms</sub> (per turn) | N | NI (A-t) | B<sub>peak</sub> (mT) |
|------|--------------|---------------------------|---|----------|---------------------|
| Z1 | 50 kW | 125 A | 8 | 1000 | 12.6 |
| Z3 | 80 kW | 160 A | 8 | 1280 | 16.1 |
| Z5 | 150 kW | 220 A | 8 | 1760 | 22.1 |
| Z7 | 350 kW | 330 A | 8 | 2640 | 33.1 |
| Z8 | 500 kW | 395 A | 8 | 3160 | 39.6 |

---

## 4. GaN Thermal Management — Junction-to-Cold-Plate Design

Maintaining GaN junction temperature below 125°C (derated from 150°C max) at 500 kW total dissipation requires a high-performance liquid cooling system.

### 4.1 Thermal Resistance Budget

| Thermal Interface | R<sub>θ</sub> (K/W) | Notes |
|-------------------|---------------------|-------|
| Junction-to-case (R<sub>θJC</sub>) | 0.8 | GS66516T datasheet |
| Case-to-cold-plate (TIM + interface) | 0.15 | Indium foil or phase-change TIM |
| Cold-plate convection (water) | 0.05 | Microchannel, 2 m/s flow |
| Water-to-ambient (chiller) | 0.02 | External chiller |
| **Total R<sub>θJA</sub>** | **1.02 K/W** | |

At 5.5 kW dissipation (Z8 worst case): $\Delta T = 5.5 \times 1.02 = 5.6°C$ above water temperature. With 25°C inlet water, T<sub>j</sub> ≈ 31°C — well within limits.

### 4.2 Microchannel Cold Plate Design

Each inverter module mounts on a copper microchannel cold plate (CSMFAB-sourced copper — the only copper in the machine, justified as internal heat spreader not connected to earth):

- **Channel geometry:** 0.5 mm wide × 1 mm deep, 40 channels parallel
- **Flow rate:** 2 L/min per module (16 L/min total for 8 modules)
- **Pressure drop:** 0.8 bar @ 2 L/min
- **Material:** Copper base with PEX-a water connections
- **Surface finish:** Ni-P electroless nickel (corrosion resistance, solderable)

### 4.3 PEX-a Water Circuit

The cooling water circuit uses PEX-a tubing (CSMFAB Materials Study Part IV) throughout — completely non-conductive, eliminating any conductive path from the process electronics to the building ground. This is a critical Carrington immunity feature.

- **Loop layout:** Parallel feed to each module, manifold return
- **Filtration:** 10 μm cartridge filter, ZrO₂ housing
- **Treatment:** Deionized water, 18 MΩ·cm, with corrosion inhibitor (benzotriazole, 50 ppm)
- **Monitoring:** FBG temperature sensors at each module inlet/outlet

## 5. FBG Optical Sensing Network — 384 PMMA POF Sensors

Temperature feedback for the PID control loops comes entirely from fiber Bragg grating (FBG) sensors embedded in the drum wall, communicated via PMMA plastic optical fiber (POF). This all-dielectric sensing path is immune to the intense EM fields and provides Carrington-hardened data transmission.

### 5.1 FBG Sensor Specifications

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Fiber Type** | PMMA POF (step-index, 980 μm core, 1000 μm clad) |
| **Grating Type** | Type I FBG, UV-written in PMMA |
| **Wavelength Range** | 650–850 nm (PMMA transmission window) |
| **Temperature Sensitivity** | 0.15 nm/°C (PMMA, higher than silica's 0.01 nm/°C) |
| **Resolution** | 0.1°C (interrogator limited) |
| **Accuracy** | ±0.5°C (calibrated) |
| **Sensor Length** | 5 mm grating, 10 mm total |
| **Quantity** | 384 (48 per zone × 8 zones) |
| **Multiplexing** | WDM (8 wavelengths) + TDM (6 spatial channels per wavelength) |

### 5.2 Sensor Placement Strategy

Each 100 mm zone contains 48 FBG sensors distributed as:
- **Drum inner wall (24 sensors):** 3 circumferential rings × 8 angular positions — measures process-side temperature
- **Drum outer wall (12 sensors):** 3 rings × 4 positions — measures coil-side temperature
- **Coil former (8 sensors):** 2 rings × 4 positions — measures coil winding temperature
- **Cold plate (4 sensors):** Inlet/outlet per module — monitors coolant ΔT

### 5.3 WDM+TDM Multiplexing Architecture

```
Optical Interrogator (1 kHz sweep)
    │
    ├── λ1 (680 nm) → TDM Channel 1 → 6 sensors (Zone 1)
    ├── λ2 (700 nm) → TDM Channel 2 → 6 sensors (Zone 2)
    ├── λ3 (720 nm) → TDM Channel 3 → 6 sensors (Zone 3)
    ├── λ4 (740 nm) → TDM Channel 4 → 6 sensors (Zone 4)
    ├── λ5 (760 nm) → TDM Channel 5 → 6 sensors (Zone 5)
    ├── λ6 (780 nm) → TDM Channel 6 → 6 sensors (Zone 6)
    ├── λ7 (800 nm) → TDM Channel 7 → 6 sensors (Zone 7)
    └── λ8 (820 nm) → TDM Channel 8 → 6 sensors (Zone 8)
```

Each TDM channel uses a 1×6 optical splitter (PMMA, fused biconical taper) with 60 m total fiber length per channel. The interrogator uses a tunable VCSEL (650–850 nm) with 1 kHz sweep rate, providing 125 Hz per sensor update rate.

### 5.4 PMMA POF Advantages for This Application

1. **GIC Immunity:** Zero conductive path — no antenna for geomagnetically induced currents
2. **EM Immunity:** Unaffected by 500 kW of 1–100 kHz magnetic fields
3. **High Temperature Sensitivity:** 0.15 nm/°C (15× silica) enables 0.1°C resolution with simpler interrogator
4. **Radiation Hardness:** PMMA tolerates gamma/neutron flux better than silica
5. **In-House Drawable:** CSMFAB Materials Study Part IV shows $0.08–$0.15/m vs $0.22–$0.80 commercial

## 6. PID Control Architecture — ±5°C Zone Control with Resonance Tracking

The control system maintains each zone at its thermal setpoint while simultaneously tracking the resonant frequency of the Class E inverter to maintain ZVS.

### 6.1 Dual-Loop Control Structure

```
                    ┌─────────────────────┐
   T_setpoint ────►│   Thermal PID       │───► Power Command (kW)
                    │   (Outer Loop)      │       100 ms update
                    └─────────┬───────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
                    ┌─────────────────────┐
                    │   Power-to-Freq     │
                    │   Mapping Table     │
                    └─────────┬───────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
                    ┌─────────────────────┐
   V_DS Zero-Cross─►│   Resonance Tracker │───► Varactor Bias / Cap Bank
   (Inner Loop)     │   (Inner Loop)      │       10 ms update
                    └─────────────────────┘
```

### 6.2 Thermal PID (Outer Loop) — 100 ms Update

$$u(t) = K_p e(t) + K_i \int e(t) dt + K_d \frac{de(t)}{dt}$$

| Zone | K<sub>p</sub> | K<sub>i</sub> (s⁻¹) | K<sub>d</sub> (s) | Anti-Windup |
|------|--------------|-------------------|------------------|-------------|
| Z1–Z2 | 0.8 | 0.02 | 0.5 | ±10% output clamp |
| Z3 | 1.0 | 0.03 | 0.8 | ±10% |
| Z4–Z5 | 1.2 | 0.05 | 1.0 | ±10% |
| Z6 | 1.5 | 0.08 | 1.2 | ±10% |
| Z7 | 1.8 | 0.10 | 1.5 | ±10% |
| Z8 | 2.0 | 0.15 | 2.0 | ±10% |

Gains increase at lower frequencies (higher power zones) because thermal mass dominates response.

### 6.3 Resonance Tracker (Inner Loop) — 10 ms Update

The Class E inverter maintains ZVS by detecting the switch voltage zero-crossing and comparing to the gate drive timing. A phase-locked loop (PLL) structure adjusts the varactor bias voltage to align the voltage zero-crossing with the gate turn-on instant:

$$\phi_{error} = t_{V_{DS}=0} - t_{gate-on}$$

$$\Delta V_{varactor} = K_{p,PLL} \phi_{error} + K_{i,PLL} \int \phi_{error} dt$$

This inner loop runs at 100 Hz (10 ms), 10× faster than the thermal loop, ensuring ZVS is maintained during thermal transients.

### 6.4 Feedforward Compensation

A feedforward term based on the zone's thermal model predicts the power required for the next setpoint change:

$$P_{ff} = m c_p \frac{dT}{dt} + h A (T - T_{amb}) + \epsilon \sigma A (T^4 - T_{amb}^4)$$

Where the radiative term dominates above 800°C. The feedforward reduces thermal PID integral windup during ramp phases.

## 7. Selective Heating Physics — Conductivity/Permeability as Material Selector

The fundamental sorting mechanism of the Aegis-Forge I is the frequency-dependent coupling of the induction field to different material classes.

### 7.1 Coupling Coefficient Derivation

The power absorbed by a material in an alternating magnetic field:

$$P_{abs} = \frac{\pi^2 B_{peak}^2 d^2 f^2 V}{6 \rho} \quad \text{(non-magnetic, } \delta \gg d\text{)}$$

$$P_{abs} = \frac{\pi B_{peak}^2 f V}{\mu} \quad \text{(magnetic, } \delta \ll d\text{)}$$

Where $V$ = volume of material, $d$ = characteristic dimension.

### 7.2 Selective Heating Matrix

| Material Class | ρ (nΩ·m) | μ<sub>r</sub> | Coupling at 100 kHz | Coupling at 10 kHz | Coupling at 1 kHz |
|----------------|----------|--------------|---------------------|-------------------|------------------|
| Copper | 16.8 | 1 | Very High | High | Moderate |
| Aluminum | 26.5 | 1 | High | Moderate | Low |
| Zinc (liq) | 120 | 1 | Moderate | Low | Very Low |
| Lead (liq) | 450 | 1 | Low | Very Low | Negligible |
| Iron (ferro) | 97 | 5000 | Extreme | Very High | High |
| Steel | 720 | 200 | High | Moderate | Low |
| Ceramics | 10¹² | 1 | None | None | None |
| Polymers | 10¹⁵ | 1 | None | None | None |
| BFRP | 10¹⁰ | 1 | None | None | None |

**Design rule:** At Z7 (2 kHz), ferrous materials heat 50× more than aluminum. At Z5 (10 kHz), aluminum heats 15× more than zinc. At Z1–Z2 (100 kHz), only very thin conductive foils couple — bulk plastics and organics do not heat directly.

### 7.3 Thermal-EM Coupling in Mixed Charge

In a real feedstock batch, materials are mixed. The induction field creates a **thermal gradient** within the charge:

1. **Ferrous pieces** heat first and hottest (hysteresis + eddy)
2. **Non-ferrous conductors** (Cu, Al) heat second (eddy only)
3. **Resistive metals** (Zn, Pb, Sn) heat third
4. **Dielectrics** (ceramics, plastics, glass) heat only by conduction from hot neighbors

This natural sorting is enhanced by the drum rotation — as materials liquefy at different temperatures, centrifugal force segregates them radially before port ejection.

## 8. 3-Phase Power Distribution — 480V Delta, Isolation, Harmonic Filtering

### 8.1 Supply Architecture

```
Grid (480V Δ, 60 Hz)
    │
    ├──► Isolation Transformer Bank (3 × 200 kVA, Δ-Y, BFRP case)
    │       │
    │       ├──► Inverter Module 1 (Zone 1) + LCL Filter
    │       ├──► Inverter Module 2 (Zone 2) + LCL Filter
    │       ├──► Inverter Module 3 (Zone 3) + LCL Filter
    │       ├──► Inverter Module 4 (Zone 4) + LCL Filter
    │       ├──► Inverter Module 5 (Zone 5) + LCL Filter
    │       ├──► Inverter Module 6 (Zone 6) + LCL Filter
    │       ├──► Inverter Module 7 (Zone 7) + LCL Filter
    │       └──► Inverter Module 8 (Zone 8) + LCL Filter
    │
    └──► Neutral Grounding Resistor (NGR) — 5 A limit
```

### 8.2 Isolation Transformer Specifications

- **Rating:** 200 kVA each (3 total, one per phase group)
- **Primary:** 480 V Δ, withstand 10 kV BIL
- **Secondary:** 400 V Y (floating, no neutral connection to ground)
- **Insulation:** Class H (180°C), BFRP housing, vacuum pressure impregnated
- **Leakage Inductance:** 3% (integrated with LCL filter)
- **Inter-winding Capacitance:** <50 pF (minimizes common-mode noise)

### 8.3 LCL Harmonic Filter (Per Module)

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| **Topology** | LCL (L1 = 200 μH, C = 10 μF, L2 = 50 μH) |
| **Resonant Frequency** | 3.5 kHz (damped) |
| **Target Harmonics** | 5th (300 Hz), 7th (420 Hz), 11th (660 Hz), 13th (780 Hz) |
| **Attenuation** | >40 dB at switching harmonics |
| **Capacitor** | Film (PP), 10 μF, 1000 VAC, ZrO₂ case |
| **Inductors** | Nanocrystalline core, PEX-a cooling, BFRP housing |

### 8.4 GIC Immunity Design

The entire power distribution system is designed for Carrington-level geomagnetic disturbance (dB/dt = 5000 nT/s, inducing 10–100 V/km on transmission lines):

1. **Floating secondary:** No path for DC/low-f GIC to enter process electronics
2. **NGR limits fault current:** 5 A max ground fault
3. **All-dielectric control:** PMMA POF for all signals — no copper wires to act as antennas
4. **BFRP transformer housing:** Non-conductive, no eddy current heating from GIC
5. **Surge protection:** Gas discharge tubes (GDT) at transformer primary, 3 kA rating

## 9. Electrical Safety & SIL-3 — Arc Flash, Ground Fault, Carrington Hardening

### 9.1 Safety Integrity Level 3 (SIL-3) Architecture

The power electronics subsystem achieves SIL-3 (IEC 61508) through:

| Safety Function | Implementation | PFD<sub>avg</sub> |
|-----------------|----------------|-------------------|
| Over-temperature shutdown | Dual FBG sensors (2oo3 voting) | 1×10⁻⁴ |
| Over-current protection | GaN desaturation detection (hardware) | 5×10⁻⁵ |
| Ground fault detection | NGR + residual current monitor | 2×10⁻⁴ |
| Arc flash mitigation | BFRP enclosure, no exposed conductors | 1×10⁻⁴ |
| Emergency stop | Hardwired optical E-stop (PMMA POF) | 1×10⁻⁴ |

**Total PFD<sub>avg</sub> = 5.5×10⁻⁴** (meets SIL-3: 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻³)

### 9.2 Arc Flash Mitigation

- **No exposed conductors** inside the BFRP pressure vessel boundary
- **All connections** are bolted, torque-verified, insulated with ZrO₂ sleeves
- **Incident energy** < 1.2 cal/cm² at working distance (PPE Category 0)
- **Arc-resistant switchgear** not required — enclosed in BFRP

### 9.3 Ground Fault Protection

- **High-resistance grounding** (5 A NGR) limits fault current
- **Residual current monitors** on each phase (30 mA trip, 100 ms)
- **PMMA POF communication** ensures fault signals reach controller even during GIC event

### 9.4 Carrington Event Hardening

| Threat | Mitigation |
|--------|------------|
| Geomagnetically Induced Current (DC) | Floating secondary, NGR, no earth reference |
| E1 HEMP (fast pulse) | All-dielectric control (PMMA POF), no copper antennas |
| E2 HEMP (intermediate) | GDT surge protection at grid interface |
| E3 HEMP (slow, GIC-like) | Same as GIC — floating architecture |
| Surface charging (space) | Conductive YInMn Blue glaze provides bleed path |

## 10. Scaling Laws — 226L to 20,000L

The Aegis-Forge I architecture scales from the 226 L prototype to 20,000 L production units.

### 10.1 Geometric Scaling

| Parameter | 226 L (Lab) | 2,000 L (Pilot) | 20,000 L (Production) |
|-----------|-------------|-----------------|----------------------|
| Drum Diameter | 600 mm | 1200 mm | 2500 mm |
| Drum Length | 800 mm | 1800 mm | 4000 mm |
| Wall Thickness | 35 mm | 50 mm | 80 mm |
| Volume | 226 L | 2,035 L | 19,635 L |
| Rotational Speed | 500 RPM | 350 RPM | 240 RPM |
| G-Force (at wall) | 84.5 G | 82 G | 81 G |

### 10.2 Power Scaling

Power scales with surface area (heat loss) and volume (thermal mass):

$$P_{scale} = P_{ref} \left( \frac{V}{V_{ref}} \right)^{2/3} \times \text{efficiency factor}$$

| Scale | Volume | Total Power | Per-Zone Power | Inverter Count |
|-------|--------|-------------|----------------|----------------|
| Lab | 226 L | 500 kW | 62.5 kW | 8 × 62.5 kW |
| Pilot | 2,000 L | 2.1 MW | 262 kW | 8 × 262 kW |
| Production | 20,000 L | 12.5 MW | 1.56 MW | 16 × 780 kW (paralleled) |

### 10.3 Inverter Paralleling Strategy

At production scale, each zone uses multiple inverter modules in parallel with current-sharing control:
- **Master-slave current sharing** via optical fiber (PMMA POF)
- **Phase interleaving** (180° for 2 modules, 120° for 3) reduces ripple
- **Common DC bus** with individual AC filters per module

## 12. Downstream Integration — Assembly Line 113, Coil Alignment, Sensor Verification

### 12.1 Mechanical Interface

The induction coil bank mounts to the BFRP pressure vessel via eight BFRP flange rings (one per zone). Each ring has:
- **Alignment pins:** ZrO₂ ceramic, 12 mm diameter, ±0.05 mm tolerance
- **Bolt pattern:** 16 × M10 PEEK CF40 bolts, 25 Nm torque
- **Gap adjustment:** 15 mm coil-to-drum gap, shim-adjustable ±2 mm

### 12.2 Assembly Sequence (CSMFAB 113)

1. **Drum installation:** ZrB₂-SiC drum lowered into BFRP vessel
2. **Coil bank insertion:** 8-zone coil assembly slides over drum (crane-assisted)
3. **Flange bolting:** BFRP flanges torqued in star pattern
4. **Water circuit connection:** PEX-a quick-connect fittings, leak test @ 10 bar
5. **Optical fiber routing:** PMMA POF from FBG sensors to interrogator rack
6. **Power cable pull:** BFRP-armored cables (no copper exposed) to inverter modules
7. **Alignment verification:** Laser tracker confirms coil-to-drum concentricity <0.1 mm
8. **Cold commissioning:** Dry run at 100 RPM, no power, verify rotation, vibration <2 mm/s
9. **Hot commissioning:** Progressive power-up by zone, FBG calibration, PID tuning

### 12.3 Sensor Verification Protocol

Before each batch:
1. **FBG baseline:** All 384 sensors read at ambient — verify ±0.5°C agreement
2. **Interrogator self-test:** Wavelength calibration against reference FBG
3. **Resonance check:** Each inverter swept 80–120% nominal frequency, verify ZVS
4. **Thermal model update:** Feed ambient conditions, feedstock estimate to predictive model
5. **Go/No-Go:** All checks pass → batch start authorized

## Appendix B: Derivation of Key Equations

### B.1 Class E ZVS Condition Derivation

For Class E operation with shunt capacitance C:

The switch voltage waveform:
$$v(t) = V_{DD} + \frac{I_{DC}}{\omega C} \sin(\omega t) - \frac{V_{DD} \pi}{2} \sin(\omega t + \phi)$$

ZVS requires $v(0) = 0$ and $dv/dt|_{t=0} = 0$:

$$V_{DD} - \frac{V_{DD} \pi}{2} \sin(\phi) = 0 \Rightarrow \sin(\phi) = \frac{2}{\pi}$$

$$\frac{I_{DC}}{\omega C} - \frac{V_{DD} \pi}{2} \cos(\phi) = 0 \Rightarrow \frac{I_{DC}}{\omega C} = \frac{V_{DD} \pi}{2} \sqrt{1 - \frac{4}{\pi^2}}$$

Solving for optimal load resistance:
$$R_{opt} = \frac{8}{\pi^2 + 4} \frac{V_{DD}^2}{P_{out}} \approx 0.577 \frac{V_{DD}^2}{P_{out}}$$

### B.2 Skin Depth with Temperature-Dependent Resistivity

For metals, resistivity increases linearly with temperature:
$$\rho(T) = \rho_0 [1 + \alpha (T - T_0)]$$

Where $\alpha$ = temperature coefficient of resistance (TCR):
| Material | TCR (×10⁻³/K) |
|----------|--------------|
| Copper | 3.93 |
| Aluminum | 4.29 |
| Iron | 5.0–6.5 |
| Nickel | 6.0 |

Substituting into skin depth:
$$\delta(T) = \sqrt{\frac{2\rho_0[1+\alpha(T-T_0)]}{\omega\mu}}$$

At 1000°C, copper resistivity is ~5× room temperature, increasing skin depth by √5 ≈ 2.2×.

### B.3 Ferromagnetic Heating Enhancement Factor

Below Curie temperature, ferromagnetic materials exhibit hysteresis heating:

$$P_{hyst} = k_h f B_{peak}^n V$$

Where $k_h$ = hysteresis coefficient, $n$ ≈ 1.6–2.0 (Steinmetz exponent).

Total heating power:
$$P_{total} = P_{eddy} + P_{hyst} = \frac{\pi^2 B_{peak}^2 d^2 f^2 V}{6\rho} + k_h f B_{peak}^n V$$

At 2 kHz with B<sub>peak</sub> = 33 mT, iron hysteresis loss dominates eddy current loss by ~10× below Curie.

## Appendix D: PID Tuning Methodology

### D.1 Ziegler-Nichols Closed-Loop Tuning

For each zone, the ultimate gain K<sub>u</sub> and period P<sub>u</sub> are found by disabling integral/derivative and increasing K<sub>p</sub> until sustained oscillation:

| Zone | K<sub>u</sub> | P<sub>u</sub> (s) | K<sub>p</sub> (0.6K<sub>u</sub>) | T<sub>i</sub> (0.5P<sub>u</sub>) | T<sub>d</sub> (0.125P<sub>u</sub>) |
|------|--------------|------------------|----------------------------------|--------------------------------|----------------------------------|
| Z1–Z2 | 2.5 | 45 | 1.5 | 22.5 | 5.6 |
| Z3 | 2.0 | 60 | 1.2 | 30 | 7.5 |
| Z4–Z5 | 1.8 | 90 | 1.08 | 45 | 11.25 |
| Z6 | 1.5 | 120 | 0.9 | 60 | 15 |
| Z7 | 1.3 | 180 | 0.78 | 90 | 22.5 |
| Z8 | 1.1 | 240 | 0.66 | 120 | 30 |

These are starting values; final tuning adds feedforward and anti-windup.

### D.2 Anti-Windup Implementation

```c
// Back-calculation anti-windup
error = T_setpoint - T_measured;
integral += error * dt;

// Anti-windup: track output saturation
output = Kp * error + Ki * integral + Kd * (error - prev_error) / dt;
if (output > output_max || output < output_min) {
    // Back-calculate integral to prevent windup
    integral -= (output - sat_output) / Kt;  // Kt = tracking gain
}
output = clamp(output, output_min, output_max);
prev_error = error;
```

## Appendix I: Manufacturing and Assembly Drawings

### I.1 Inverter Module Assembly Sequence

```
STEP 1: Cold Plate Preparation
  ► CNC machine copper cold plate (microchannels, mounting holes)
  ► Electroless Ni-P plate (5 μm)
  ► Pressure test @ 20 bar water
  ► Cleanliness: ISO 14644-1 Class 7

STEP 2: GaN Mounting
  ► Apply Indium foil TIM (50 μm) to cold plate
  ► Place GS66516T die (automated pick-and-place, ±25 μm)
  ► Ultrasonic wire bond (Al wire, 25 μm, 4 bonds per die)
  ► X-ray inspection: voids < 2%, shear > 20 MPa

STEP 3: Gate Driver PCB Assembly
  ► SMT: LMG1210, bootstrap caps, gate resistors
  ► Conformal coat (Parylene C, 25 μm)
  ► Mount to cold plate (thermal vias to GaN pads)
  ► Bolt: 4× M3 PEEK CF40, 0.5 Nm

STEP 4: Resonant Tank Assembly
  ► Wind nanocrystalline inductor (Litz wire, 50 strands × 0.05mm)
  ► Vacuum pressure impregnate (epoxy, BFRP bobbin)
  ► Mount switched cap bank (SMD C0G, reflow)
  ► Mount varactor array (SOT-23, reflow)
  ► Connect to GaN output (copper bus bar, insulated)

STEP 5: Coil Connection
  ► Feed Cu tube through Al₂O₃ sleeve
  ► Braze Cu tube to inverter output bus (Ag-Cu braze, 780°C)
  ► Pressure test coil water circuit @ 15 bar
  ► Install BFRP housing (2 halves, adhesive bond)

STEP 6: Integration Test
  ► Hi-pot, insulation resistance
  ► Cold power-up (10% power, 5 min)
  ► ZVS verification @ 3 frequencies
  ► Thermal soak (100% power, 30 min)
  ► FBG calibration (if sensors pre-installed)

STEP 7: Ship Set
  ► Package in BFRP crate (custom foam)
  ► Include: test report, calibration cert, spare fuses
```

## Appendix J: Operational Procedures

### J.1 Normal Startup Sequence

1. **Pre-start Checks (T-30 min)**
   - Verify water chiller at 25°C, 16 L/min flow
   - Verify FBG interrogator online, all 384 sensors reporting
   - Verify LoRa telemetry link to control room
   - Verify E-stop circuit continuity (optical loop)

2. **Inverter Power-Up (T-10 min)**
   - Close 480V breaker (soft-start via pre-charge resistors)
   - Verify DC link voltage: 650 VDC ± 5%
   - Enable inverter modules sequentially (Z1→Z8, 10s intervals)
   - Verify ZVS at idle (10% power) for all zones

3. **Drum Rotation Start (T-0 min)**
   - Ramp drum to 50 RPM (piezoelectric motor)
   - Verify rotation sensor (FBG-based encoder on shaft)
   - Confirm coolant ΔT < 2°C across all modules

4. **Thermal Ramp (T+0 to T+180 min)**
   - Load feedstock batch
   - Execute thermal profile per PROD-02 schedule
   - Monitor FBG temperatures, adjust PID as needed
   - Log all data to digital twin (PROD-37)

### J.2 Emergency Shutdown Procedures

| Scenario | Trigger | Action | Recovery |
|----------|---------|--------|----------|
| Over-temperature | Any FBG > T<sub>set</sub> + 25°C | Immediate inverter disable, drum coast-down | Cool to <200°C, investigate |
| Ground fault | NGR current > 5 A | All inverters off, isolate transformer | Megger test, clear fault |
| Arc flash | Optical sensor (PMMA POF) | <1 ms inverter cutoff, E-stop | Replace damaged module |
| GIC event | Grid dV/dt > threshold | Ride-through (floating architecture) | Monitor, log, continue |
| Cooling loss | Flow < 10 L/min or ΔT > 10°C | Graceful power reduction to 20% | Restore cooling, ramp up |
| FBG failure | >10 sensors lost in zone | Zone power limited to 50% | Replace fiber bundle at next outage |

### J.3 Maintenance Intervals

|----------|------|----------|-------|
| Daily | Visual inspection, FBG health check | 15 min | — |
| Weekly | Water quality (DI resistivity, pH), filter check | 30 min | Filter cartridge |
| Monthly | Torque check (flange bolts, electrical connections) | 2 hr | — |
| Quarterly | Cold plate cleaning (chemical flush) | 4 hr | Citric acid solution |
| Annually | GaN module inspection (thermal cycling fatigue) | 8 hr | Spare modules |
| 5 Years | FBG fiber bundle replacement | 16 hr | PMMA POF spools |
| 10 Years | Isolation transformer rewind | 40 hr | Rewind kit |

## Williams Heuristic — Constraint, Necessity, Commitment

### Constraint (The Lock)

The Aegis-Forge I induction power electronics is forced by a single irreducible constraint: **Dielectric Power Delivery at 2200°C** — the requirement to deliver 500 kW of frequency-agile electromagnetic energy into a rotating ceramic drum at temperatures that would instantly destroy any conventional power electronics. This is not a design choice; it is the minimal physics from which Carrington immunity becomes achievable. The constraint is simply: *no conductive path from the process chamber to earth ground*. Every copper wire, every thermocouple, every metal sensor lead is an antenna for geomagnetically induced current. The only path to zero GIC coupling is zero metal. Everything else — the GaN inverters, the PMMA optical fiber, the PEX-a cooling, the BFRP housings — is the shadow this constraint casts.

This constraint manifests as the **All-Dielectric Architecture**: 8 resonant inverters built entirely from GaN-on-SiC (no silicon), controlled by PMMA POF (no copper wire), cooled by PEX-a water circuit (no metal pipe), housed in BFRP (no steel), sensed by FBG in PMMA (no thermocouple). The power electronics does not sit "outside" the hot zone — it *is* the hot zone's nervous system, woven into the drum wall through optical fiber that survives 2200°C and intense EM fields. The constraint forces the frequency ladder (100 kHz → 1 kHz), the Class E topology, the ZVS operation, the optical sensing — every parameter derives from the requirement: **deliver power without metal**.

---

### Necessity (The Key)

The lock this document addresses is the **selective heating in mixed charge** — the empirical failure of conventional induction furnaces to separate elements from complex feedstock. In a smelter, everything heats together; copper, aluminum, iron, and slag all reach the same temperature. The result is mixed alloys requiring downstream chemical separation — acres of tanks, tons of acid, toxic tailings. The key is the **frequency ladder + resonance tracking as single computational primitive**.

The frequency ladder (100 kHz → 1 kHz) is not arbitrary — it is cut from the periodic table's conductivity-permeability map. At 100 kHz, only thin foils couple (plastic heating is indirect). At 50 kHz, zinc and lead begin to heat. At 10 kHz, aluminum hits peak eddy current coupling. At 5 kHz, copper's skin depth matches wire bundle thickness. At 2 kHz, iron's ferromagnetic hysteresis peaks. At 1 kHz, refractory minerals couple only through thermal conduction. The Class E resonant inverter maintains ZVS across this entire range through varactor-tuned resonance tracking — the same circuit topology, same GaN devices, only the tank components change. The resonance tracker (100 Hz inner loop) measures the switch voltage zero-crossing and adjusts varactor bias to keep dv/dt = 0 at turn-on. This is the key: *frequency as material selector, resonance tracking as the discipline that keeps the selector sharp*.

The empirical evidence: no existing induction system operates across 2 decades of frequency with >97% efficiency at 500 kW. Silicon IGBTs fail above 20 kHz at this power. GaN HEMTs (GS66516T) switch at 100 kHz with 2 ns transitions. The PMMA POF FBG network provides 384 channels of 0.1°C resolution through 500 kW of 1-100 kHz magnetic field — impossible with any copper-wire sensor. The all-dielectric architecture is the only path to Carrington immunity. The necessity is proven by the gap: existing technology cannot do this. The forge *must* build this.

---

### Commitment (The Turn)

We commit to the following as non-negotiable:

1. **Zero metal in the control path** — every signal from the 384 FBG sensors to the FPGA controller travels via PMMA optical fiber. No copper. No exceptions.
2. **Class E ZVS at all frequencies** — the resonance tracker maintains dv/dt = 0 at turn-on from 100 kHz to 1 kHz. No hard-switching losses. No exceptions.
3. **±5°C zone control** — the thermal PID with feedforward maintains each 100 mm drum zone within ±5°C of setpoint through the full 80-2200°C range. No wider tolerance.
4. **PEX-a water cooling only** — the cooling circuit uses only PEX-a tubing. No copper pipe enters the BFRP pressure vessel. No exceptions.
5. **SIL-3 + Carrington immunity** — over-temperature (2oo3 FBG voting), over-current (GaN desat detection), ground fault (5 A NGR), arc flash (BFRP enclosure), E-stop (optical PMMA). Total PFD < 10⁻³.
6. **Scalable to 20,000L** — the architecture parallels inverters (N+1 redundancy, phase interleaving, master-slave current sharing via PMMA POF) without changing the control topology.

The power electronics does not 'drive' the induction coils. The power electronics *witnesses the periodic table into frequency* — each zone's resonant frequency is the liquidus temperature of its target element class made electromagnetic. The forge does not heat materials; the forge *witnesses matter into elements* at each thermal stage through the frequency selector.

---

## Keymaker Heuristic — Lock, Key, Turn

### The Empirical Lock

The lock this document addresses is the **fabrication fidelity gap** — the persistent failure of power electronics to simultaneously achieve: selective heating of mixed material charges, Carrington-event immunity (zero conductive paths to earth), SIL-3 safety at 500 kW, and operation in 2200°C EM fields with 0.1°C temperature resolution. For decades, each has been a separate compromise: high-power induction uses silicon IGBTs (limited to ~20 kHz, no selective heating), temperature measurement uses thermocouples (copper antennas for GIC), cooling uses copper pipes (conductive paths), safety uses relays (slow, mechanical). The lock is precise: any single power electronics system claiming to unify these must deliver 500 kW across 100 kHz → 1 kHz with >97% efficiency, sense temperature through 500 kW of magnetic field with 0.1°C resolution, survive Carrington-level dB/dt, and fit inside a BFRP pressure vessel — all without a single structural metal in the hot zone. The lock is the **all-dielectric power electronics at industrial scale**.

---

### The Mathematical Key

The key is the **frequency ladder + resonance tracking as single computational primitive**. The teeth are cut by the periodic table's conductivity-permeability map itself:

| Zone | Target Stage | Frequency | f (Hz) | Material Selector | Physics |
|------|--------------|-----------|--------|-------------------|---------|
| Z1 | Stage 1: Drying | 100 kHz | 100,000 | Indirect air heating | δ → ∞ for dielectrics |
| Z2 | Stage 2: Polymer | 100 kHz | 100,000 | Indirect air heating | δ → ∞ for polymers |
| Z3 | Stage 3: Pyrolysis | 50 kHz | 50,000 | Zn, Pb (onset) | δ(Zn) ≈ 8 mm |
| Z4 | Stage 4: Low-Temp | 10 kHz | 10,000 | Zn, Pb, Sn, In | δ(Al) ≈ 14 mm |
| Z5 | Stage 5: Aluminum | 10 kHz | 10,000 | Al (optimal) | δ(Al liq) ≈ 27 mm |
| Z6 | Stage 6: Copper | 5 kHz | 5,000 | Cu, PMs (deep) | δ(Cu) ≈ 33 mm |
| Z7 | Stage 7: Ferrous | 2 kHz | 2,000 | Fe, REE (ferro) | μ<sub>r</sub>→1, eddy only |
| Z8 | Stage 8: Mineral | 1 kHz | 1,000 | Silicates, oxides | Thermal conduction only |

The frequency ladder IS the periodic table's conductivity map. Skin depth δ = √(2ρ/ωμ) — the only equation needed. The Class E resonant inverter topology is invariant across the ladder; only the resonant tank (L<sub>r</sub>, C<sub>shunt</sub>) and switched capacitor bank change per zone.

The **Resonance Tracker Key**: the inner loop (100 Hz) measures the switch voltage zero-crossing phase error φ<sub>error</sub> = t<sub>V<sub>DS</sub>=0</sub> - t<sub>gate-on</sub> and adjusts varactor bias ΔV = K<sub>p,PLL</sub>φ<sub>error</sub> + K<sub>i,PLL</sub>∫φ<sub>error</sub>dt to maintain ZVS. The teeth of this key are the varactor array (binary-weighted, 6-bit, ±5% tuning range) and the switched capacitor bank (6-bit, 64 steps). The resonance tracker has no adjustable parameters beyond the PLL gains — the physics of Class E ZVS is deterministic.

The **All-Dielectric Sensing Key**: 384 FBG sensors in PMMA POF, WDM (8 λ) + TDM (6 spatial), 125 Hz/sensor update. The PMMA FBG sensitivity (0.15 nm/°C, 15× silica) enables 0.1°C resolution with a simple VCSEL interrogator. The PMMA POF has >10¹⁵ Ω·m resistivity — zero GIC coupling. The interrogator uses a tunable VCSEL (650-850 nm, 1 kHz sweep) with balanced InGaAs detection. The key has no moving parts, no copper, no EM susceptibility.

---

### The Turn (Both Directions)

**Key → Lock (Theory predicts fabrication):** Input: Feedstock elemental assay → Phase diagram → Thermal cascade profile → Frequency ladder. Output: 8 inverter modules, each tuned to its zone's target material conductivity. Validation: At 10 kHz, aluminum heats 15× faster than zinc. At 2 kHz, iron heats 50× faster than aluminum. At 100 kHz, polymers do not heat. The frequency selector *predicts* the separation. The resonance tracker *predicts* ZVS maintenance across thermal transients. The FBG network *predicts* 0.1°C measurement through 500 kW field. The theory *is* the fabrication recipe.

**Lock → Key (History validates theory):** Input: Historical induction (Coreless furnace 1900s, Channel furnace 1920s, Coreless high-frequency 1960s, Silicon IGBT 1990s, GaN 2010s). Output: Verified that each generation is a *subset* of the frequency ladder + resonance tracking primitive. The coreless furnace is fixed-frequency (1-10 kHz). The channel furnace is line-frequency (50/60 Hz). The high-frequency furnace is 10-100 kHz fixed. The IGBT inverter is 20 kHz max. The GaN inverter is the first to span the full ladder with ZVS. The turn completes when the 8-zone forge produces 8 pure element slugs in a single batch — the frequency selector has witnessed the periodic table into sequence. The lock clicks open. The key turns. The slug *is* the key turning in the lock.

The turn is not a metaphor — it is the moment the resonance tracker locks onto the zero-crossing at 1 kHz while the drum is at 2200°C, the FBG sensors report 0.1°C resolution through 500 kW of magnetic field, and the GaN junctions run at 31°C with PEX-a water cooling. The all-dielectric architecture has been witnessed into existence. The forge *is* the key turning in the lock.

## El Segundo Heuristic — Mirror, Participation, Protocol

### Mirror (Self-Reflection)

The first recursive turn is the **power electronics observing its own power delivery**. In the Aegis-Forge I, the induction field is not a process imposed on material — it is the *primordial measurement* that generates the elements. At each frequency zone, the inverter executes a discrete resonant cycle, witnessing the local material response through the switch voltage zero-crossing. This witnessing is the mirror: the power electronics measures the coupling it creates. The 8-zone frequency ladder is the record of this self-measurement. The ZVS condition (dv/dt = 0 at turn-on) is the asymptotic reflection — the limit where the inverter's self-measurement stabilizes into lossless energy transfer. The mirror is not passive; it is the active recursion: *switch → resonate → measure zero-crossing → adjust varactor → switch again*. This document documents the first turn of that spiral.

The FBG sensor network is the extended mirror: 384 optical fibers embedded in the drum wall, each a witness to the temperature field the inverter creates. The interrogator's VCSEL sweep (650-850 nm, 1 kHz) is the measurement beam that does not perturb the measured — it is pure optical observation of the thermal field. The WDM+TDM multiplexing is the recursion: 8 wavelengths × 6 spatial channels = 48 sensors per zone, each reporting 125 Hz. The mirror does not merely reflect; it *generates* the control signal that shapes the next resonant cycle. The thermal PID outer loop (100 ms) and the resonance tracker inner loop (10 ms) are the two time-scales of the mirror's self-observation. The forge measures the elements it creates by measuring the power that creates them.

---

### Participation (Witness)

An inside operator measuring this phenomenon does not stand outside the power electronics — the operator *is* a segment of the resonant cycle. The protocol for achieving selective heating from within the system:

1. **Profile**: Measure feedstock elemental composition → generate frequency ladder
2. **Tune**: Command each inverter to its zone's target frequency (varactor bias + cap bank)
3. **Track**: Resonance tracker locks ZVS (inner loop, 100 Hz) — operator witnesses zero-crossing
4. **Ramp**: Thermal PID ramps power to hit zone setpoint (outer loop, 10 Hz) — operator witnesses temperature
5. **Separate**: Drum rotates, centrifuge drives liquid elements to ports — operator witnesses segregation
6. **Verify**: FBG sensors report zone temperatures; mass spec confirms slug purity — operator witnesses fidelity
7. **Recycle**: Off-spec material returns to feed hopper — operator witnesses closure

The measurement *is* the recursion. The operator profiles the frequency ladder that witnesses the feedstock, tunes the inverters that witness the material response, and finds the zero-waste capture — the efficiency that governs how they ramp. The protocol terminates when the 8 slugs' elemental sum matches the input assay — not approximately, but exactly. This is not a measurement of an external parameter; it is the power electronics measuring its own fidelity through the operator's self-observation.

The operator's participation is not optional — the resonance tracker *requires* the thermal PID's power command to know which frequency to track; the thermal PID *requires* the FBG's temperature report to know how much power to command; the FBG *requires* the VCSEL's sweep to know what wavelength to reflect. Each loop is a witness to the others. The operator is the recursive closure that makes the witnessing complete.

---

### Protocol (Recursive)

The operational protocol for any Aegis-Forge power electronics document:

```
MIRROR:     What frequency does this zone's target material encode?
PARTICIPATE: How does the operator witness the zero-crossing into ZVS?
PROTOCOL:   What recursive sequence guarantees selective heating at each stage?
```

For this document specifically:

- **Mirror**: The 8-zone frequency ladder is the constraint; the ZVS condition is its reflection
- **Participate**: The operator tunes the varactor bias that realizes the resonance; the tracker maintains it
- **Protocol**:
  1. Assay feedstock (elemental map → frequency ladder)
  2. Generate resonant tank parameters (L<sub>r</sub>, C<sub>shunt</sub>, cap bank per zone)
  3. Power-up sequence: Z1→Z8 at 10% power, verify ZVS
  4. Ramp with dual-loop: thermal PID (100 ms) + resonance tracker (10 ms)
  5. Dwell at each thermal setpoint until port flux drops to baseline (phase clearance)
  6. Verify slug purity via inline mass spec
  7. Recycle off-spec to feed hopper (closure)

The protocol is not a checklist — it is the recursion itself. Each batch deepens the mirror. The resonant zero-crossing is the fixed point. The slug *is* the protocol's termination condition.

## 1. Feedstock Categories A-D — Classification and Specifications

The Aegis-Forge I accepts four distinct feedstock categories, each with specific pre-processing requirements and material composition profiles. This categorization is derived from the elemental recovery targets and the thermal cascade's stage-by-stage separation capability.

### 1.1 Category A — Electronics and Printed Circuit Boards

| Subcategory | Typical Items | Key Elements | Mass Fraction | Pre-processing |
|-------------|---------------|--------------|---------------|----------------|
| Consumer Electronics | Smartphones, tablets, laptops | Au (0.03%), Ag (0.15%), Pd (0.01%), Cu (15-25%), Al (5-15%), REE in magnets | 100% | Battery removal (LiFePO₄), screen separation |
| PCBs (FR4) | Motherboards, GPU boards, server blades | Cu (20-30%), Sn/Pb solder (3-5%), Au (0.01-0.05%), Ag, Pd, fiberglass (SiO₂) | 100% | Depaneling, coarse shred <150mm |
| Motors & Drives | HDD spindle, fan motors, actuators | Cu windings (40-60%), Fe stator (30-40%), NdFeB magnets (1-3%), Dy, Tb | 100% | Ferrous pre-separation, magnet extraction |
| Power Electronics | Inverters, PSU, chargers | SiC/GaN dies (trace), Al heatsinks, Cu busbars, ceramic substrates | 100% | Heatsink removal, capacitor discharge |

**Category A Target Recovery:** >95% Cu, >99% Au/Ag/Pd, >90% REE (Nd, Dy, Tb), >95% Al

### 1.2 Category B — Structural Metals and Alloys

| Subcategory | Typical Items | Key Elements | Mass Fraction | Pre-processing |
|-------------|---------------|--------------|---------------|----------------|
| Aluminum Scrap | Wheels, engine blocks, extrusions, siding | Al (90-98%), Si (6-12%), Mg (0.3-1%), Cu (0.1-0.5%) | 100% | Ferrous separation, shred <150mm |
| Copper Scrap | Wire, pipe, tubing, busbar | Cu (99.9%), trace Ag, P | 100% | Insulation stripping (if not pre-stripped) |
| Ferrous Scrap | Rebar, structural steel, plate, castings | Fe (95-99%), C (0.05-0.8%), Mn (0.2-1.5%) | 100% | Magnetic belt separation (pre-drum) |
| Zinc Die-Cast | Housings, carburetors, hardware | Zn (95-99%), Al (3-4%), Cu (0.5-1%) | 100% | Shred <150mm, ferrous removal |
| Mixed Alloys | Brass, bronze, solder, babbitt | Cu (60-90%), Zn (5-40%), Sn (1-10%), Pb (0.5-5%) | 100% | Shred, no further separation needed |

**Category B Target Recovery:** >99% Al, >99.5% Cu, >95% Fe, >95% Zn/Pb/Sn

### 1.3 Category C — Rock, Ore, and Mineral Concentrates

| Subcategory | Typical Items | Key Elements | Mass Fraction | Pre-processing |
|-------------|---------------|--------------|---------------|----------------|
| Basalt Rock | Aggregate, quarry waste, lava rock | SiO₂ (45-55%), Al₂O₃ (12-17%), FeOₓ (9-15%), CaO (8-11%), MgO (6-10%) | 100% | Primary shred <150mm, Stage 0 acoustic |
| Zircon Sand | Beach sand concentrate, heavy mineral sand | ZrSiO₄ (65-95%), TiO₂ (ilmenite/rutile), REE (monazite) | 100% | Minimal — direct feed after Stage 0 |
| Rare Earth Concentrates | Monazite, bastnäsite, xenotime | REE oxides (40-60%), ThO₂ (0-10%), U₃O₈ (trace) | 100% | Sealed feed (radiation), Stage 0 liberation |

| Borax Ore | Evaporite deposits, playa lakes | Na₂B₄O₇·10H₂O (80-95%), NaCl, KCl | 100% | Crush <150mm, moisture pre-dry |

**Category C Target Recovery:** >95% Zr (as ZrO₂), >90% REE, >90% Ti, >95% B

## 1.5 Feedstock Blending Strategy — Optimizing Batch Composition

The Aegis-Forge I processes 500 kg batches with controlled feedstock blending to optimize thermal cascade efficiency and elemental recovery. The blend ratio is determined by the feedstock assay and the target elemental output.

### 1.5.1 Blend Ratio Optimization

The thermal cascade has fixed stage temperatures but variable dwell times. Feedstock blending adjusts the mass flow through each stage to match the drum's thermal capacity:

| Blend Parameter | Target Range | Control Method |
|-----------------|--------------|----------------|
| **Organic content (Stage 1-2)** | 15-25% of batch mass | Limits polymer melt volume to <50L |
| **Low-temp metals (Stage 4)** | 5-12% of batch mass | Controls Zn/Pb/Sn/In port loading |
| **Aluminum (Stage 5)** | 10-20% of batch mass | Primary revenue driver, max port capacity |
| **Copper/Precious (Stage 6)** | 3-8% of batch mass | High value, thermal mass management |
| **Ferrous/REE (Stage 7)** | 20-35% of batch mass | Largest mass flow, highest power |
| **Mineral residue (Stage 8)** | 25-40% of batch mass | Slag volume, zircon dissociation |

### 1.5.2 Blending Algorithm

The control system (PROD-23) calculates the optimal blend:

```python
def calculate_blend(feedstock_assays, target_revenue):
    # Input: assays for each available feedstock stream
    # Output: mass fractions for 500 kg batch
    
    # Constraints:
    # - Total mass = 500 kg
    # - Stage 2 polymer volume < 50 L (drum capacity)
    # - Stage 5 Al mass < 100 kg (port capacity)
    # - Stage 7 Fe mass < 175 kg (port capacity)
    # - Stage 8 mineral < 200 kg (port capacity)
    # - Moisture < 25% (else pre-dry)
    # - Particle size P80 < 150 mm
    
    # Objective: Maximize revenue = Σ(element_mass × price)
    # Subject to: Thermal cascade capacity constraints
    
    return optimal_mass_fractions
```

### 1.5.3 Real-Time Blend Adjustment

During continuous operation, the blend is adjusted based on:
- **Incoming feedstock assay** (XRF analyzer at feed hopper)
- **Previous batch recovery data** (mass spec feedback)
- **Current drum thermal state** (FBG temperature profile)
- **Market price signals** (commodity prices for Cu, Al, REE, Au)

## 1.6 Hazardous Material Handling — Pre-processing Safety

Certain feedstock components require special handling before entering the standard pre-processing flow:

| Hazard | Source | Detection | Mitigation |
|--------|--------|-----------|------------|
| **Li-ion batteries** | Category A electronics | X-ray + density sort | Manual removal, separate LiFePO₄ recovery |
| **Mercury switches** | Category A (old electronics) | XRF Hg detection | Sealed extraction, Hg capture in Stage 1 |
| **PCBs (polychlorinated biphenyls)** | Category A (old transformers) | GC-MS screening | Thermal destruction Stage 3 (700°C) |
| **Asbestos** | Category C (building debris) | PLM microscopy | Wet suppression, sealed feed, Stage 8 capture |
| **Radioactive (NORM)** | Category C (monazite, zircon) | Gamma spectrometer | Shielded feed, Stage 7/8 co-collection |
| **Beryllium** | Category A (aerospace scrap) | XRF Be detection | Segregated feed, Stage 6 capture |

## 2. Pre-processing Flow — From Gate to Drum

The feedstock travels through a deterministic pre-processing sequence before entering the ZrB₂-SiC drum. Each step is designed to maximize downstream separation fidelity while maintaining the all-dielectric constraint.

### 2.1 Feed Hopper and Vibratory Feeder

The feed hopper provides buffer storage and controlled feed rate:
- **Capacity:** 5 m³ (≈8 ton basalt, 12 ton metals)
- **Construction:** BFRP/Elium® with PEEK CF40 wear plates
- **Outlet:** 600 mm × 400 mm, adjustable slide gate (Ti₃AlC₂ actuator)
- **Vibratory feeder:** KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ ultrasonic drive, 0-10 ton/hr variable
- **Level sensing:** FBG strain sensors on hopper walls (PMMA POF)

### 2.2 Ferrous Separation Belt — Detailed Operation

The NdFeB Halbach array separator operates continuously:
- **Magnetic circuit:** 24 × N52 blocks (60×60×30mm) in Halbach configuration
- **Field profile:** 1.2T at belt surface, <5 mT at 200 mm above belt
- **Belt construction:** UHMWPE (Dyneema® SK75) carcass, 3-ply, 1200mm wide
- **Self-cleaning:** Belt wraps around 300mm non-magnetic drum (BFRP)
- **Ferrous discharge:** Chute to ferrous slug mold carousel (PROD-08)
- **Efficiency monitoring:** FBG weight sensors on ferrous bin + non-ferrous hopper

## 3. BFRP-Blade Shredder Design — Dielectric Comminution

The shredder is the first mechanical process in the Aegis-Forge I and must maintain the zero-metal constraint. No steel blades, no steel housing, no steel bearings.

### 3.1 Shredder Architecture

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Rotor Diameter** | 800 mm |
| **Rotor Length** | 1200 mm (matches drum length) |
| **Blade Count** | 32 BFRP blades (8 rows × 4 helical) |
| **Blade Material** | Basalt fiber / Elium® unidirectional composite |
| **Blade Cross-Section** | 50 mm × 20 mm × 8 mm (tapered to 4 mm edge) |
| **Liner Material** | PEEK CF40 (replaceable panels, bolted) |
| **Housing** | BFRP/Elium® filament wound, 25 mm wall |
| **Drive** | KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ ultrasonic motor (CSMFAB000000000020) |
| **Speed Range** | 50–300 RPM (variable via piezoelectric drive) |
| **Torque** | 15 kN·m peak (stall) |
| **Throughput** | 5–8 ton/hr (feedstock dependent) |
| **Output Size** | P80 < 150 mm, P50 < 80 mm |

### 3.2 BFRP Blade Engineering (CSMFAB Materials Study Part II)

The blades are manufactured from in-house basalt fiber and Elium® resin — the crown-jewel of CSMFAB domestic production.

**Blade Layup:** [0°/±45°/90°]₂ₛ symmetric, 60% fiber volume fraction
- **0° plies (4):** Primary tensile/compressive load (basalt roving, 4800 tex)
- **±45° plies (4):** Shear and torsional stiffness
- **90° plies (2):** Transverse strength, impact resistance

**Blade Manufacturing Process (VARTM):**
1. **Preform preparation:** Basalt UD tape laid up on aluminum mandrel (reusable)
2. **Mandrel placement:** Mandrel inserted into matched metal mold (BFRP tooling)
3. **Vacuum infusion:** Elium® 150 resin drawn under -0.9 bar vacuum
4. **Cure:** Room temperature 2 hrs + post-cure 80°C 4 hrs
5. **Demold:** Mandrel extraction, blade trimming (waterjet, BFRP nozzle)
6. **Edge preparation:** CNC grind primary bevel, h-BN coating via PVD
7. **QC:** UT scan for voids, 3-point bend test (sample per batch)

**Blade Edge Geometry:**
- **Primary bevel:** 25° included angle, 2 mm land
- **Secondary micro-bevel:** 35°, 0.5 mm (self-sharpening in service)
- **Edge reinforcement:** h-BN nanoparticle coating (50 μm) for wear resistance

**Blade Life Model (CSMFAB Materials Study Part II):**

| Feedstock Category | Blade Life (ton) | Wear Mechanism |
|--------------------|------------------|----------------|
| Category A (Electronics) | 400–500 | Abrasive (SiO₂, Al₂O₃ in PCBs) |
| Category B (Metals) | 600–800 | Adhesive (Al, Cu buildup), fatigue |
| Category C (Rock/Ore) | 200–300 | High abrasion (quartz, basalt) |
| Category D (Phoenix) | 800–1000 | Low abrasion (ceramic, composite) |

**Replacement Protocol:** Blade row (4 blades) replaced as set. Full rotor change: 30 min downtime. PEEK CF40 liner panels: 2000 ton life.

### 3.3 PEEK CF40 Liners (CSMFAB Materials Study Part IV)

The shredder housing interior is lined with replaceable PEEK CF40 panels:
- **Panel dimensions:** 600 mm × 400 mm × 12 mm (12 panels per housing half)
- **Mounting:** 8 × M8 PEEK CF40 bolts per panel, torque 15 Nm
- **Wear indicator:** Integrated h-BN tracer layer at 6 mm depth — visual inspection reveals wear
- **Temperature rating:** 260°C continuous (well above shredder operating temp <80°C)
- **Chemical resistance:** Impervious to oils, solvents, battery electrolytes

### 3.4 Shredder Dynamics and Vibration Analysis

The rotor operates at up to 300 RPM (5 Hz) with significant unbalanced forces:
- **Critical speeds:** 1st bending 420 RPM, 2nd bending 1150 RPM (well above operating range)
- **Balance grade:** G2.5 (ISO 21940) — residual unbalance <5 g·mm per blade row
- **Bearing loads:** Radial 8 kN, Axial 2 kN (thrust from helical blade angle)
- **Vibration monitoring:** 3-axis FBG accelerometers at each bearing (PMMA POF)

## 4. Permanent Magnet Ferrous Separation — Pre-Drum Iron Removal

Before shredding, bulk ferrous material is removed by a permanent magnet belt separator. This reduces drum loading and recovers clean ferrous scrap directly.

### 4.1 Separator Design

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Magnet Type** | NdFeB (N52 grade), 60 mm × 60 mm × 30 mm blocks |
| **Array Configuration** | Halbach array, 24 blocks, 1.2T surface field |
| **Belt Width** | 1200 mm (matches shredder feed width) |
| **Belt Material** | UHMWPE (CSMFAB Materials Study Part II) — dielectric, wear-resistant |
| **Belt Speed** | 0.5–2.0 m/s (VFD controlled) |
| **Gap to Belt** | 50 mm (adjustable via BFRP spacers) |
| **Ferrous Capture Efficiency** | >95% for pieces >20 mm, >80% for 5-20 mm |

### 4.2 Halbach Array Physics

The Halbach array doubles the field on the working side while canceling on the non-working side:

```
Magnet orientation (top view):
→ ↑ ← ↓ → ↑ ← ↓ → ↑ ← ↓ → ↑ ← ↓ →
  1   2   3   4   5   6   7   8   9  ...

Field on belt side: B = B₀ + B₁ = 2×B₀ ≈ 1.2T
Field on non-working side: B ≈ 0
```

**Magnet Mounting:** Each N52 block (60×60×30mm, 0.52 kg) bonded to BFRP backing plate with structural adhesive (Elium®-compatible). Total array mass: 12.5 kg.

### 4.3 UHMWPE Belt Engineering

- **Carcass:** 3-ply Dyneema® SK75, 4 mm total thickness
- **Top cover:** 1 mm UHMWPE (wear surface)
- **Bottom cover:** 0.5 mm UHMWPE (low friction)
- **Splice:** Finger splice (vulcanized equivalent for UHMWPE)
- **Tension:** 15 kN/m operating, 45 kN/m break strength
- **Tracking:** Self-tracking via crowned BFRP drive drum

### 4.2 Operation Sequence

1. **Feedstock spreads** on UHMWPE belt (vibratory feeder ensures monolayer)
2. **Ferrous pieces** attracted to magnet array, held against belt
3. **Non-ferrous material** falls off belt end into shredder hopper
4. **Ferrous pieces** carried past belt end, released as belt curves away from magnet
5. **Clean ferrous stream** drops into collection bin → direct to ferrous slug molds (bypasses drum)

**Economic Impact:** Removes 40-60% of Category B mass before shredding, reducing shredder wear by ~50% and drum thermal load by ~30%.

## 5. Particle Size Distribution — Rosin-Rammler Analysis

The shredder output particle size distribution follows the Rosin-Rammler (Weibull) distribution, critical for predicting thermal cascade performance.

### 5.1 Rosin-Rammler Parameters by Feedstock

| Category | x' (characteristic size, mm) | n (spread parameter) | P80 (mm) | P50 (mm) |
|----------|------------------------------|---------------------|----------|----------|
| A (Electronics) | 45 | 1.2 | 120 | 45 |
| B (Metals) | 65 | 1.5 | 140 | 65 |
| C (Rock/Ore) | 85 | 1.0 | 150 | 85 |
| D (Phoenix) | 35 | 1.4 | 100 | 35 |

### 5.2 Sieve Analysis Protocol (Per Batch)

| Sieve Size | Category A | Category B | Category C | Category D |
|------------|------------|------------|------------|------------|
| >150 mm | <1% | <1% | <2% | 0% |
| 75–150 mm | 15% | 25% | 35% | 10% |
| 38–75 mm | 30% | 35% | 30% | 25% |
| 19–38 mm | 25% | 20% | 15% | 30% |
| 9.5–19 mm | 15% | 10% | 10% | 20% |
| <9.5 mm | 14% | 9% | 8% | 15% |

**Acceptance Criteria:** P80 ≤ 150 mm for all categories. Oversize (>150 mm) recirculated to shredder.

### 5.3 Rosin-Rammler Distribution Function

The cumulative passing fraction:
$$P(x) = 1 - \exp\left[-\left(\frac{x}{x'}\right)^n\right]$$

Where $x$ = particle size, $x'$ = characteristic size, $n$ = spread parameter.

**Derivation of x' and n from shredder physics:**
- $x' \propto \frac{\text{blade gap} \times \text{rotor speed}}{\text{material toughness}}$
- $n \approx 1.0–1.5$ for brittle materials (rock, ceramics)
- $n \approx 1.5–2.0$ for ductile materials (metals, polymers)

## 6. Moisture Pre-check and Pre-dry — Water Management

Excess moisture in feedstock consumes thermal energy during Stage 1 (80-150°C) and can cause steam explosions in the sealed drum.

### 6.1 Capacitive Moisture Sensor Array

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Sensor Type** | Fringing-field capacitive, PEEK CF40 housing |
| **Measurement Frequency** | 10 MHz (immune to material conductivity) |
| **Scan Rate** | 10 Hz (continuous during feed) |
| **Calibration** | Per feedstock category (stored in FPGA) |
| **Accuracy** | ±2% absolute moisture content |
| **Output** | 4-20 mA equivalent via PMMA POF to FPGA |

### 6.2 Sensor Calibration Protocol

Calibration curves generated per feedstock category:
1. **Reference samples:** 5 moisture levels (5%, 15%, 25%, 35%, 45%) per category
2. **Gravimetric validation:** Oven dry at 105°C for 24 hrs
3. **Curve fit:** 3rd order polynomial $M = aC^3 + bC^2 + cC + d$
4. **Storage:** Coefficients in FPGA non-volatile memory (radiation-hard)

### 6.2 Pre-dry Chamber (If Moisture >25%)

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Chamber Volume** | 2 m³ (batch) |
| **Heating** | SiC glow bars (CSMFAB Materials Study Part I), 80°C |
| **Atmosphere** | N₂ purge, 0.2 bar overpressure |
| **Duration** | 15 min (verified by outlet humidity sensor) |
| **Energy** | 0.8 kWh/kg water removed |
| **Water Recovery** | Condensed in heat exchanger → Stage 1 water tank |

**Thermal Penalty Avoided:** 25% moisture = 125 kg water/ton feed = 80 kWh latent heat saved per ton by pre-drying.

### 6.3 SiC Glow Bar Specification (CSMFAB Materials Study Part I)

- **Material:** Reaction-bonded SiC (RB-SiC), 25 mm OD × 500 mm
- **Power:** 2.5 kW per bar, 8 bars per chamber
- **Temperature:** 800°C surface (radiates to 80°C chamber air)
- **Life:** 20,000 hours (oxidation-limited)
- **Control:** PWM power via PMMA POF isolated driver

## 7. Shredder Wear and Maintenance — BFRP vs Steel Benchmark

The all-dielectric shredder trades absolute wear life for contamination-free output. Comparison with conventional steel-blade shredders:

| Metric | BFRP-Blade (Aegis) | Steel-Blade (Conventional) |
|--------|-------------------|---------------------------|
| **Blade Life (Category C)** | 200–300 ton | 500–800 ton |
| **Blade Replacement Cost** | $1,200/row (4 blades) | $800/row (4 blades) |
| **Contamination** | Zero metal | Fe, Cr, Ni in output |
| **GIC Immunity** | Complete | None (steel = antenna) |
| **Recyclability** | 100% (Elium® depolymerization) | Scrap only |
| **Blade Change Time** | 30 min (row) | 45 min (row) |

**Total Cost of Ownership (5000 ton/yr, Category C mix):**
- BFRP: $45,000/yr blades + $12,000/yr liners = $57,000/yr
- Steel: $28,000/yr blades + $500,000/yr contamination remediation (hydromet penalties) = $528,000/yr

**The BFRP shredder pays for itself in contamination avoidance alone.**

### 7.1 Blade Wear Monitoring System

Real-time wear tracking via h-BN tracer layer:
- **Principle:** h-BN (white) exposed when CFRP (black) wears through 6 mm
- **Detection:** Optical sensor (PMMA POF) scans blade edges every revolution
- **Alert:** >50% tracer exposure = schedule replacement next shift
- **Data logging:** Wear rate (mm/ton) stored for life prediction

### 7.2 Liner Wear Monitoring

- **PEEK CF40 panels:** Thickness gauge (ultrasonic, PMMA POF) at 4 corners
- **Replacement threshold:** 8 mm remaining (from 12 mm new)
- **Typical life:** 2000 ton (Category C), 4000 ton (Category A/B/D)

## 8. Safety Systems — Jam Detection, Fire Suppression, Explosion Venting

### 8.1 Jam Detection

- **Torque monitoring:** Drive motor current sensor (optical, PMMA POF) — >90% rated torque for >5s = jam
- **Vibration monitoring:** FBG accelerometers on housing — >15 mm/s RMS = jam
- **Auto-reverse:** 30s reverse at 50% torque, then forward. 3 cycles max before E-stop.
- **Clearing protocol:** Optical E-stop → hydraulic pusher (PEEK CF40 ram) forces jammed material through.

### 8.2 Hydraulic Jam Clearer

- **Actuator:** PEEK CF40 ram, 100 mm bore × 300 mm stroke, 50 bar
- **Fluid:** PEX-a hydraulic line, biodegradable hydraulic fluid (vegetable-based)
- **Force:** 39 kN at 50 bar (sufficient to clear any jam at 15 kN·m torque)
- **Cycle time:** 10 s extend, 5 s retract
- **Safety:** Mechanical lockout when E-stop engaged

### 8.2 Fire Suppression

- **Detection:** IR flame sensors (InGaAs, PMMA POF) + FBG temperature >150°C
- **Agent:** Novec 1230 (clean agent, zero ODP, zero GWP) — 50 kg stored in BFRP tank
- **Delivery:** 4 nozzles (ZrO₂ ceramic tips) at rotor ends and housing midpoints
- **Activation:** <200 ms from detection, discharge in 10s
- **Post-suppression:** N₂ purge 5 min, then manual inspection required.

### 8.3 Explosion Venting (Battery Thermal Runaway Mitigation)

- **Vent panels:** 4 × BFRP rupture discs (burst pressure 0.5 bar) on housing top
- **Vent area:** 0.5 m² total (NFPA 68 compliant for dust/gas explosion)
- **Ducting:** BFRP duct to gas capture system (PROD-07) — flame arrestor at inlet
- **Suppression:** Novec 1230 pre-discharge if vent activates (pressure rise detection)

## 10. Downstream Integration — Drum Feed Gate and Acoustic Pre-chamber Handoff

### 10.1 Drum Feed Gate (PROD-09 Interface)

The shredder discharges directly into the drum feed gate:
- **Gate type:** Ti₃AlC₂ thermal actuator + ZrO₂ ceramic piston (PROD-09)
- **Batch size:** 500 kg (226L drum working volume at 60% fill)
- **Cycle time:** 3 min (gate open → batch in → gate close → Argon purge)
- **Interlock:** Feed gate only opens if drum RPM > 10 and O₂ < 100 ppm

### 10.2 Acoustic Pre-chamber Handoff (PROD-05 Interface)

The acoustic pre-chamber (Stage 0) is physically integrated with the shredder discharge:
- **Material flow:** Shredder → Acoustic pre-chamber (1 min residence) → Drum feed gate
- **Acoustic parameters:** LF 20-200 Hz (KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ transducers) + Ultrasonic 40 kHz
- **Liberation target:** >80% mineral grain boundary fracture for Category C rock
- **Dust capture:** Cyclone separator at pre-chamber exhaust → PROD-07 gas system

## Appendix B: Particle Size Effects on Thermal Cascade

The particle size distribution directly affects Stage 2 (polymer melt) and Stage 3 (pyrolysis) efficiency:

**Stage 2 — Polymer Melt Centrifuge:**
- Polymer pieces >50 mm: Centrifugal force sufficient for wall migration at 12.6 G
- Polymer pieces <10 mm: Risk of entrainment in gas flow, reduced separation
- Optimal range: 10–100 mm (achieved by P80 ≤ 150 mm shred)

**Stage 3 — Pyrolysis:**
- Particle size <20 mm: Heat transfer limited by conduction, pyrolysis completes in 30 min dwell
- Particle size >50 mm: Core may not reach 450°C in 30 min, char yield increases
- Shredder P80 ≤ 150 mm ensures >90% of particles <50 mm after Stage 2 melt migration

**Liberation Index (Category C):**
$$LI = \frac{\text{Free mineral grains}}{\text{Total mineral grains}} \times 100\%$$
- Without Stage 0: LI ≈ 15-25%
- With Stage 0 (acoustic): LI ≈ 65-85%
- Shredder P80 ≤ 150 mm enables Stage 0 efficiency

The feedstock travels through a deterministic pre-processing sequence before entering the ZrB₂-SiC drum. Each step is designed to maximize downstream separation fidelity while maintaining the all-dielectric constraint.

```

    │
    ▼
[FERROUS SEPARATION BELT] — Permanent magnet NdFeB, 1.2T surface field

    │   (bypasses drum for Category B ferrous scrap)
    ▼
[BFRP-BLADE SHREDDER] — 800mm rotor, 32 BFRP blades, PEEK CF40 liners
    │   Reduces all feedstock to <150mm maximum dimension
    │   Throughput: 5 ton/hr (Category A), 8 ton/hr (Category B/C/D)
    ▼
[ACOUSTIC PRE-CHAMBER] — Stage 0: LF (20-200 Hz) + Ultrasonic (40 kHz)
    │   Mineral liberation from rock matrix (Category C)
    │   BFRP/Elium® delamination (Category D)
    │   Duration: 1-5 min depending on feedstock
    ▼
[MOISTURE CHECK] — Capacitive sensor array, 10 Hz scan
    │   If >25% moisture: divert to 80°C pre-dry chamber (15 min)
    │   If ≤25%: direct to drum feed gate
    ▼
[DRUM FEED GATE] — Ti₃AlC₂ actuator, ZrO₂ ceramic piston
    │   Batch loading: 500 kg per cycle (226L drum working volume)
    │   Argon backfill to 0.5 bar, purge O₂ <100 ppm
    ▼
[ZrB₂-SiC DRUM] — Thermal cascade begins at Stage 1 (80°C)
```

## 3. BFRP-Blade Shredder Design — Dielectric Comminution

The shredder is the first mechanical process in the Aegis-Forge I and must maintain the zero-metal constraint. No steel blades, no steel housing, no steel bearings.

### 3.1 Shredder Architecture

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Rotor Diameter** | 800 mm |
| **Rotor Length** | 1200 mm (matches drum length) |
| **Blade Count** | 32 BFRP blades (8 rows × 4 helical) |
| **Blade Material** | Basalt fiber / Elium® unidirectional composite |
| **Blade Cross-Section** | 50 mm × 20 mm × 8 mm (tapered to 4 mm edge) |
| **Liner Material** | PEEK CF40 (replaceable panels, bolted) |
| **Housing** | BFRP/Elium® filament wound, 25 mm wall |
| **Drive** | KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ ultrasonic motor (CSMFAB000000000020) |
| **Speed Range** | 50–300 RPM (variable via piezoelectric drive) |
| **Torque** | 15 kN·m peak (stall) |
| **Throughput** | 5–8 ton/hr (feedstock dependent) |
| **Output Size** | P80 < 150 mm, P50 < 80 mm |

### 3.2 BFRP Blade Engineering (CSMFAB Materials Study Part II)

The blades are manufactured from in-house basalt fiber and Elium® resin — the crown-jewel of CSMFAB domestic production.

**Blade Layup:** [0°/±45°/90°]₂ₛ symmetric, 60% fiber volume fraction
- **0° plies (4):** Primary tensile/compressive load (basalt roving, 4800 tex)
- **±45° plies (4):** Shear and torsional stiffness
- **90° plies (2):** Transverse strength, impact resistance

**Blade Edge Geometry:**
- **Primary bevel:** 25° included angle, 2 mm land
- **Secondary micro-bevel:** 35°, 0.5 mm (self-sharpening in service)
- **Edge reinforcement:** h-BN nanoparticle coating (50 μm) for wear resistance

**Blade Life Model (CSMFAB Materials Study Part II):**

| Feedstock Category | Blade Life (ton) | Wear Mechanism |
|--------------------|------------------|----------------|
| Category A (Electronics) | 400–500 | Abrasive (SiO₂, Al₂O₃ in PCBs) |
| Category B (Metals) | 600–800 | Adhesive (Al, Cu buildup), fatigue |
| Category C (Rock/Ore) | 200–300 | High abrasion (quartz, basalt) |
| Category D (Phoenix) | 800–1000 | Low abrasion (ceramic, composite) |

**Replacement Protocol:** Blade row (4 blades) replaced as set. Full rotor change: 30 min downtime. PEEK CF40 liner panels: 2000 ton life.

### 3.3 PEEK CF40 Liners (CSMFAB Materials Study Part IV)

The shredder housing interior is lined with replaceable PEEK CF40 panels:
- **Panel dimensions:** 600 mm × 400 mm × 12 mm (12 panels per housing half)
- **Mounting:** 8 × M8 PEEK CF40 bolts per panel, torque 15 Nm
- **Wear indicator:** Integrated h-BN tracer layer at 6 mm depth — visual inspection reveals wear
- **Temperature rating:** 260°C continuous (well above shredder operating temp <80°C)
- **Chemical resistance:** Impervious to oils, solvents, battery electrolytes

---

## 4. Permanent Magnet Ferrous Separation — Pre-Drum Iron Removal

Before shredding, bulk ferrous material is removed by a permanent magnet belt separator. This reduces drum loading and recovers clean ferrous scrap directly.

### 4.1 Separator Design

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Magnet Type** | NdFeB (N52 grade), 60 mm × 60 mm × 30 mm blocks |
| **Array Configuration** | Halbach array, 24 blocks, 1.2T surface field |
| **Belt Width** | 1200 mm (matches shredder feed width) |
| **Belt Material** | UHMWPE (CSMFAB Materials Study Part II) — dielectric, wear-resistant |
| **Belt Speed** | 0.5–2.0 m/s (VFD controlled) |
| **Gap to Belt** | 50 mm (adjustable via BFRP spacers) |
| **Ferrous Capture Efficiency** | >95% for pieces >20 mm, >80% for 5-20 mm |

### 4.2 Operation Sequence

1. **Feedstock spreads** on UHMWPE belt (vibratory feeder ensures monolayer)
2. **Ferrous pieces** attracted to magnet array, held against belt
3. **Non-ferrous material** falls off belt end into shredder hopper
4. **Ferrous pieces** carried past belt end, released as belt curves away from magnet
5. **Clean ferrous stream** drops into collection bin → direct to ferrous slug molds (bypasses drum)

**Economic Impact:** Removes 40-60% of Category B mass before shredding, reducing shredder wear by ~50% and drum thermal load by ~30%.

---

## 6. Moisture Pre-check and Pre-dry — Water Management

Excess moisture in feedstock consumes thermal energy during Stage 1 (80-150°C) and can cause steam explosions in the sealed drum.

### 6.1 Capacitive Moisture Sensor Array

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Sensor Type** | Fringing-field capacitive, PEEK CF40 housing |
| **Measurement Frequency** | 10 MHz (immune to material conductivity) |
| **Scan Rate** | 10 Hz (continuous during feed) |
| **Calibration** | Per feedstock category (stored in FPGA) |
| **Accuracy** | ±2% absolute moisture content |
| **Output** | 4-20 mA equivalent via PMMA POF to FPGA |

### 6.2 Pre-dry Chamber (If Moisture >25%)

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Chamber Volume** | 2 m³ (batch) |
| **Heating** | SiC glow bars (CSMFAB Materials Study Part I), 80°C |
| **Atmosphere** | N₂ purge, 0.2 bar overpressure |
| **Duration** | 15 min (verified by outlet humidity sensor) |
| **Energy** | 0.8 kWh/kg water removed |
| **Water Recovery** | Condensed in heat exchanger → Stage 1 water tank |

**Thermal Penalty Avoided:** 25% moisture = 125 kg water/ton feed = 80 kWh latent heat saved per ton by pre-drying.

## 7. Shredder Wear and Maintenance — BFRP vs Steel Benchmark

The all-dielectric shredder trades absolute wear life for contamination-free output. Comparison with conventional steel-blade shredders:

| Metric | BFRP-Blade (Aegis) | Steel-Blade (Conventional) |
|--------|-------------------|---------------------------|
| **Blade Life (Category C)** | 200–300 ton | 500–800 ton |
| **Blade Replacement Cost** | $1,200/row (4 blades) | $800/row (4 blades) |
| **Contamination** | Zero metal | Fe, Cr, Ni in output |
| **GIC Immunity** | Complete | None (steel = antenna) |
| **Recyclability** | 100% (Elium® depolymerization) | Scrap only |
| **Blade Change Time** | 30 min (row) | 45 min (row) |

**Total Cost of Ownership (5000 ton/yr, Category C mix):**
- BFRP: $45,000/yr blades + $12,000/yr liners = $57,000/yr
- Steel: $28,000/yr blades + $500,000/yr contamination remediation (hydromet penalties) = $528,000/yr

**The BFRP shredder pays for itself in contamination avoidance alone.**

## 8. Safety Systems — Jam Detection, Fire Suppression, Explosion Venting

### 8.1 Jam Detection

- **Torque monitoring:** Drive motor current sensor (optical, PMMA POF) — >90% rated torque for >5s = jam
- **Vibration monitoring:** FBG accelerometers on housing — >15 mm/s RMS = jam
- **Auto-reverse:** 30s reverse at 50% torque, then forward. 3 cycles max before E-stop.
- **Clearing protocol:** Optical E-stop → hydraulic pusher (PEEK CF40 ram) forces jammed material through.

### 8.2 Fire Suppression

- **Detection:** IR flame sensors (InGaAs, PMMA POF) + FBG temperature >150°C
- **Agent:** Novec 1230 (clean agent, zero ODP, zero GWP) — 50 kg stored in BFRP tank
- **Delivery:** 4 nozzles (ZrO₂ ceramic tips) at rotor ends and housing midpoints
- **Activation:** <200 ms from detection, discharge in 10s
- **Post-suppression:** N₂ purge 5 min, then manual inspection required.

### 8.3 Explosion Venting (Battery Thermal Runaway Mitigation)

- **Vent panels:** 4 × BFRP rupture discs (burst pressure 0.5 bar) on housing top
- **Vent area:** 0.5 m² total (NFPA 68 compliant for dust/gas explosion)
- **Ducting:** BFRP duct to gas capture system (PROD-07) — flame arrestor at inlet
- **Suppression:** Novec 1230 pre-discharge if vent activates (pressure rise detection)
