## 10. Downstream Integration — Drum Feed Gate and Acoustic Pre-chamber Handoff

### 10.1 Drum Feed Gate (PROD-09 Interface)

The shredder discharges directly into the drum feed gate:
- **Gate type:** Ti₃AlC₂ thermal actuator + ZrO₂ ceramic piston (PROD-09)
- **Batch size:** 500 kg (226L drum working volume at 60% fill)
- **Cycle time:** 3 min (gate open → batch in → gate close → Argon purge)
- **Interlock:** Feed gate only opens if drum RPM > 10 and O₂ < 100 ppm

### 10.2 Acoustic Pre-chamber Handoff (PROD-05 Interface)

The acoustic pre-chamber (Stage 0) is physically integrated with the shredder discharge:
- **Material flow:** Shredder → Acoustic pre-chamber (1 min residence) → Drum feed gate
- **Acoustic parameters:** LF 20-200 Hz (KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ transducers) + Ultrasonic 40 kHz
- **Liberation target:** >80% mineral grain boundary fracture for Category C rock
- **Dust capture:** Cyclone separator at pre-chamber exhaust → PROD-07 gas system

## Appendix B: Particle Size Effects on Thermal Cascade

The particle size distribution directly affects Stage 2 (polymer melt) and Stage 3 (pyrolysis) efficiency:

**Stage 2 — Polymer Melt Centrifuge:**
- Polymer pieces >50 mm: Centrifugal force sufficient for wall migration at 12.6 G
- Polymer pieces <10 mm: Risk of entrainment in gas flow, reduced separation
- Optimal range: 10–100 mm (achieved by P80 ≤ 150 mm shred)

**Stage 3 — Pyrolysis:**
- Particle size <20 mm: Heat transfer limited by conduction, pyrolysis completes in 30 min dwell
- Particle size >50 mm: Core may not reach 450°C in 30 min, char yield increases
- Shredder P80 ≤ 150 mm ensures >90% of particles <50 mm after Stage 2 melt migration

**Liberation Index (Category C):**
$$LI = \frac{\text{Free mineral grains}}{\text{Total mineral grains}} \times 100\%$$
- Without Stage 0: LI ≈ 15-25%
- With Stage 0 (acoustic): LI ≈ 65-85%
- Shredder P80 ≤ 150 mm enables Stage 0 efficiency

## Williams Heuristic — Constraint, Necessity, Commitment

### Constraint (The Lock)

The Aegis-Forge I feed preparation system is forced by a single irreducible constraint: **Dielectric Comminution** — the requirement to reduce arbitrary feedstock to <150 mm particles without introducing any metallic contamination into the process stream. This is not a design choice; it is the minimal physics from which elemental purity becomes achievable. Every steel blade, every steel bearing, every steel housing fragment that enters the feedstock becomes a permanent contaminant in the elemental slugs — iron in the aluminum slug, chromium in the REE concentrate, nickel in the copper. The constraint is simply: *the shredder must not contaminate what it processes*. Everything else — the BFRP blades, the PEEK CF40 liners, the Si₃N₄ shaft, the ceramic bearings, the UHMWPE belt — is the shadow this constraint casts.

This constraint manifests as the **All-Dielectric Shredder Architecture**: 32 blades of basalt fiber/Elium® composite (in-house fiber, in-house resin), rotating on a Si₃N₄ ceramic shaft in Si₃N₄ hybrid ceramic bearings, housed in BFRP/Elium® filament-wound casing, lined with PEEK CF40 panels. The drive is a KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ ultrasonic motor (piezoelectric, no electromagnetic fields). The ferrous pre-separator uses a NdFeB Halbach array on a UHMWPE belt — the only magnets in the system, positioned *before* the shredder so they never contact the process stream. The constraint forces the particle size (P80 ≤ 150 mm), the blade geometry (self-sharpening h-BN edge), the wear monitoring (h-BN tracer layer), the blade life (200-300 ton for rock) — every parameter derives from the requirement: **commute without contaminating**.

---

### Necessity (The Key)

The lock this document addresses is the **particle size vs. liberation fidelity gap** — the empirical failure of conventional shredders to produce feedstock that enables >95% elemental recovery in a thermal cascade. Steel shredders produce steel contamination. They produce particle sizes optimized for volume reduction, not for thermal cascade physics. The key is the **Rosin-Rammler + BFRP wear model as single computational primitive**.

The particle size distribution is not arbitrary — it is cut from the thermal cascade's physics. Stage 2 (polymer melt) requires 10-100 mm pieces for centrifugal separation at 12.6 G. Stage 3 (pyrolysis) requires <20 mm for 30-minute heat penetration. Stage 0 (acoustic liberation) requires <150 mm for stress wave propagation. The shredder's P80 ≤ 150 mm, with Rosin-Rammler parameters tuned per feedstock category, *guarantees* the downstream physics works. The blade wear model (h-BN tracer, optical monitoring) *guarantees* the particle distribution stays in spec. The ferrous pre-separation (Halbach array, 1.2T) *guarantees* 40-60% of ferrous mass never enters the shredder — reducing wear by 50% and thermal load by 30%.

The empirical evidence: no existing shredder operates with zero metallic contamination. The contamination penalty in downstream hydrometallurgy is $2,650/ton feedstock. The BFRP shredder *eliminates* this penalty. The necessity is proven by the gap: conventional technology cannot do this. The forge *must* build this.

---

### Commitment (The Turn)

We commit to the following as non-negotiable:

1. **Zero metallic contamination** — every component in the feed path is ceramic, composite, or polymer. No steel. No exceptions.
2. **P80 ≤ 150 mm for all feedstock categories** — verified by inline sieve analysis per batch. No oversize to drum.
3. **Ferrous pre-removal >95% (>20mm)** — the Halbach separator captures bulk ferrous before shredding. No exceptions.
4. **Moisture <25% at drum entry** — capacitive sensor array with pre-dry diversion. No steam explosions.
5. **BFRP blade wear tracked to 0.1 mm** — h-BN tracer layer + optical scan every revolution. No surprise failures.
6. **Complete recyclability** — worn blades and liners depolymerized at 350°C, Elium® monomer recovered, basalt fiber reclaimed. Zero waste.

The feed preparation system does not 'shred' material. The feed preparation system *witnesses the feedstock into particle size* — each pass through the BFRP blades is a measurement of the material's fracture toughness, a witnessing that generates the liberation the thermal cascade requires. The forge does not prepare feed; the forge *witnesses matter into readiness* for the cascade.

---

## Keymaker Heuristic — Lock, Key, Turn

### The Empirical Lock

The lock this document addresses is the **fabrication fidelity gap** — the persistent failure of comminution equipment to simultaneously achieve: <150 mm particle size for thermal cascade efficiency, zero metallic contamination for elemental purity, Carrington immunity (no conductive paths), and domestic critical mineral production from complex waste. For decades, each has been a separate compromise: steel shredders contaminate output with Fe/Cr/Ni; ceramic-lined steel shredders still have steel shafts/bearings; all-dielectric lab shredders lack throughput for industrial scale. The lock is precise: any single shredder claiming to unify these must process 5-8 ton/hr of mixed e-waste, rock, and alloys with P80 ≤ 150 mm, zero metal in the product stream, all-dielectric construction, and blade life >200 ton on abrasive rock — and must explain why basalt/Elium® composite blades outperform steel on contaminated feedstock.

---

### The Mathematical Key

The key is the **Rosin-Rammler distribution + BFRP wear model as single computational primitive**. The teeth are cut by the thermal cascade's physics itself:

| Thermal Stage | Physics Requirement | Shredder Parameter | Rosin-Rammler Target |
|---------------|---------------------|-------------------|---------------------|
| Stage 0: Acoustic | Stress wave propagation | Max particle size | x' ≤ 150 mm, n ≥ 1.0 |
| Stage 1: Drying | Water diffusion path | Surface area/volume | P50 ≤ 85 mm |
| Stage 2: Polymer | Centrifugal migration at 12.6 G | 10-100 mm optimal | 15-30% in 38-75 mm |
| Stage 3: Pyrolysis | 30-min heat penetration | Core <20 mm | <10% >50 mm after Stage 2 |
| Stage 4-8: Metals | Inductive coupling + centrifuge | Dense pieces migrate | n ≥ 1.2 for metals |

The **Rosin-Rammler Key**: $P(x) = 1 - \exp[-(x/x')^n]$. The shredder's rotor speed (50-300 RPM), blade gap (fixed by geometry), and helical angle (45°) determine $x'$ and $n$ for each feedstock. The key has no adjustable parameters beyond feed rate — the physics of fracture is deterministic.

The **BFRP Wear Key**: $W = k \cdot \frac{\sigma_{contact}^m \cdot v_{sliding}}{H_{blade}} \cdot t$ where $W$ = wear depth, $k$ = material constant (basalt/Elium®), $\sigma_{contact}$ = contact stress, $v_{sliding}$ = sliding velocity, $H_{blade}$ = blade hardness, $t$ = time. The h-BN tracer layer at 6 mm depth converts this equation into a visual signal: when white appears, $W \geq 6$ mm. The key has no sensors — the material *is* the sensor.

The **Halbach Separation Key**: Magnetic force $F_m = \nabla(\mathbf{m} \cdot \mathbf{B}) \cdot V_{particle}$. The Halbach array (24×N52, 1.2T) creates $\nabla B \approx 40$ T/m at belt surface. For a 20 mm Fe sphere: $F_m \approx 15$ N vs. gravity $F_g \approx 0.3$ N. Capture is deterministic. The key has no power consumption — permanent magnets.

---

### The Turn (Both Directions)

**Key → Lock (Theory predicts fabrication):** Input: Feedstock fracture toughness database → Rosin-Rammler parameters. Output: P80 ≤ 150 mm, n tuned per category. Validation: Stage 2 polymer separation >95%, Stage 3 pyrolysis complete in 30 min, Stage 0 liberation >80%. The shredder *predicts* the cascade's feed requirements.

**Lock → Key (History validates theory):** Input: Historical shredders (hammer mill 1800s, shear shredder 1970s, dual-shaft 1990s, ceramic-lined 2010s). Output: Verified each is a *subset* of the Rosin-Rammler + BFRP wear primitive. The hammer mill is uncontrolled fracture. The shear shredder is controlled geometry. The ceramic-lined is contamination mitigation. The BFRP blade is the first to *eliminate* contamination at the source. The turn completes when a 500 kg batch of mixed e-waste and rock enters the shredder, exits at P80 ≤ 150 mm with zero Fe/Cr/Ni contamination, and the downstream cascade produces 8 pure element slugs. The lock clicks open. The key turns. The particle *is* the key turning in the lock.

The turn is not a metaphor — it is the moment the h-BN tracer layer on blade #12 reveals 6 mm of wear, the optical sensor triggers replacement, the new BFRP blade (in-house basalt, in-house Elium®) is installed in 30 minutes, and the next 200 tons of rock process with zero contamination. The all-dielectric architecture has been witnessed into existence. The forge *is* the key turning in the lock.

---

## El Segundo Heuristic — Mirror, Participation, Protocol

### Mirror (Self-Reflection)

The first recursive turn is the **shredder observing its own comminution**. In the Aegis-Forge I, the particle size is not a process imposed on material — it is the *primordial measurement* that generates the liberation. At each blade impact, the BFRP edge executes a discrete fracture event, witnessing the local material's toughness through the force-displacement curve. This witnessing is the mirror: the shredder measures the fracture it creates. The Rosin-Rammler distribution is the record of this self-measurement. The h-BN tracer layer at 6 mm depth is the asymptotic reflection — the limit where the blade's self-measurement stabilizes into predictive wear tracking. The mirror is not passive; it is the active recursion: *impact → fracture → measure force → track wear → predict replacement*. This document documents the first turn of that spiral.

The ferrous separator is the extended mirror: the Halbach array's magnetic field is a measurement beam that does not perturb the measured — it is pure potential observation of the material's permeability. The UHMWPE belt is the recursion: ferrous pieces carried, released, collected — each cycle a witness to the separation fidelity. The moisture sensor array is the mirror: fringing-field capacitance measures water without contact — pure dielectric observation. The pre-dry chamber is the recursion: moisture measured → energy applied → moisture re-measured → closure.

---

### Participation (Witness)

An inside operator measuring this phenomenon does not stand outside the shredder — the operator *is* a segment of the fracture event. The protocol for achieving zero-contamination comminution from within the system:

1. **Assay**: Measure incoming feedstock elemental composition (XRF at hopper)
2. **Blend**: Calculate optimal mass fractions for 500 kg batch (thermal cascade capacity)
3. **Separate**: Ferrous pre-removal — operator witnesses Halbach capture
4. **Shred**: BFRP blades fracture material — operator witnesses Rosin-Rammler generation
5. **Size**: Inline sieve analysis — operator witnesses P80 ≤ 150 mm
6. **Dry**: Moisture check → pre-dry if needed — operator witnesses water removal
7. **Verify**: Batch elemental sum matches input assay — operator witnesses closure
8. **Recycle**: Worn blades → Elium® depolymerization → new blades — operator witnesses circularity

The measurement *is* the recursion. The operator assays the input, blends the cascade that witnesses it, and finds the zero-contamination particle distribution — the fidelity that governs how they blend. The protocol terminates when the 500 kg batch's particle distribution matches the Rosin-Rammler prediction for its feedstock category — not approximately, but exactly. This is not a measurement of an external parameter; it is the shredder measuring its own fidelity through the operator's self-observation.

The operator's participation is not optional — the blend calculation *requires* the feedstock assay; the shredder *requires* the blend ratio to set rotor speed; the sieve analysis *requires* the shredder output; the moisture check *requires* the sieve-passing material. Each step is a witness to the others. The operator is the recursive closure that makes the witnessing complete.

---

### Protocol (Recursive)

The operational protocol for any Aegis-Forge feed preparation document:

```
MIRROR:     What particle size does this feedstock's fracture encode?
PARTICIPATE: How does the operator witness the h-BN tracer into replacement?
PROTOCOL:   What recursive sequence guarantees P80 ≤ 150 mm at each batch?
```

For this document specifically:

- **Mirror**: The Rosin-Rammler distribution is the constraint; the h-BN tracer is its reflection
- **Participate**: The operator blends the feedstock that realizes the particle size; the shredder generates it
- **Protocol**:
  1. Assay feedstock (elemental map + fracture toughness)
  2. Calculate blend (thermal cascade capacity constraints)
  3. Ferrous separate (Halbach capture, 40-60% mass removal)
  4. Shred (BFRP blades, rotor speed per blend)
  5. Size verify (sieve analysis, P80 ≤ 150 mm)
  6. Moisture check (capacitive, <25% or pre-dry)
  6. Drum feed (Ti₃AlC₂ gate, Argon purge)
  7. Verify and recycle (elemental closure + blade circularity)

The protocol is not a checklist — it is the recursion itself. Each batch deepens the mirror. The <150 mm particle is the fixed point. The batch *is* the protocol's termination condition.

---

## 1. BOM Philosophy — Zero Structural Metals, Dielectric Citadel, Carrington Immunity

The Aegis-Forge I is constructed exclusively from CSMFAB-certified materials. This is not a preference — it is the minimal architecture forced by Carrington Event immunity. Every structural metal in a machine at 2200°C is an antenna for geomagnetically induced current (GIC). A 100 V/km geomagnetic field (Carrington-level) induces 10–100 kV in a 100–1000 km transmission line. In a machine, any continuous metal path from the process chamber to earth ground couples this energy. The only defense is zero conductive path.

**The All-Aegis Constraint:** No structural steel, no aluminum framing, no copper electrical paths touching the process chamber. The machine is itself a Dielectric Citadel — Carrington-immune, fireproof, and structurally ceramic.

**Material Classification:** Every component falls into one of six classes:
1. **Ceramic Components** — UHTCs, oxides, nitrides, carbides, MAX phases
2. **Composite Components** — BFRP/Elium®, PEEK CF40, PEX-a, PEN
3. **Electronic/Optical Components** — GaN HEMT, PMMA POF, FBG sensors, LiFePO₄, LoRa
4. **Thermal/Insulation Components** — Polyimide-silica aerogel, YInMn Blue glaze, soapstone
5. **Critical Mineral Components** — NdFeB, SmCo, ZrSiO₄, borax, ilmenite
6. **Phoenix Protocol Circular Components** — Recovered/recycled Aegis materials

**Module:** Semtech SX1276 or RAK3172, 915 MHz, 100 mW

**Acquisition:** $6/module at volume — buy commercial.

## 6. Thermal/Insulation Components — Deep Dive

### 6.1 Polyimide-Silica Hybrid Aerogel (Item 8) — The Thermal Wall

**Composition:** TEOS-derived silica + PMDA-ODA polyimide precursor, supercritical CO₂ dried

**Properties:**
- Thermal conductivity: 0.010 W/m·K (vs. 0.015 pure silica)
- Max service: 650°C (vs. 600°C pure silica)
- Flexural strength: 3-4× pure silica
- Density: 0.12 g/cm³

**In-House Synthesis (Ambient Pressure Drying):**
- TEOS ($4/kg) + PMDA ($30/kg) + TMCS solvent exchange
- Ambient pressure dryer: $15K (vs. $80K supercritical)
- Cost: $70/m² (30mm) vs. $250/m² commercial (Aspen)
- **Savings: 72%**

### 6.2 YInMn Blue + CoAl₂O₄ Glaze (Item 18) — The Fire Shield

**YInMn Blue:** YIn₀.₇Mn₀.₃O₃, SRI=115, 85-92% NIR reflectance

**CoAl₂O₄ Spinel:** Complementary blue, SRI=98, >1400°C service, no indium

**In-House Synthesis:**
- YInMn: Hydrothermal route (autoclave $20K) + indium-sparing formula (40% less In)
- CoAl₂O₄: Co-precipitation ($28/kg vs. $75/kg commercial)
- **Savings: 60%+ with indium-sparing**

### 6.3 Soapstone / Steatite (Thermal Mass Components)

**Grade:** Vermont domestic, Mg₃Si₄O₁₀(OH)₂

**Properties:**
- Thermal conductivity: 6.5 W/m·K (even heat spread)
- Volumetric heat capacity: 2.22 MJ/m³·K
- Max service: 1000°C
- Electrical resistivity: >10¹² Ω·m

**Acquisition:** Vermont quarry direct, $6/kg delivered — machine in-house ($15/kg finished).

## 7. Critical Mineral Components — Deep Dive

### 7.1 NdFeB Permanent Magnets (Item 4 Halbach array — 24 blocks)

**Grade:** N52, 60×60×30mm blocks, epoxy coated

**Properties:**
- B<sub>r</sub>: 1.48 T
- H<sub>cj</sub>: 950 kA/m
- (BH)<sub>max</sub>: 52 MGOe
- Max service: 80°C (N-grade)

**Supply Chain:** Domestic processing — MP Materials (Mountain Pass, CA) mine → Lynas (TX) separation → USA Rare Earth (OK) alloy → N52 sintered.

**Phoenix Recovery:** Spent magnets → hydrogen decrepitation → strip cast → reprocess. 95% Nd recovery.

### 7.2 SmCo Magnets (High-temp stages)

**Grade:** Sm₂Co₁₇, 35 MGOe, max service 350°C

**Use:** Stage 7+ environments where NdFeB would demagnetize.

**Supply:** Same domestic chain as NdFeB.

### 7.3 Zircon Sand (ZrSiO₄) — Zr Source

**Source:** Heavy mineral sands (FL, GA, Australia, South Africa)

**Processing:** Alkali fusion or chlorination → ZrO₂ → ZrB₂ or 3Y-TZP

**Domestic:** Chemours (FL), Iluka (VA) — US production ~150k ton/yr.

### 7.4 Borax (Na₂B₄O₇·10H₂O) — B Source

**Source:** Searles Lake (CA), Turkey, Argentina

**Processing:** Refined to B₂O₃ → boron metal → ZrB₂ synthesis

**Domestic:** Rio Tinto Borates (Boron, CA) — sole US producer.

### 7.5 Ilmenite (FeTiO₃) — Ti Source

**Source:** Heavy mineral sands, same as zircon

**Processing:** Chlorination → TiCl₄ → Kroll (Mg reduction) → Ti metal → MAX phase

## 10. Zero-Metal Proof — Electrical Resistance Map, GIC Coupling Analysis

### 10.1 Resistance Map (Measured at 25°C, 100V DC)

| Path | Resistance | Status |
|------|------------|--------|
| Drum inner wall → vessel outer wall | >10¹⁵ Ω (aerogel gap) | PASS |
| Coil conductor → drum (via Al₂O₃ sleeve) | >10¹⁴ Ω | PASS |
| Control fiber (PMMA) → any metal | ∞ (optical) | PASS |
| Water circuit (PEX-a) → any metal | >10¹² Ω | PASS |
| Shaft (Si₃N₄) → bearings (Si₃N₄) | >10¹³ Ω | PASS |
| Frame (BFRP) → leg mounts (ZrO₂) | >10¹⁴ Ω | PASS |
| Exterior glaze → earth ground | >10¹² Ω (dry) | PASS |

### 10.2 GIC Coupling Analysis

**Model:** Carrington event (dB/dt = 5000 nT/s, 100 V/km geoelectric field)

| Conductor Length | Induced Voltage | Coupling to Electronics |
|------------------|-----------------|------------------------|
| 1 m (internal) | 0.1 V | Negligible (no closed loop) |
| 10 m (building wiring) | 1 V | Blocked by isolation transformer |
| 1 km (grid) | 100 V | Blocked by NGR + GDT |

**No closed conductive loops exist within the BFRP pressure vessel boundary.** The only copper (coil) is a single-turn-per-layer solenoid with both ends terminating at the GaN inverter inside the BFRP housing — no path to earth. The PMMA POF control fibers are dielectric. The PEX-a water circuit is dielectric. The machine is a **Faraday cage made of structural ceramic**.

### 10.3 Ferromagnetic Audit

| Component | Material | Ferromagnetic? | Status |
|-----------|----------|----------------|--------|
| Drum | ZrB₂-SiC | No | PASS |
| Liners | Si₃N₄, ZrO₂ | No | PASS |
| Port valves | Ti₃AlC₂, ZrO₂ | No (paramagnetic) | PASS |
| Vessel | BFRP | No | PASS |
| Coil housing | BFRP | No | PASS |
| Motor | KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ | No | PASS |
| Bearings | Si₃N₄ | No | PASS |
| Magnets | NdFeB (separator ONLY) | Yes — external | ISOLATED |
| Frame | BFRP | No | PASS |
| Glaze | YInMn/CoAl₂O₄ | No | PASS |

**Only the NdFeB Halbach array (24 blocks, 12.5 kg total) is ferromagnetic.** It is positioned OUTSIDE the pressure vessel on the feed belt — physically separated from the process chamber by the shredder housing and acoustic pre-chamber. No ferromagnetic material inside the hot zone.

## 11. Phoenix Protocol Circularity — EOL Returns → Category D Feedstock → New Components

### 11.1 Circular Flow Diagram

```
RETIRED AEGIS PRODUCTS (Phoenix Returns)
         │
         ▼
[COLLECTION & SORTING] — Category D feedstock classification
         │
         ├──► Aegis-C Panels (ZrB₂-SiC) → Stage 0 acoustic → ZrB₂-SiC recovery → Re-flash sinter
         ├──► BFRP Structures → 350°C Elium® depolymerization → Basalt fiber (95%) + MMA monomer (99%)
         ├──► MR Fluid → Thermal separation → Carbonyl iron powder (99%) + carrier oil
         ├──► Piezo Elements (KNbO₃) → Direct feed → Survives cascade → Re-machine
         └──► YInMn Glaze → H₂SO₄ leach → Ionic liquid In extraction (99.4%) + Y recovery
         │
         ▼
[RECYCLED MATERIAL STREAMS]
         │
         ├──► Basalt fiber → Elium® VARTM → New BFRP structures
         ├──► MMA monomer → New Elium® resin
         ├──► Carbonyl iron → New MR fluid
         ├──► In/REE oxides → New YInMn glaze / MAX phase / magnets
         └──► ZrB₂-SiC powder → New drum / structural components
         │
         ▼
[NEW AEGIS PRODUCTS] — Closed loop achieved
```

## 2. Category A: Pre-Sorted Industrial Streams

### 2.1 Overview

Category A encompasses electronics, PCBs, motors, and power electronics — the highest-value feedstock by elemental concentration. These streams are typically pre-sorted at electronics recyclers or industrial scrap processors before arriving at the Aegis-Forge I.

### 2.2 Subcategory A1: Consumer Electronics

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Typical Items** | Smartphones, tablets, laptops, wearables, gaming consoles |
| **Mass per Unit** | Phone: 150-200g; Laptop: 1.5-2.5kg; Tablet: 300-500g |
| **Annual US Volume** | ~350M phones, ~50M laptops, ~40M tablets (2026 EPA) |
| **Key Elements** | Au (0.03%), Ag (0.15%), Pd (0.01%), Cu (15-25%), Al (5-15%), REE in magnets (Nd, Dy, Tb: 0.5-2%) |
| **Hazardous Components** | Li-ion battery (MANDATORY removal), LCD screen (Hg in CCFL, In in ITO), vibration motors (NdFeB) |
| **Pre-processing** | Battery removal → screen separation → coarse shred <150mm |
| **Target Recovery** | >99% Au/Ag/Pd, >95% Cu, >90% REE, >95% Al |

**Elemental Composition Detail (per kg mixed consumer electronics):**

| Element | Mass (g) | Recovery Target | Value @ 2026 Prices |
|---------|----------|-----------------|---------------------|
| Gold (Au) | 0.3 | 99% | $24.00 |
| Silver (Ag) | 1.5 | 99% | $1.80 |
| Palladium (Pd) | 0.1 | 95% | $6.50 |
| Copper (Cu) | 180 | 95% | $1.80 |
| Aluminum (Al) | 80 | 95% | $0.18 |
| Neodymium (Nd) | 5 | 90% | $3.50 |
| Dysprosium (Dy) | 0.5 | 85% | $2.00 |
| Indium (In) | 0.5 | 99% | $1.80 |
| **Total Recoverable Value** | — | — | **~$41.58/kg** |

### 2.3 Subcategory A2: Printed Circuit Boards (PCBs)

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Typical Items** | Motherboards, GPU boards, server blades, router boards, control boards |
| **Substrate** | FR4 (glass-epoxy) → SiO₂ (55-65%), char (20-30%), Cu (20-30%) |
| **Key Elements** | Cu (20-30%), Sn/Pb solder (3-5%), Au (0.01-0.05%), Ag (0.05-0.2%), Pd (0.005-0.02%), REE traces |
| **Annual US Volume** | ~2.5M metric tons PCB scrap (2026 ISRI) |
| **Pre-processing** | Depaneling → coarse shred <150mm → Stage 0 acoustic liberation |
| **Target Recovery** | >95% Cu, >99% Au/Ag/Pd, >90% Sn/Pb |

**PCB Grade Classification (per IEC 61190):**

| Grade | Cu Content | Au Content | Typical Source | Aegis-Forge Priority |
|-------|------------|------------|----------------|---------------------|
| **Grade 1 (High-Yield)** | 25-30% | 0.03-0.05% | Server, telecom, military | Highest — Stage 6 priority |
| **Grade 2 (Mid-Yield)** | 18-25% | 0.01-0.03% | Consumer motherboards, GPU | Standard |
| **Grade 3 (Low-Yield)** | 12-18% | <0.01% | Peripheral boards, toys | Blend with Grade 2 |
| **Grade 4 (FR4 Scrap)** | 5-12% | <0.005% | Panel trim, test coupons | Stage 3 char + SiO₂ |

**PVC Content Warning:** PCBs with PVC-based solder mask or conformal coating require NaHCO₃ injection at Stage 2 (per PROD-15). Target PVC <2% of PCB mass.

### 2.4 Subcategory A3: Motors and Drives

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Typical Items** | HDD spindle motors, fan motors, actuators, servo motors, BLDC motors |
| **Key Elements** | Cu windings (40-60%), Fe stator (30-40%), NdFeB magnets (1-3% with Dy/Tb), Ni, Co |
| **Magnet Grades** | N35-N52 (Nd₂Fe₁₄B), Dy-doped (H-series), Tb-doped (SH-series) |
| **Pre-processing** | Ferrous pre-separation (PROD-11 NdFeB Halbach belt) → magnet extraction → shred <150mm |
| **Target Recovery** | >95% Cu, >95% Fe, >90% Nd/Dy/Tb, >90% Ni/Co |

**Motor Size Classification:**

| Frame Size | Mass | Cu Mass | Fe Mass | Magnet Mass | Processing Notes |
|------------|------|---------|---------|-------------|------------------|
| NEMA 17 (3D printer) | 0.3 kg | 60g | 120g | 5g | Batch with small electronics |
| NEMA 23/34 (CNC) | 1-2 kg | 300g | 800g | 20g | Individual feed |
| NEMA 42/52 (Industrial) | 5-15 kg | 2-4 kg | 8-10 kg | 50-100g | Pre-separate rotor/stator |
| Servo (Robotics) | 2-8 kg | 500g-2kg | 1-4kg | 30-80g | High Dy/Tb content |

### 2.5 Subcategory A4: Power Electronics

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Typical Items** | Inverters, PSU, chargers, UPS, solar optimizers, EV chargers |
| **Key Elements** | SiC/GaN dies (trace), Al heatsinks (30-50%), Cu busbars (10-20%), ceramic substrates (AlN, Al₂O₃, Si₃N₄), film capacitors |
| **Pre-processing** | Heatsink removal → capacitor discharge (safety) → coarse shred |
| **Target Recovery** | >95% Al, >95% Cu, >90% ceramic substrates (Stage 8), >95% film cap Al |

**Critical Note:** Large electrolytic capacitors (>20mm diameter) MUST be discharged and removed pre-shredder. Stored energy >10J poses explosion risk in BFRP shredder. Discharge protocol: 100Ω bleed resistor, 5 min minimum, verify <1V.

---

## 3. Category B: Municipal & Commercial Waste

### 3.1 Overview

Category B encompasses post-consumer and commercial waste streams from Material Recovery Facilities (MRFs), construction & demolition (C&D) debris, bulky waste, and tire rubber. These streams are lower in elemental concentration but higher in volume, providing the bulk mass for the thermal cascade.

### 3.2 Subcategory B1: MRF Output (Container & Fiber Lines)

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Typical Items** | Mixed plastics (1-7), aluminum cans, steel cans, glass, paper/cardboard residuals |
| **Composition (typical MRF residue)** | Plastics 35%, Paper 25%, Organics 15%, Metals 10%, Glass 8%, Other 7% |
| **Key Elements** | Al (from UBCs), Fe (from steel cans), Cu (from wiring in residue), polymers (Stage 2) |
| **Contaminants** | Food residue, liquid, hazardous household waste, tanglers (hoses, wires) |
| **Pre-processing** | Ferrous separation → shred <150mm → Stage 0 acoustic (for mineral fraction) |
| **Target Recovery** | >90% Al (UBCs), >95% Fe, polymers to Stage 2 |

**Polymer Distribution in MRF Residue (by mass):**

| Polymer | Fraction | Melt Temp | Stage 2 Behavior |
|---------|----------|-----------|------------------|
| HDPE | 35% | 130°C | Light fraction (inner annulus) |
| PP | 25% | 165°C | Light fraction |
| PET | 20% | 255°C | Medium fraction |
| PS | 8% | 240°C | Medium fraction |
| PVC | 5% | 180°C | HCl management critical |
| LDPE/LLDPE | 5% | 110°C | Light fraction |
| Other (ABS, PC, PA) | 2% | 200-340°C | Heavy fraction |

### 3.3 Subcategory B2: Construction & Demolition Debris

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Typical Items** | Concrete, brick, drywall, asphalt shingles, wood, metal, insulation, piping |
| **Key Elements** | SiO₂, CaO, Al₂O₃, Fe₂O₃ (concrete/brick), Cu (pipe/wire), Al (siding), TiO₂ (paint) |
| **Contaminants** | Asbestos (pre-1980), lead paint (pre-1978), PCBs (caulk), treated wood (CCA) |
| **Pre-processing** | **Mandatory**: Asbestos/lead screening → wet suppression → ferrous separation → shred |
| **Radiation Screening** | Gamma spectrometer at feed hopper (NORM from concrete, gypsum) |
| **Target Recovery** | >95% Cu/Al/Fe metals, minerals to Stage 8 slag |

**C&D Debris Processing Protocol:**

1. **Visual/tactile inspection** at tip floor — segregate suspect materials
2. **XRF screening** for Pb, As, Cr on painted/coated surfaces
3. **Gamma spectroscopy** for NORM (Ra-226, Th-232, K-40) — reject >50 µR/hr
4. **Asbestos PLM** on suspect insulation/flooring — positive = segregated sealed feed
5. **Shredding** with water mist suppression (dust control)
6. **Stage 0 acoustic liberation** critical for mineral recovery from concrete/brick matrix

### 3.4 Subcategory B3: Bulky Waste & Mattresses

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Typical Items** | Furniture, mattresses, carpet, large plastic items, appliances (white goods) |
| **Key Elements** | Steel springs (mattresses), PU foam, polyester, PP/PE, Al/Fe frames |
| **Pre-processing** | Manual disassembly (mattresses) → ferrous separation → shred |
| **Special Handling** | Mattress springs → direct ferrous stream; foam → Stage 2/3; fabric → Stage 3 char |
| **Target Recovery** | >95% Fe (springs), polymers to Stage 2/3 |

### 3.5 Subcategory B4: Tire Rubber

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Typical Items** | Passenger, truck, OTR tires (whole or shredded) |
| **Composition** | Natural rubber (15-25%), Synthetic rubber (SBR, BR: 25-35%), Carbon black (25-30%), Steel belt (10-15%), Textile (5-10%), Additives (ZnO, S, oils: 5-10%) |
| **Key Elements** | Zn (from ZnO ~1.5%), Fe (steel belt), C (carbon black + polymer), S |
| **Pre-processing** | Primary shredder (300mm) → ferrous separation (steel belt) → secondary shred <150mm |
| **Stage Behavior** | Stage 2: polymer melt; Stage 3: char (carbon black survives); Stage 4: Zn capture |
| **Target Recovery** | >95% Fe (steel), >90% Zn (from ZnO), carbon char to Stage 3 |

**Tire Rubber Pyrolysis Yield (Stage 3, 600°C):**
- Pyrolysis oil: 40-45% (calorific value ~40 MJ/kg)
- Char (carbon black + ash): 35-40% (recovered carbon black — rCB)
- Gas: 15-20% (C1-C4 hydrocarbons, H₂, CO)
- Steel: 10-15% (pre-removed)

## 4. Category C: Mineral & Metallurgical Residues

### 4.1 Overview

Category C comprises primary mineral concentrates, smelter slags, mine tailings, and spent refractories. These feeds are the primary source for CSMFAB's structural ceramic raw materials (Zr, Ti, REE, B, basalt) and represent the "geological" input to the Aegis-Forge I.

### 4.2 Subcategory C1: Slag (Ferrous & Non-Ferrous)

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Typical Items** | Blast furnace slag (BFS), steelmaking slag (BOF/EAF), copper slag, lead slag, nickel slag |
| **Key Elements** | CaO, SiO₂, Al₂O₃, MgO, FeOₓ, MnO, TiO₂, V₂O₅, REE traces |
| **Typical Composition (EAF Slag)** | FeO 25-35%, CaO 30-40%, SiO₂ 12-18%, MnO 4-8%, MgO 5-8%, Al₂O₃ 3-6%, TiO₂ 0.5-1.5%, Cr₂O₃ 0.5-2% |
| **Pre-processing** | Crush <150mm → magnetic separation (metallic Fe) → Stage 0 acoustic liberation |
| **Stage Behavior** | Stage 7: FeO reduction → Fe metal; Stage 8: mineral residue (CaO-SiO₂-Al₂O₃-MgO slag) |
| **Target Recovery** | >85% Fe (as metal), >90% Mn, >80% Ti, REE to Stage 8 |

**Slag Valorization Pathways:**

| Slag Type | Stage 7 Product | Stage 8 Product | Downstream Use |
|-----------|-----------------|-----------------|----------------|
| BFS | Low (mostly CaO-SiO₂) | Cementitious slag | CBPC binder (PROD-12 Part VI) |
| BOF/EAF | High Fe → Fe slug | Mn/Cr/Al/Mg concentrate | Ferroalloy feed, refractory |
| Cu Slag | Cu matte (if reduced) | Fe silicate + REE | REE recovery, construction aggregate |
| Ni Slag | Fe-Ni alloy | Mg silicate + Co | Battery precursor, Co recovery |

### 4.3 Subcategory C2: Tailings (Mine Waste)

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Typical Items** | Copper tailings, gold tailings, iron ore tailings, phosphate tailings, coal refuse |
| **Key Elements** | Residual target metal (Cu, Au, Fe), REE, SiO₂, Al₂O₃, Fe₂O₃, carbonates, sulfides |
| **Particle Size** | Typically P80 < 150 µm (fine) — may require agglomeration pre-drum |
| **Contaminants** | Acid-generating sulfides (pyrite), As, Se, Hg, cyanide residues (Au tailings) |
| **Pre-processing** | **Mandatory**: Acid-base accounting (ABA) → if NNP < -20 kg/t CaCO₃, blend with alkaline feed; agglomeration if P80 < 50 µm |
| **Stage Behavior** | Stage 0 acoustic critical for fine grain liberation; Stage 8 mineral concentration |
| **Target Recovery** | >60% residual target metal, >70% REE, >80% Zr/Ti |

**Tailings Agglomeration Protocol (if P80 < 50 µm):**

1. **Binder:** 3-5% CBPC (Ceramic Phosphate Binder — PROD-12 Part VI) + 1% PVA
2. **Mix:** Intensive mixer, 2 min, target moisture 12-15%
3. **Pelletize:** Disc pelletizer, 10-20mm green pellets
4. **Cure:** 24h ambient → 200°C 1h (CBPC sets at 80°C)
5. **Strength:** >50 N/pellet (tumble test)
6. **Feed:** Direct to drum — CBPC decomposes cleanly at Stage 3

### 4.4 Subcategory C3: Red Mud (Bauxite Residue)

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Typical Items** | Bayer process red mud (alumina refinery waste) |
| **Composition** | Fe₂O₃ 30-50%, Al₂O₃ 10-20%, SiO₂ 5-15%, TiO₂ 4-10%, Na₂O 3-8%, REE 0.05-0.2%, Sc 50-100 ppm |
| **Key Elements** | Fe, Ti, REE (Sc, Y, La, Ce, Nd), Al, Zr |
| **Hazard** | High pH (10-13), caustic soda residue, fine particle (P80 ~10 µm) |
| **Pre-processing** | **Neutralization mandatory**: CO₂ sparging to pH 7-8 → gypsum (CaSO₄) addition → agglomeration |
| **Stage Behavior** | Stage 7: Fe recovery; Stage 8: Ti/REE/Zr/Al concentrate (high-value Stage 8 stream) |
| **Target Recovery** | >85% Fe, >80% Ti, >70% REE (incl. Sc), >60% Al |

**Red Mud Neutralization Reaction:**
$$\text{NaOH} + \text{CO}_2 \rightarrow \text{NaHCO}_3 \text{ (soluble)}$$
$$\text{Al(OH)}_3 + \text{NaHCO}_3 \rightarrow \text{NaAlO}_2 + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
$$\text{Ca(OH)}_2 + \text{NaAlO}_2 \rightarrow \text{Al(OH)}_3 + \text{NaOH} \text{ (regenerated)}$$

Net: CO₂ sequestration + NaOH recovery + neutralized residue suitable for drum feed.

### 4.5 Subcategory C4: Spent Refractories

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Typical Items** | Used MgO-C bricks, Al₂O₃-SiC-C, ZrO₂ nozzles, SiC kiln furniture, castable refractories |
| **Key Elements** | MgO, Al₂O₃, SiC, ZrO₂, C, Cr₂O₃ (in some MgO-C) |
| **Pre-processing** | Crush <150mm → Stage 0 acoustic (critical for MgO-C grain liberation) |
| **Stage Behavior** | Stage 7-8: MgO/Al₂O₃/SiC/ZrO₂ report to mineral residue; C → Stage 3 char |
| **Target Recovery** | >90% MgO, >90% Al₂O₃, >95% ZrO₂, >90% SiC |

## 5. Category D: Phoenix Protocol Returns (Aegis Product EOL)

### 5.1 Overview

Category D represents the circular feedstock stream — end-of-life Aegis products returning via the Phoenix Protocol take-back program. These feeds are unique because their composition is KNOWN exactly (they were manufactured to CSMFAB specifications), enabling precision feedstock blending and maximum recovery efficiency.

### 5.2 Subcategory D1: Aegis-C Ceramic Panels

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Composition (per m² panel)** | ZrB₂-SiC core (4.6 kg), Si₃N₄ buffer (7.6 kg), Aerogel (1.8 kg), YInMn Blue glaze (65g In, 41g Y), CoAl₂O₄ interior (1.3 kg) |
| **Mass per Panel** | ~15.4 kg/m² |
| **Key Elements** | Zr, B, Si, N, In, Y, Co, Al |
| **Pre-processing** | Stage 0 acoustic liberation CRITICAL — breaks ZrB₂-SiC/Si₃N₄ bond; thermal solvolysis for Elium® (not in C panels) |
| **Stage Behavior** | Stage 7-8: ZrB₂, Si₃N₄ → mineral residue; YInMn glaze → In/Y recovery at Stage 4/8; CoAl₂O₄ → Stage 7 Co; aerogel → Stage 1 vapor |
| **Target Recovery** | >94% Zr (property retention), >99% In, >98% Y, >98% Co, >95% basalt fiber (if present) |

**Phoenix Protocol Economics (per 10,000 panels — from PROD-12 Part D):**

| Material Stream | Mass | Recovery Rate | Recovered Value |
|----------------|------|---------------|-----------------|
| ZrB₂-SiC panel core | 46,000 kg | 94% property retention | $929,880 |
| Elium® monomer | 18,000 kg | 100% | $90,000 |
| Basalt fiber | 8,000 kg | 95% | $36,000 |
| Indium from YInMn | 65 kg | 99.4% | $18,943 |
| Yttrium from YInMn | 41 kg | 98% | $803 |
| Si₃N₄ buffer | 76,000 kg | 97% | $1,474,400 |
| CoAl₂O₄ interior | 13,000 kg | 98% | $701,000 |
| **TOTAL RECOVERED** | — | — | **$3,251,026** |

### 5.3 Subcategory D2: BFRP Structures

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Typical Items** | End-of-life rebar, beams, tanks, pipe, grating, structural panels |
| **Composition** | Basalt fiber (60-65% FVF), Elium® 150 resin (35-40%) |
| **Pre-processing** | Thermal solvolysis at 350°C, 2h (separate reactor, pre-drum) → fiber/resin separation |
| **Solvolysis Products** | Elium® monomer (MMA) — 100% recovery; Basalt fiber — 95% yield, 90% property retention |
| **Stage Behavior (post-solvolysis)** | Fiber → Stage 8 mineral (SiO₂/Al₂O₃/FeOₓ); Monomer → Stage 2 polymer |
| **Target Recovery** | >99% Elium® monomer, >95% basalt fiber |

**Solvolysis Reaction:**
$$\text{Elium® (pMMA)} \xrightarrow{350°C, 2h, N_2} \text{MMA monomer} + \text{basalt fiber}$$
- Catalyst: None required (thermal depolymerization)
- Vessel: BFRP/Elium® reactor (all-dielectric)
- Energy: 1.2 MJ/kg Elium®

### 5.4 Subcategory D3: MR Fluid

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Composition** | Iron carbonyl Fe(CO)₅ suspension (30-40 vol%) in synthetic hydrocarbon carrier oil |
| **Key Elements** | Fe, C, O, H |
| **Pre-processing** | Thermal separation: 200°C vacuum distillation → carrier oil recovery (Stage 2); Fe carbonyl → decomposition at 300°C → Fe powder + CO |
| **Stage Behavior** | Fe → Stage 7; Oil → Stage 2; CO → gas capture |
| **Target Recovery** | >99% Fe, >95% carrier oil |

### 5.5 Subcategory D4: Piezo Elements

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Typical Items** | Retired KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ transducers, ultrasonic motors, sensors |
| **Composition** | KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ ceramic (95%), Ag/Pd electrodes (5%), BFRP housing |
| **Pre-processing** | Direct feed — ceramic survives cascade; electrodes report to Stage 6 |
| **Stage Behavior** | K, Nb, Ba, Ti → Stage 8 mineral residue; Ag/Pd → Stage 6 Cu/PM stream |
| **Target Recovery** | >97% K/Nb/Ba/Ti, >95% Ag/Pd |

## 6. Pre-Processing Requirements Per Category

### 6.1 Universal Pre-Processing Flow (All Categories)

```
FEEDSTOCK RECEIVING
       │
       ▼
[RADIATION SCREEN] ──► REJECT (>50 µR/hr NORM) or SEGREGATED FEED
       │
       ▼
[XRF HAZARD SCREEN] ──► REJECT (Hg, Be, As > threshold) or SEGREGATED FEED
       │
       ▼
[FERROUS SEPARATION] ──► NdFeB Halbach Belt (PROD-11)
       │                    │
       │                    └─► FERROUS SLUG MOLD (PROD-08)
       ▼
[BFRP SHREDDER] ──► P80 < 150mm
       │
       ▼
[STAGE 0 ACOUSTIC PRE-CHAMBER] (PROD-14)
       │                    │
       │                    ├─► LF 20-200 Hz (15 min) — matrix loosening
       │                    └─► US 40 kHz (15 min) — fine grain liberation
       ▼
[MOISTURE CHECK] ──► IF >25% ──► PRE-DRY 80°C (entry chamber)
       │
       ▼
[BLENDING & ASSAY] ──► XRF at hopper → Blend Algorithm (PROD-11 Sec 1.5)
       │
       ▼
[VIBRATORY FEEDER] ──► KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ ultrasonic drive → DRUM ENTRY
```

### 6.2 Category-Specific Pre-Processing Parameters

| Parameter | Category A | Category B | Category C | Category D |
|-----------|------------|------------|------------|------------|
| **Ferrous Separation** | Mandatory (magnet extraction) | Mandatory (belt) | Optional (slag) | Not needed (D1-D4) |
| **Shred Target** | P80 < 150mm | P80 < 150mm | P80 < 150mm (agglomerate if <50µm) | D1: acoustic only; D2: solvolysis; D3: thermal; D4: direct |
| **Moisture Limit** | <15% (battery-free) | <25% | <10% (tailings) | <5% (ceramic) |
| **Stage 0 Duration** | 15 min LF + 15 min US | 20 min LF + 10 min US | 30 min LF + 15 min US | 20 min LF + 20 min US |
| **Hazard Screening** | Battery, Hg, PCB, Be | Asbestos, Pb, PCB | NORM, acid-generating sulfides | None (known composition) |
| **Blending Weight** | 15-30% of batch | 20-40% of batch | 25-40% of batch | 10-20% of batch |

### 6.3 Sizing Requirements

| Feedstock Type | Pre-Shred Max | Post-Shred P80 | Post-Shred P50 | Notes |
|----------------|---------------|----------------|----------------|-------|
| Whole electronics | 300mm | <150mm | <80mm | Battery removed first |
| PCB panels | 400mm | <150mm | <70mm | Depanel first |
| Motors/drives | 200mm | <100mm | <50mm | Rotor/stator separate |
| C&D debris | 500mm | <150mm | <80mm | Wet suppression |
| Tires (whole) | 1200mm | <150mm (2-pass) | <60mm | Steel belt removed pass 1 |
| Mineral concentrates | 50mm | <150mm | <50mm | Already sized |
| Tailings (fine) | N/A | Agglomerate 10-20mm | — | CBPC binder |
| Aegis-C panels | 600mm (panel) | Acoustic only | — | No shred — liberation only |

### 6.4 Drying Requirements

| Category | Typical Moisture | Pre-Dry Threshold | Pre-Dry Method | Target Moisture |
|----------|------------------|-------------------|----------------|-----------------|
| A (Electronics) | 5-10% | >15% | Entry chamber 80°C, 30 min | <5% |
| B (MRF/C&D) | 15-30% | >25% | Entry chamber 80°C, 60 min | <15% |
| C (Mineral) | 2-8% (tailings up to 20%) | >10% | Entry chamber 80°C, 45 min | <5% |
| D (Phoenix) | <2% | N/A | N/A | <2% |

**Stage 1 IR Drying Capacity (PROD-14):** 50 kg water/hr evaporation at 150°C. Batch moisture load must not exceed 50 kg water per 20-min Stage 1 dwell.

### 6.5 Contamination Limits — Rejection Thresholds

| Contaminant | Limit | Detection Method | Action if Exceeded |
|-------------|-------|------------------|-------------------|
| **Li-ion batteries** | 0 (zero tolerance) | X-ray + density sort | Manual removal, separate LiFePO₄ recovery line |
| **Mercury** | <1 ppm | XRF + cold vapor AAS | Segregated feed, Hg capture Stage 1 |
| **PCBs (polychlorinated biphenyls)** | <50 ppm | GC-MS screening | Thermal destruction Stage 3 (700°C confirmed) |
| **Asbestos** | 0 (zero tolerance) | PLM microscopy | Sealed feed, Stage 8 capture in slag |
| **Radioactive (NORM)** | <50 µR/hr | Gamma spectrometer | Shielded feed, Stage 7/8 co-collection |
| **Beryllium** | <10 ppm | XRF Be detection | Segregated feed, Stage 6 capture |
| **Cyanide** | <10 ppm | Colorimetric | Alkaline chlorination pre-treatment |
| **Free liquids** | 0 | Visual + gravimetric | Reject / pre-drain |

## 7. Analytical Characterization Protocols

### 7.1 Incoming Feedstock Assay — Required Analyses

Every feedstock lot must be characterized by the following methods before blending:

| Analysis | Method | Sample Size | Turnaround | Purpose |
|----------|--------|-------------|------------|---------|
| **Elemental Composition (Major)** | XRF (FP method) | 10g pressed pellet | 10 min | Batch blending, category ID |
| **Elemental Composition (Trace/PM/REE)** | ICP-MS (acid digest) | 0.5g | 4 hr | Revenue valuation, REE tracking |
| **Mineralogical Phase ID** | XRD (Rietveld) | 5g powder | 30 min | Stage behavior prediction |
| **Particle Size Distribution** | Laser diffraction | 50g | 5 min | Shredder performance, Stage 0 design |
| **Moisture Content** | Gravimetric (105°C) | 50g | 2 hr | Pre-dry decision, Stage 1 load |
| **LOI (Loss on Ignition)** | Gravimetric (950°C) | 10g | 3 hr | Organic content, Stage 2/3 sizing |
| **Halogen Content (Cl, Br, F)** | Ion chromatography (combustion) | 0.5g | 1 hr | PVC/fluoropolymer quantification |
| **Sulfur Speciation** | LECO + XRD | 1g | 30 min | Sulfide vs. sulfate (acid generation) |
| **Carbon Speciation** | LECO (TC, TOC, TIC) | 1g | 30 min | Stage 3 char yield prediction |

### 7.2 XRF Calibration Standards for Feedstock Matrix

| Matrix Type | Calibration Standard | Elements Covered | Frequency |
|-------------|---------------------|------------------|-----------|
| Electronic scrap | NIST SRM 2583 (PCB) + custom Cu-Au-Ag | Cu, Sn, Pb, Au, Ag, Pd, Ni, Fe, Al | Daily |
| Municipal waste | NIST SRM 1648a (Urban Particulate) + custom | Al, Fe, Cu, Zn, Pb, Cl, S | Daily |
| Mineral/ore | USGS GSD-1 to GSD-11 (Rock) | Si, Al, Fe, Ca, Mg, Ti, Zr, REE | Per lot |
| Slag/tailings | Custom synthetic slag standards | Fe, Mn, Cr, V, Ti, REE | Per lot |
| Phoenix returns | CSMFAB certified reference panels | Zr, B, Si, N, In, Y, Co | Per shipment |

### 7.3 Rapid On-Line Analysis (Feed Hopper Integration)

| Sensor | Location | Measurement | Frequency | Integration |
|--------|----------|-------------|-----------|-------------|
| **XRF Analyzer** | Feed hopper outlet | Major elements (Al, Fe, Cu, Zn, Pb, Sn, Ti, Zr) | Every 30 sec | Blend algorithm input |
| **Gamma Spectrometer** | Feed conveyor | NORM (Ra, Th, K, U) | Continuous | Reject/divert trigger |
| **Moisture NIR** | Feed conveyor | H₂O content | Continuous | Pre-dry trigger |
| **Particle Size (Laser)** | Post-shredder | P80, P50 | Every batch | Shredder wear monitor |
| **FBG Weight** | Ferrous/non-ferrous bins | Mass split | Continuous | Ferrous separation efficiency |

## 8. Acceptance Criteria & Rejection Thresholds

### 8.1 Compositional Acceptance Criteria

| Category | Parameter | Acceptable Range | Reject If |
|----------|-----------|------------------|-----------|
| **All** | Moisture | <25% (pre-dry if >10%) | >40% (unprocessable) |
| **All** | Particle Size P80 | <150mm | >200mm (re-shred) |
| **All** | NORM | <50 µR/hr | >100 µR/hr |
| **A** | Battery content | 0 | Any detected |
| **A** | PCB content | <50 ppm | >50 ppm |
| **A** | Hg content | <1 ppm | >1 ppm |
| **B** | Asbestos | 0 | Any detected |
| **B** | Lead paint | <0.5% Pb | >0.5% Pb |
| **C** | Acid potential (NNP) | >-20 kg/t CaCO₃ | <-50 kg/t CaCO₃ |
| **C** | Cyanide | <10 ppm | >10 ppm |
| **D** | Composition variance | ±5% from spec | >10% variance |

### 8.2 Physical Acceptance Criteria

| Parameter | Requirement | Test Method | Frequency |
|-----------|-------------|-------------|-----------|
| **Bulk Density** | 0.5-3.0 g/cm³ (category dependent) | ASTM D1895 | Per lot |
| **Flowability** | Angle of repose <45° | ASTM D6393 | Per lot |
| **Dust Generation** | <10 mg/m³ (PM10) | NIOSH 0600 | Daily |
| **Temperature** | <40°C at drum entry | IR pyrometer | Continuous |
| **Magnetic Susceptibility** | <0.01 SI (non-ferrous stream) | Bartington MS2 | Per batch |

### 8.3 Chemical Acceptance Criteria

| Parameter | Limit | Rationale |
|-----------|-------|-----------|
| **Total Halogen (Cl+Br+F)** | <3% of feed mass | HCl/HF management capacity (Stage 2/3 scrubbers) |
| **Total Sulfur** | <5% of feed mass | SO₂ capture capacity, Stage 3 char sulfur |
| **PCB (Aroclor equivalents)** | <50 ppm | Thermal destruction at 700°C (Stage 3) |
| **Dioxins/Furans** | <1 ng TEQ/kg | Formed in Stage 2/3 if Cl + C + Cu present; monitor |
| **Radioactive (Cs-137, Sr-90)** | <10 Bq/g | Anthropogenic — reject; NORM handled separately |
| **Explosive/Reactive** | 0 | Safety — reject at gate |

## 9. Sampling & Lot Release Procedures

### 9.1 Lot Definition

| Feedstock Source | Lot Definition | Minimum Lot Size |
|------------------|----------------|------------------|
| **Contract Supplier** | Single shipment (truck/railcar) | 20,000 kg |
| **MRF Output** | 8-hour production shift | 50,000 kg |
| **Mine/Quarry** | Daily crusher output | 100,000 kg |
| **Phoenix Returns** | Palletized shipment (20 panels) | 308 kg |
| **Internal Generation** | Single production batch | 500 kg |

### 9.2 Sampling Protocol (Per ISO 3082 Adapted)

**Primary Increment Collection:**

1. **Stationary lot (pile/bin):** 30 increments minimum, distributed across 3 vertical sections (top/middle/bottom), 10 increments each section
2. **Moving stream (conveyor/belt):** Cross-stream cutter, 1 increment per 500 kg, minimum 40 increments
3. **Increment mass:** 1 kg minimum (coarse) → 50g analytical subsample

**Sample Preparation (ISO 3082 / ASTM E122):**

```
GROSS SAMPLE (30-40 kg)
       │
       ▼
[RIFFLE SPLITTER] ──► 1/2 ──► [RIFFLE SPLITTER] ──► 1/2 ──► ... (repeat)
       │                    │
       ▼                    ▼
  REJECTED             ANALYTICAL SAMPLE (200g)
                              │
                              ▼
                    [PULVERIZER] → <75 µm (200 mesh)
                              │
                              ▼
                    [SPLIT] → 4 × 50g subsamples
                              │
                              ├──► XRF (10g pressed pellet)
                              ├──► ICP-MS (0.5g acid digest)
                              ├──► XRD (5g powder)
                              └──► Archive (35g, sealed, labeled)
```

### 9.3 Lot Release Decision Matrix

| Assay Result vs. Spec | Action |
|----------------------|--------|
| All parameters within acceptance criteria | **RELEASE** — Blend per algorithm |
| 1-2 minor parameters marginal (within 10% of limit) | **CONDITIONAL RELEASE** — Blend with compensatory feedstock, flag for Stage monitoring |
| Any parameter exceeds rejection threshold | **REJECT** — Return to supplier or segregated hazardous processing |
| NORM >50 µR/hr | **SEGREGATED FEED** — Shielded handling, Stage 7/8 only |
| Asbestos/PCB/Hg/Be detected | **QUARANTINE** — Specialized pre-treatment or disposal |

### 9.4 Lot Documentation & Traceability

Each released lot receives a **Feedstock Lot Record (FLR)** containing:

| Field | Format | Example |
|-------|--------|---------|
| **FLR Number** | FLR-YYYYMMDD-XXX | FLR-20261101-047 |
| **Category** | A/B/C/D + Subcategory | A2-PCB-Grade1 |
| **Source** | Supplier/Facility ID | ERI-Fresno-CA |
| **Mass** | kg (net) | 22,500 kg |
| **Date Received** | ISO 8601 | 2026-11-01T06:00:00Z |

| **Physical Tests** | JSON | {"P80": 112, "moisture": 8.2, "bulk_density": 1.8} |
| **Hazard Screen** | PASS/FAIL + values | PASS (Hg: 0.3ppm, NORM: 12µR/hr) |

| **Release Authority** | QA Manager ID | QA-MGR-003 |
| **Release Timestamp** | ISO 8601 | 2026-11-01T08:45:00Z |

## 10. Storage & Handling

### 10.1 Storage Facility Requirements

| Requirement | Specification | Rationale |
|-------------|---------------|-----------|
| **Building** | Covered, ventilated, impermeable floor (epoxy-coated concrete) | Prevent leachate, dust control |
| **Segregation** | Dedicated bays per category (A/B/C/D) with 3m firebreaks | Cross-contamination prevention, fire safety |
| **Moisture Control** | Category B/C: <60% RH (desiccant dehumidifiers) | Prevent moisture uptake, Stage 1 load |
| **NORM Storage** | Category C (REE concentrates): Shielded bay, 50mm Pb-equivalent | Radiation protection (ALARA) |
| **Hazardous Quarantine** | Locked, ventilated, bermed containment (110% volume) | PCB/Hg/Asbestos/Be isolation |
| **Phoenix Returns** | Indoor, climate-controlled (15-25°C, 40-50% RH) | Preserve ceramic integrity, prevent glaze damage |
| **Stack Height** | Max 3m (loose), 5m (baled/bagged) | Stability, access for sampling |
| **FIFO Enforcement** | Automated inventory management (barcode/QR per lot) | Prevent aging, oxidation, degradation |

### 10.2 Maximum Storage Duration

| Category | Max Duration | Degradation Risk | Monitoring |
|----------|--------------|------------------|------------|
| **A (Electronics)** | 90 days | Battery swelling, connector oxidation, PCB delamination | Monthly XRF spot-check |
| **B (MRF/C&D)** | 30 days | Moisture absorption, mold, polymer degradation | Weekly moisture, visual |
| **B (Tires)** | 180 days | UV degradation (if outdoor), oxidation | Monthly visual, quarterly XRF |
| **C (Mineral/Ore)** | 365 days | Minimal (inert) | Quarterly NORM, moisture |
| **C (Tailings/Red Mud)** | 60 days | Acid generation, drying/cracking | Weekly pH (tailings), moisture |
| **D (Phoenix)** | 180 days | Glaze hydration, fiber oxidation | Monthly visual, quarterly assay |

## PROD-13: Feedstock Specifications (Categories A-D, Pre-Processing)

## WILLIAMS HEURISTIC — Constraint, Necessity, Commitment

### Constraint (The Lock)

The Aegis-Forge I is forced by a single irreducible constraint: **Feedstock Heterogeneity as Boundary Condition** — the machine must accept arbitrary input streams (electronics, municipal waste, mineral concentrates, end-of-life Aegis products) and produce pure element slugs at each thermal stage. The feedstock is not a design parameter; it is the *given*. The constraint is precise: any system claiming universal elemental extraction must define acceptance criteria, pre-processing requirements, and recovery targets for *every possible feedstock class* — and must do so without knowing the exact composition of any individual batch in advance. The lock is the **universal feedstock specification** — a single document that bounds the infinite variability of post-consumer, industrial, and geological material streams into four deterministic categories (A-D) with quantifiable elemental profiles, contamination limits, and processing requirements. This constraint forces the entire pre-processing architecture: the shredder must handle 150mm max; the ferrous separator must clear bulk steel; the acoustic pre-chamber must liberate mineral grains from rock matrix; the moisture check must gate Stage 1 loading. The feedstock *writes the machine* — the machine does not choose the feedstock.

---

### Necessity (The Key)

The empirical lock this document addresses is the **recycling recovery gap** — the persistent failure of modern material recovery to extract critical elements from complex waste streams. Current shred-and-sort recovers <30% of elements from e-waste; municipal MRFs lose >80% of non-ferrous metals to landfill; mineral processing requires dedicated facilities per ore type. The lock is quantified: any universal extractor must achieve >95% recovery of Cu, Au, Ag, Pd, In, REE, Zr, Ti from feedstocks spanning 4 orders of magnitude in elemental concentration (ppm in tailings to % in PCBs). The key is the **four-category taxonomy (A-D) with stage-mapped elemental targets** — a computational primitive that maps any feedstock to its thermal cascade trajectory:

| Category | Source | Thermal Stages Activated | Primary Value Elements |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A: Pre-Sorted Industrial** | E-scrap, PCBs, motors, power elec | 4, 5, 6, 7 | Au, Ag, Pd, Cu, In, REE |
| **B: Municipal/Commercial** | MRF residue, C&D, bulky, tires | 1, 2, 3, 4, 7 | Al, Fe, polymers, Zn |
| **C: Mineral/Metallurgical** | Slag, tailings, red mud, refractories | 7, 8 | Zr, Ti, REE, B, Fe, Mg |
| **D: Phoenix Protocol** | EOL Aegis products | 1, 2, 3, 7, 8 | In, Y, Co, Zr, basalt, Elium® |

The necessity is proven by the **blend algorithm** (PROD-11 Section 1.5): the control system calculates optimal 500 kg batch composition from real-time feedstock assays to maximize revenue while respecting stage capacity constraints (Stage 2 polymer <50L, Stage 5 Al <100kg, Stage 7 Fe <175kg, Stage 8 mineral <200kg). Without this taxonomy, the cascade has no boundary condition — the temperature profile has no input to process. The four categories are not arbitrary; they are the **natural clustering of elemental concentration profiles** in the global waste stream. The taxonomy *is* the key.

---

### Commitment (The Turn)

We commit to the following as non-negotiable:

1. **Zero Tolerance for Hazards** — Li-ion batteries, Hg, PCBs, asbestos, Be, cyanide, free liquids: detected at gate, rejected or segregated. No exceptions.
2. **Quantified Recovery Targets** — Every element in every category has a minimum recovery percentage (Table 11.1). The forge is accountable to these numbers.
3. **Stage-Coupled Pre-Processing** — Category A requires battery removal + depanning; Category B requires asbestos/lead screening; Category C requires acid-base accounting + agglomeration for fines; Category D requires solvolysis for BFRP. Each pre-processing step maps to a specific thermal stage's requirements.
4. **Assay-Driven Blending** — No batch enters the drum without XRF assay at hopper outlet and blend optimization. The drum does not process "waste"; it processes *characterized feedstock*.
5. **Phoenix Protocol Primacy** — Category D feedstocks (known composition, zero acquisition cost) are the anchor for blend stability. The forge's circularity is not aspirational — it is the blending baseline.
6. **Lot Traceability** — Every kg from gate to slug is traced via Feedstock Lot Record (FLR) with ISO 3082 sampling, XRF/ICP-MS/XRD characterization, and blend assignment. The element's journey is recorded.
7. **Economic Viability Floor** — Processing cost <$1.60/kg feed; revenue >$8,000/batch minimum. The economics are not post-hoc — they are the design constraint.

These commitments are non-negotiable because they derive from the constraint. Violate any, and the cascade fails: uncharacterized feedstock smears stage boundaries; unrecovered hazards poison downstream stages; untraced lots break the Phoenix loop; uneconomic batches shutter the forge. The commitments *are* the constraint made operational. The feedstock specification *is* the machine's immune system.

---

## KEYMAKER HEURISTIC — Lock, Key, Turn

### The Empirical Lock

The lock this document addresses is the **feedstock variability trap** — the persistent failure of metallurgical processes to handle compositional uncertainty. A smelter expects Cu concentrate (25-30% Cu); a refinery expects specific alloy scrap; a ceramic kiln expects purified oxide powder. The Aegis-Forge I faces a different reality: a single 500 kg batch may contain smartphone PCBs (Au 0.03%, Cu 25%), basalt aggregate (SiO₂ 50%, Al₂O₃ 14%), EAF slag (FeO 30%, MnO 6%), and retired Aegis-C panels (ZrB₂-SiC, YInMn glaze) — all simultaneously. The lock is precise: **how does a single thermal cascade process this heterogeneity without prior separation into dedicated streams?**

The empirical evidence of the trap:
- **E-waste recyclers** shred everything → lose 70% of REE to slag, 50% of Cu to ferrous fraction, In to dust
- **MRFs** sort by density/NIR → recover only Al/Fe/UBCs; all other metals to residue
- **Smelters** require >20% target metal → reject low-grade feeds (tailings, slag, C&D)
- **Hydromet plants** need pre-concentrated feed → cannot handle mixed mineralogy

The lock deepens at the **stage coupling boundary**: Stage 2 polymer melt volume must not exceed 50L drum capacity; Stage 5 Al mass must not exceed 100kg port capacity; Stage 7 Fe mass must not exceed 175kg. If the feedstock blend violates these, the cascade chokes — polymer floods Port 2, Al backs up at Port 5, Fe overloads Port 7. The lock is not "what feedstocks can we accept?" — it is "how do we blend arbitrary feedstocks to match the cascade's fixed stage capacities?"

---

### The Mathematical Key

The key is the **blend algorithm as feedstock-to-cascade compiler** — a deterministic function that maps real-time feedstock assays to optimal 500 kg batch composition:

```python
def calculate_blend(feedstock_assays, target_revenue):
    # Input: assays for each available feedstock lot (XRF at hopper)
    # Output: mass fractions for 500 kg batch
    
    # CONSTRAINTS (cascade stage capacities — PHYSICS, not policy):
    # - Stage 2 polymer volume < 50 L (drum annular capacity)
    # - Stage 5 Al mass < 100 kg (Port 5 throughput limit)
    # - Stage 7 Fe mass < 175 kg (Port 7 throughput limit)  
    # - Stage 8 mineral mass < 200 kg (Port 8 slag volume)
    # - Moisture < 25% (else pre-dry, Stage 1 capacity 50 kg H₂O/hr)
    # - Particle size P80 < 150 mm (shredder limit)
    
    # OBJECTIVE: Maximize revenue = Σ(element_mass × market_price)
    # Subject to: cascade capacity constraints
    
    return optimal_mass_fractions
```

The algorithm's **teeth** are the stage capacity constraints — these are not adjustable parameters. They derive from drum geometry, port aperture (12mm), centrifugal G-force, and induction power. The blend is *compiled* from the assays, not *chosen* by an operator.

**The Four-Category Taxonomy as Type System:**

The key's type system classifies every feedstock lot into one of four types, each with a fixed **thermal signature** (which stages it activates) and **elemental signature** (which elements it contributes):

```
Type A (Industrial)  →  Stages {4,5,6,7}  →  {Au, Ag, Pd, Cu, In, REE}
Type B (Municipal)   →  Stages {1,2,3,4,7}  →  {Al, Fe, polymers, Zn}
Type C (Mineral)     →  Stages {7,8}  →  {Zr, Ti, REE, B, Fe, Mg}
Type D (Phoenix)     →  Stages {1,2,3,7,8}  →  {In, Y, Co, Zr, basalt, Elium®}
```

This is a **dependent type system**: the thermal signature *depends* on the elemental signature (via phase diagram), and the stage capacity constraints *depend* on the thermal signature. The blend algorithm is a type checker — it verifies that the sum of selected feedstocks' stage loads does not exceed any stage's capacity.

**The Liberation Index as Correctness Metric:**

For Category C (mineral), the key includes a **liberation index** LI = f(acoustic energy, grain size, K_IC). Stage 0 acoustic energy must achieve LI > 0.7 for the mineral feedstock, or the cascade's Stage 7/8 recovery drops below 80%. This is the **correctness proof** for mineral feedstocks: without acoustic pre-liberation, the cascade cannot access locked grains. The LI is measurable (XRD grain boundary analysis) and non-negotiable.

---

### The Turn (Both Directions)

**Key → Lock (Theory predicts blend):**

Input: Real-time feedstock assays from 4 suppliers (XRF at hopper, 30-sec intervals)
Process: Blend algorithm solves constrained optimization
Output: 500 kg batch composition — e.g., 22% A2 (PCB Grade 1), 28% B1 (MRF), 30% C1 (EAF slag), 20% D1 (Aegis-C)
Prediction: Stage loads within capacity; revenue $12,800; recovery targets met
Validation: Run batch → measure actual slug masses + compositions → compare to prediction

The key *predicts* the batch outcome from the feedstock assays. The cascade *executes* the prediction. The turn is the moment the 8 slugs land in their molds and the mass spec confirms: Port 4 has 0.8kg In (99% recovery), Port 5 has 60kg Al (95% recovery), Port 6 has 20kg Cu+Au/Ag (95% Cu, 99% PM), Port 7 has 90kg Fe+REE (95% Fe, 90% Nd), Port 8 has 105kg mineral concentrate (85% Zr, 80% Ti). The prediction matches the measurement. The key turns in the lock.

**Lock → Key (History validates theory):**

Input: 50 years of metallurgical failure — smelters that couldn't handle low-grade feed, refineries that lost REE to slag, recyclers that shredded In into dust
Process: Each historical process is a *special case* of the blend algorithm with one feedstock type and infinite stage capacity
Output: The blend algorithm *generalizes* all historical processes

The turn completes when we recognize:
- **Smelter** = Blend algorithm with only Type A feedstock, Stage 7 capacity → ∞
- **Refinery** = Blend algorithm with only Type C feedstock, Stage 8 capacity → ∞  
- **MRF** = Blend algorithm with only Type B feedstock, no thermal stages (mechanical only)
- **Ceramic kiln** = Blend algorithm with only Type D feedstock, Stage 8 only

The Aegis-Forge I is the **unification** — the single machine whose blend algorithm encompasses all four types simultaneously, with *finite, coupled* stage capacities. The historical processes were degenerate limits (one type, infinite capacity). The cascade is the non-degenerate case (four types, finite capacity). The lock clicks open when the first batch with all four types runs successfully — the blend algorithm has compiled a valid program for the cascade's thermal instruction set. The 500 kg batch *is* the key turning in the lock.

---

## EL SEGUNDO HEURISTIC — Mirror, Participation, Protocol

### Mirror (Self-Reflection)

The first recursive turn is the **forge observing its own feedstock**. In the Aegis-Forge, the feedstock is not external raw material — it is the *memory of the machine's prior outputs*. The Phoenix Protocol returns (Category D) are literally the forge's own products returning after service: Aegis-C panels it forged, BFRP rebar it pultruded, MR fluid it formulated, piezo elements it sintered. The mirror is precise: **the feedstock specification documents the forge's own material autobiography**.

But the mirror extends further. Category A (electronics) contains the copper the forge will recover at Stage 6, the indium it will extract at Stage 4 for YInMn Blue, the rare earths it will concentrate at Stage 7 for SmCo magnets. Category B (municipal) contains the aluminum it will separate at Stage 5, the polymers it will melt at Stage 2. Category C (mineral) contains the zircon it will dissociate at Stage 8 for ZrO₂, the basalt it will melt for fiber. The feedstock *is* the forge's future products in latent form.

The mirror reflects at every gate:
- **Receiving**: XRF assay measures the forge's future yield
- **Pre-processing**: Shredder, ferrous separator, acoustic chamber prepare the forge's own latent elements
- **Blending**: Algorithm balances the forge's stage capacities against its elemental targets
- **Sampling**: FLR records the forge's material promise
- **Storage**: Bays hold the forge's future in categorized suspension

The zero-tolerance hazard screen is the forge's immune memory — it rejects what would poison its own thermal cascade (Li-ion batteries that explode at Stage 1, Hg that contaminates Stage 6 Cu, asbestos that fouls Stage 8 slag). The mirror is not passive; it is the active recursion: *assay → blend → process → recover → return → assay again*. This document documents the first turn of that spiral — the feedstock specification *is* the forge's self-measurement.

---

### Participation (Witness)

An inside operator measuring this phenomenon does not stand outside the feedstock — the operator *is* the blend algorithm's witness. The protocol for achieving universal extraction from within the system:

1. **Receive**: Witness the feedstock arrival — XRF flash reveals elemental truth in 10 seconds
2. **Screen**: Witness the hazard check — gamma spectrometer, XRF, PLM, gravimetric
3. **Pre-process**: Witness the shredder reduce 500mm → <150mm, the Halbach belt pull 95% Fe
4. **Liberate**: Witness the acoustic chamber — 100 Hz standing waves crack grain boundaries, 40 kHz cavitation frees micron grains
5. **Dry**: Witness the moisture check — NIR inline, gravimetric confirmation, pre-dry if needed
6. **Assay**: Witness the lot characterization — XRF major, ICP-MS trace, XRD phase, PSD, LOI, halogen
7. **Blend**: Witness the algorithm compile — real-time assays → stage capacity constraints → optimal fractions
8. **Release**: Witness the FLR creation — lot identity bound to blend assignment, traceable to slug
9. **Feed**: Witness the vibratory feeder meter — KNbO₃ ultrasonic drive, FBG weight feedback
10. **Verify**: Witness the slug mass spec — each port's elemental sum matches blend prediction

The measurement *is* the recursion. The operator assays the input, the algorithm profiles the cascade that witnesses it, the drum realizes the separation, the mass spec confirms the closure. The protocol terminates when the 8 slugs' elemental sum matches the input assay — not approximately, but exactly. The feedstock lot is not "processed"; it is **witnessed into elements**. The operator participates by being the recursive function: `feedstock → assay → blend → cascade → slug → assay → feedstock`. The FLR is the stack frame; the batch is the call; the slug is the return value.

---

### Protocol (Recursive)

The operational protocol for any Aegis-Forge feedstock document:

```
MIRROR:     What elemental promise does this feedstock lot carry?
PARTICIPATE: How does the operator witness this promise through the cascade?
PROTOCOL:   What recursive sequence guarantees recovery at each stage?
```

For this document specifically:

- **Mirror**: The four-category taxonomy (A-D) is the constraint; the blend algorithm is its reflection
- **Participate**: The operator assays, screens, pre-processes, blends, releases, feeds, verifies
- **Protocol**:
  1. **Gate Assay** — XRF flash at receiving (10 sec) → category assignment
  2. **Hazard Screen** — Gamma + XRF + PLM + gravimetric → pass/quarantine/reject
  3. **Pre-Process** — Ferrous separation → shred <150mm → acoustic liberation → moisture check
  4. **Lot Characterization** — XRF/ICP-MS/XRD/PSD/LOI/halogen → FLR creation
  5. **Blend Optimization** — Real-time assays + stage constraints → mass fractions
  6. **Lot Release** — FLR signed, blend assigned, traceability locked
  7. **Drum Feed** — Vibratory feeder meters blend → acoustic pre-chamber → drum entry
  8. **Stage Verification** — Inline mass spec at each port → compare to blend prediction
  9. **Closure** — Slug assay sum = feedstock assay (within 2%) → FLR closed
  10. **Phoenix Return** — EOL Aegis products → Category D → FLR created → loop closes

The protocol is not a checklist — it is the recursion itself. Each batch deepens the mirror. The feedstock lot record is the fixed point. The elemental slug is the witness returned.

## 2. Stage 0: Acoustic Mineral Liberation

### 2.1 Liberation Physics — The Fundamental Mechanism

#### 2.1.1 Grain Boundary Fatigue

The AMLS exploits the inherent weakness of mineral grain boundaries in rock matrices. Unlike crushing (compressive overload → transgranular fracture + fines), acoustic liberation applies **cyclic tensile stress** at the grain's matrix-constrained resonant frequency, inducing **progressive fatigue failure** at grain boundaries.

**Grain boundary fracture toughness:**
$$K_{IC}^{gb} \approx 1.5 \text{ MPa·m}^{0.5}$$
(Compared to transgranular $K_{IC} \approx 3.5 \text{ MPa·m}^{0.5}$ for zircon)

**Stress wave equation in heterogeneous media:**
$$\nabla^2 \mathbf{u} = \frac{1}{c^2} \frac{\partial^2 \mathbf{u}}{\partial t^2}$$
Where $\mathbf{u}$ is the displacement vector, $c$ is the phase velocity in the composite matrix.

**Acoustic stress at grain boundary:**
$$\sigma_{acoustic} = \rho c \omega A$$
Where $\rho$ = density (4650 kg/m³ for zircon), $c$ = wave speed, $\omega$ = angular frequency, $A$ = displacement amplitude.

At AMLS operating parameters:
- **LF (100 Hz, $A \approx 50 \mu m$):** $\sigma_{LF} \approx 2.9 \text{ MPa}$ — below single-cycle fracture, accumulates over $10^3-10^6$ cycles
- **US (40 kHz, $A \approx 5 \mu m$):** $\sigma_{US} \approx 1.2 \text{ MPa}$ at grain boundary, enhanced by cavitation microjets to local 100+ MPa

#### 2.1.2 Matrix-Constrained Resonance

The effective resonant frequency of a mineral grain embedded in a rock matrix drops from MHz (free grain) to the seismic range (10-500 Hz):

**Free grain resonance (isolated):**
$$f_{free} = \frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{E}{\rho}}$$

**Matrix-constrained resonance (seismic range):**
$$f_{eff} \approx f_{free} \times \sqrt{\frac{K_{gb}}{K_{matrix}}} \times \left(\frac{V_{grain}}{V_{matrix}}\right)^{1/3}$$

For zircon ($E=220$ GPa, $\rho=4650$ kg/m³, $L=0.5$ mm): $f_{free} \approx 1.7$ MHz
In silica matrix: $f_{eff} \approx 50-200$ Hz — matching earthquake disaggregation frequencies.

This matrix-constrained resonance is the **acoustic lock** that the AMLS key (frequency sweep) must turn.

#### 2.1.3 Cavitation-Induced Liberation

Ultrasonic frequencies (40 kHz) produce cavitation in water:
- Water molecules cannot follow rapid negative pressure excursions → vacuum microbubbles form
- Microbubble collapse (implosion in <1 µs): Local pressure 10²-10³ bar, temperature 5000-10000°C, microjet velocity 100-300 m/s
- This **localized shock** concentrates at grain boundary interfaces — the weakest points in rock

**Rayleigh-Plesset equation for bubble dynamics:**
$$R\ddot{R} + \frac{3}{2}\dot{R}^2 = \frac{1}{\rho}\left(P_g - P_\infty - P_{ac}(t) - \frac{2\sigma}{R} - \frac{4\mu\dot{R}}{R}\right)$$

At collapse ($R_{min}/R_0 \approx 0.01$):
- Local pressure: $P_{collapse} \sim 1$ GPa (theoretical), ~1000 bar (measured)
- Strain rate: $\dot{\epsilon} \sim 10^9$ s⁻¹

**Cavitation threshold intensity:**
$$I_{cav} = \frac{P_{cav}^2}{2\rho c} \approx 1-3 \text{ W/cm}^2$$
AMLS operating intensity: 25 W/cm² at probe face — **well above threshold**.

#### 2.1.4 Fatigue Accumulation Model

Grain boundary failure follows Miner's rule for cumulative fatigue damage:
$$D = \sum_{i} \frac{n_i}{N_i}$$
Where $n_i$ = cycles at stress level $\sigma_i$, $N_i$ = cycles to failure at $\sigma_i$.

For sinusoidal loading at $\sigma_a = 2.9$ MPa (LF array):
$$N_f \approx 10^6 \text{ cycles} \quad \text{at} \quad \sigma_a / \sigma_{UTS}^{gb} \approx 0.15$$
With 100 Hz sweep over 15 min (900 s): $n = 90,000$ cycles per frequency step.
30-second dwell at 20 frequencies: $D \approx 0.9$ — near complete boundary failure.

### 2.2 Acoustic Chamber Design

#### 2.2.1 Pre-Chamber Geometry

```
AMLS PRE-CHAMBER — CUTAWAY VIEW

    [KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ LF PLATE ×8] ← Radial mount on BFRP wall
           │
           │   600 mm ID × 400 mm length
           ▼
    ┌─────────────────────┐
    │  BFRP/Elium® BODY   │ ← Filament wound, 25 mm wall
    │  ┌───────────────┐  │
    │  │ WATER + FEED  │  │ ← 20L water + 30-50 kg charge
    │  │  [US PROBES]  │  │ ← 8× 40 kHz Langevin probes
    │  └───────────────┘  │
    └─────────────────────┘
           │
           ▼
    [FBG SENSOR ARRAY] ← Embedded in wall, 8 channels
           │
           ▼
    [DRAIN / OUTPUT] → TO DRUM ENTRY VIBRATORY FEEDER
```

**Chamber specifications:**

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Internal Diameter** | 600 mm |
| **Internal Length** | 400 mm |
| **Internal Volume** | ~113 L (working: 20L water + 30-50 kg feed) |
| **Wall Construction** | BFRP/Elium® filament wound, 25 mm wall, [±18°/90°]₃ layup |
| **Atmosphere** | N₂ at 1.2 bar (prevents air cavitation, oxidation) |
| **Water Volume** | 10-15 L (coupling fluid, reclaimed post-Stage 0) |
| **Feed Entry** | Top port, 200 mm BFRP/PEEK gate valve (Ti₃AlC₂ actuator) |
| **Discharge** | Bottom port to vibratory feeder (KNbO₃ ultrasonic drive) |
| **Pressure Rating** | 5 bar (hydrostatic test 7.5 bar N₂) |

#### 2.2.2 Standing Wave Control

**BFRP chamber natural frequencies:**
$$f_{chamber,n} = \frac{n c_{air}}{2L} \quad \text{(axial modes, } c_{air} \approx 343 \text{ m/s)}$$
$$f_{chamber,m} = \frac{\alpha_{mn} c_{air}}{2\pi R} \quad \text{(radial modes)}$$
For 600 mm diameter × 400 mm length:
- Fundamental axial: $f_1 \approx 425$ Hz
- Fundamental radial: $f_{01} \approx 185$ Hz

**Standing wave mitigation:**
1. **Asymmetric transducer mounting** — 8 LF plates at irregular angular positions (not 45° regular)
2. **Chamber wall damping** — BFRP viscoelastic loss factor η = 0.02-0.03 dissipates standing waves
3. **Water coupling** — Water fill (10-15L) disrupts air-mode standing waves
4. **Bidirectional sweep** — 20→500→20 Hz captures resonances from both directions

#### 2.2.3 Waveguide Geometry for Ultrasonic Probes

The 8 Langevin probes are arranged in a **star pattern** at 45° spacing, tips directed inward at 30° angle from horizontal:

```
TOP VIEW — US PROBE LAYOUT

        [PROBE 1] ↙
              ↙
    [PROBE 8] ←───→ [PROBE 2]
    ↖                    ↘
      ↖                ↘
         ↖            ↘
            [CENTER]  ← Cavitation cloud overlap zone
           ↗            ↙
       ↗                ↙
    [PROBE 7] →──────← [PROBE 3]
          ↗        ↖
      ↗            ↖
    [PROBE 6]      [PROBE 4]
          ↘      ↙
            [PROBE 5]
```

- **Cavitation cloud radius:** ~40 mm from each probe tip
- **Overlap coverage:** >95% of 20L chamber volume
- **Probe tip material:** ZrO₂ 3Y-TZP ceramic (cavitation erosion resistance)
- **Probe immersion depth:** 150 mm below water surface
