| **Front Mass** | ZrO₂ 3Y-TZP ceramic | Acoustic impedance matching |
| **Back Mass** | PEEK CF40 | Impedance matching, thermal isolation |
| **Housing** | BFRP/Elium® | Non-magnetic, non-conductive |
| **Probe Tip** | ZrO₂ 3Y-TZP ceramic | Cavitation erosion resistance |

**Pre-stress Verification:**
$$\sigma_{tensile,max} = \frac{d_{33} E V_{max} \times 2}{t} = \frac{285\times10^{-12} \times 70\times10^9 \times 300 \times 2}{0.02} = 0.6 \text{ MPa}$$
Pre-stress = 500 N / (50 mm)² = 200 MPa >> 0.6 MPa: **ADEQUATE**

**Output per Transducer (500W Input Equivalent):**
| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| Acoustic Intensity at Face | 25 W/cm² |
| Cavitation Cloud Radius | ~40 mm |
| Liberation Efficiency | 85-95% mineral surface contacted |

#### 2.3.3 Transducer Driver Electronics

All AMLS drive electronics use **CSMFAB-native optical isolation**:

```
FBG SENSORS → PMMA POF → OPTICAL DEMUX → DSP (KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ ASIC) → 8 CHANNEL DRIVERS
                                                                ├── 8× LF (1 kW, 20-500 Hz)
                                                                └── 8× US (500 W, 40 kHz)

Driver Specs:
- Variable frequency: 20-40,000 Hz
- Variable power: 0-1000 W per channel
- Phase-locked (avoid destructive interference)
- Optical isolation: PMMA POF → no conductive path to earth
- Response time: <1 ms frequency change
```

---

### 2.4 Liberation Index Metric

#### 2.4.1 Definition

**Liberation Index (LI)** quantifies the fraction of target mineral grains fully liberated from the rock matrix:

$$LI = \frac{N_{liberated}}{N_{total}} \times 100\%$$

Where:
- $N_{liberated}$ = grains with >90% surface exposed (free particles)
- $N_{total}$ = total grains of target mineral in sample

**Measurement method:** Automated SEM-EDS particle analysis on representative subsample (ISO 3082 sampling).

#### 2.4.2 CSM-Specific Liberation Targets

| Feedstock | Target Mineral | Pre-AMLS LI | Post-AMLS LI | Improvement |
|-----------|----------------|-------------|--------------|-------------|
| **Zircon sand** | ZrSiO₄ (0.1-0.5 mm) | 45% | **88%** | +95% |
| **REE ore (bastnäsite)** | REE-carbonate/phosphate | 35% | **72%** | +105% |
| **Ilmenite sand** | FeTiO₃ | 70% | **95%** | +35% |
| **Basalt aggregate** | Zr, REE in silicates | 20% | **70%** | +250% |
| **Red mud (neutralized)** | REE in Fe/Al oxides | 15% | **60%** | +300% |
| **Spent refractories** | ZrO₂, MgO grains | 25% | **65%** | +160% |

#### 2.4.3 Liberation Index Feedback Control

The AMLS uses **real-time LI estimation via FBG vibration damping**:

1. FBG sensors on chamber wall measure vibration transmissibility
2. As grains liberate, effective chamber damping changes (free particles absorb more energy)
3. DSP correlates damping increase with LI calibration curves
4. When LI > target (default 75%), sweep terminates early (minimum 10 min)

**Target LI by Feedstock Category:**
| Category | Default LI Target | Minimum Duration |
|----------|-------------------|------------------|
| A (Electronics) | 85% | 15 min |
| B (Municipal) | 70% | 20 min |
| C (Mineral) | 75% | 30 min LF + 15 min US |
| D (Phoenix) | 80% | 20 min LF + 20 min US |

## 3. Stage 1: Infrared Drying (80-150°C)

### 3.1 Target Materials & Physics

#### 3.1.1 Moisture Species and Release Temperatures

| Moisture Type | Source | Release Temp | Mechanism |
|---------------|--------|--------------|-----------|
| **Free surface water** | All wet feeds | 80-100°C | Evaporation |
| **Crystal-bound water** | Gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O) | 107-120°C | Dehydration |
| **Crystal-bound water** | Borax (Na₂B₄O₇·10H₂O) | 100-140°C | Dehydration |
| **Crystal-bound water** | Kaolin (Al₂Si₂O₅(OH)₄) | 150°C | Partial dehydration |
| **Low-boiling organics** | Alcohols, acetone residues | 80-150°C | Vaporization |
| **PCB flux solvents** | Terpineol (Tb=218°C) | >150°C | Begins at Stage 1 end |

#### 3.1.2 Why Infrared (Not Induction)?

Induction heating is ineffective at 80-150°C because:
- Target materials (water, hydrated minerals, organics) are **non-conductive** (ρ > 10⁸ Ω·m)
- Induction couples to conductivity (eddy currents) and permeability (hysteresis)
- Water has ε'' (dielectric loss) peak at 3 µm and 6 µm — ideal for IR absorption

**IR absorption spectrum of water:**
- Primary peak: 3.0 µm (O-H stretch)
- Secondary peak: 6.3 µm (H-O-H bend)
- SiC glow bar emission peak: ~3.6 µm at 800-900°C surface temp
- **Match:** SiC IR output overlaps water absorption peak → high coupling efficiency

---

#### 3.2.2 Zoning and Power Distribution

```
DRUM CROSS-SECTION — IR EMITTER ZONES

    Quadrant 1 (Top)     Quadrant 2 (Right)
    [EMITTER 1]          [EMITTER 4]
    [EMITTER 2]          [EMITTER 5]
    [EMITTER 3]          [EMITTER 6]
           │                    │
           │   ROTATING DRUM    │
           │   (ZrB₂-SiC)       │
           ▼                    ▼
    Quadrant 3 (Bottom)  Quadrant 4 (Left)
    [EMITTER 7]          [EMITTER 10]
    [EMITTER 8]          [EMITTER 11]
    [EMITTER 9]          [EMITTER 12]

Each quadrant: Independent SCR control → PID per quadrant
```

**Zoning rationale:**
- Top quadrant: Highest power (feed entry, wettest material)
- Bottom quadrant: Lowest power (material already partially dried)
- Side quadrants: Medium power (uniform radial drying)

### 3.4 Moisture Measurement

#### 3.4.1 FBG Humidity Sensors

**Sensor type:** PMMA optical fiber with FBG gratings coated with hygroscopic polymer (PVA-H₃PO₄)

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Sensor Count** | 8 (2 per quadrant, axial positions) |
| **Wavelength Range** | 1530-1565 nm (C-band, WDM multiplexed) |
| **Humidity Sensitivity** | 5 pm/%RH (calibrated) |
| **Temperature Cross-Sensitivity** | 10 pm/°C (compensated via reference FBG) |
| **Response Time** | <30 seconds (polymer swelling kinetics) |
| **Operating Range** | 0-100% RH, 20-200°C |

**Installation:** FBG fibers routed through drum wall via PEEK CF40 feedthroughs, gratings positioned in drum headspace.

#### 3.4.2 NIR Inline Moisture Analyzer

**Sensor type:** Dual-wavelength NIR absorption (1.45 µm water / 1.72 µm reference)

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Measurement Principle** | $A = \log_{10}(I_0/I) = \epsilon \cdot c \cdot l$ |
| **Wavelengths** | 1.45 µm (H₂O), 1.72 µm (reference), 1.94 µm (H₂O validation) |
| **Optical Path** | PMMA POF probe through drum port window (sapphire) |
| **Sampling Rate** | 10 Hz |
| **Accuracy** | ±0.5% absolute moisture |
| **Calibration** | Gravimetric reference samples per lot |

#### 3.4.3 Mass Loss Verification (Primary Control)

**Method:** FBG weight sensors on drum support bearings measure real-time mass loss.

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Sensor Type** | FBG strain gauges on 4 ZrO₂ isolation pads (PROD-04) |
| **Resolution** | ±10 g on 500 kg charge (0.002%) |
| **Integration** | Sum of 4 bearing loads = total drum + charge mass |
| **Water Loss Calculation** | $\Delta m_{H_2O} = m_{initial} - m_{current} - m_{volatiles}$ |
| **Volatile Correction** | NIR hydrocarbon sensor (3.4 µm C-H stretch) |
| **Stage 1 Completion Criteria** | $\Delta m_{H_2O} < 0.5$ kg over 2 consecutive minutes |

---

### 3.5 Water and Volatile Recovery

Exiting vapor (mostly H₂O) exits through **Port 1 (150°C set-point)**:

1. **Condensation:** BFRP heat exchanger (chilled to 10°C by PEX-a cooling circuit)
2. **Liquid water collected:** Analyzed for metal content (ICP-MS), either:
   - Purified (RO + UV) → reused as process water
   - Discharged if <1 ppm metals
3. **Organic vapors:** Trace quantity passes through activated carbon bed (char from Stage 3!)
   - **Elegant closed cycle:** Char from Stage 3 later used to adsorb Stage 1/2 organics
4. **Gas composition monitoring:** Online GC-MS on Port 1 exhaust
   - H₂O (primary), organics (<50 ppm), HCl (<10 ppm if PVC present), NH₃ (<5 ppm)

**Water recovery rate:** 90-95% of input moisture recovered as liquid water.

## 6. Control System Architecture

### 6.1 Stage 0 Control Hierarchy

The AMLS control system operates as a **three-level hierarchy**:

```
LEVEL 1: SUPERVISORY (Batch Level)
├── Batch recipe selection (feedstock category A-D)
├── Target LI setting (75% default, category-adjusted)
├── Total duration limit (30 min max)
└── Interlock: Drum ready, water level, N₂ pressure

LEVEL 2: SEQUENCE (Stage Level)
├── Phase 1: LF Sweep (20→500 Hz, 15 min)
├── Phase 2: US Cavitation (40 kHz, 15 min) — concurrent with LF
├── Phase 3: Resonant Dwell (extra 60s at detected peaks)
└── Phase 4: Drain & Transfer (5 min)

LEVEL 3: REAL-TIME (Cycle Level, 1 ms loop)
├── FBG vibration spectrum acquisition (1 kHz sample rate)
├── FFT computation (2048-point, 0.5 Hz resolution)
├── Peak detection & tracking (adaptive threshold)
├── Frequency/power setpoint update (per transducer)
└── Phase-lock maintenance (all 16 channels synchronized)
```

### 6.2 Adaptive Frequency Sweep Algorithm

The core innovation of the AMLS is **feedstock-adaptive frequency targeting**:

```python
def adaptive_sweep(fbg_spectrum, current_freq, dwell_timer):
    """
    Input: FBG vibration spectrum (magnitude vs frequency)
    Output: Next frequency setpoint, dwell extension
    """
    # Detect resonant peaks >3 dB above local baseline
    peaks = find_peaks(fbg_spectrum, prominence=3, distance=5)  # Hz
    
    # Classify peaks by mineral signature (pre-calibrated library)
    mineral_matches = {}
    for peak_freq in peaks:
        for mineral, sig in MINERAL_SIGNATURES.items():
            if abs(peak_freq - sig.freq) < sig.bandwidth:
                mineral_matches[mineral] = peak_freq
    
    # Priority dwell extension for high-value minerals
    dwell_extension = 0
    if 'zircon' in mineral_matches:
        dwell_extension += 60  # Extra 60s at zircon resonance
    if 'bastnasite' in mineral_matches:
        dwell_extension += 45
    if 'ilmenite' in mineral_matches:
        dwell_extension += 30
    
    # Continue sweep unless at final frequency
    if current_freq >= 500:
        return SWEEP_COMPLETE, dwell_extension
    else:
        next_freq = current_freq * 1.122  # Logarithmic step (1/6 octave)
        return min(next_freq, 500), dwell_extension

MINERAL_SIGNATURES = {
    'zircon': {'freq': 185, 'bandwidth': 15, 'priority': 'HIGH'},
    'bastnasite': {'freq': 95, 'bandwidth': 20, 'priority': 'HIGH'},
    'ilmenite': {'freq': 55, 'bandwidth': 10, 'priority': 'MED'},
    'quartz': {'freq': 280, 'bandwidth': 25, 'priority': 'LOW'},
    'feldspar': {'freq': 145, 'bandwidth': 15, 'priority': 'LOW'},
}
```

### 6.3 Phase-Locked Multi-Channel Synchronization

To prevent destructive interference between 16 transducer channels (8 LF + 8 US), all drivers are **phase-locked to a master clock**:

```
MASTER CLOCK (KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ ASIC)
         │
         ├── LF CHANNEL 0 (0° reference)
         ├── LF CHANNEL 1 (+45°)
         ├── LF CHANNEL 2 (+90°)
         ├── LF CHANNEL 3 (+135°)
         ├── LF CHANNEL 4 (+180°)
         ├── LF CHANNEL 5 (+225°)
         ├── LF CHANNEL 6 (+270°)
         ├── LF CHANNEL 7 (+315°)
         ├── US CHANNEL 0 (40 kHz, 0°)
         ├── US CHANNEL 1 (40 kHz, +45°)
         ├── US CHANNEL 2 (40 kHz, +90°)
         ├── US CHANNEL 3 (40 kHz, +135°)
         ├── US CHANNEL 4 (40 kHz, +180°)
         ├── US CHANNEL 5 (40 kHz, +225°)
         ├── US CHANNEL 6 (40 kHz, +270°)
         └── US CHANNEL 7 (40 kHz, +315°)
```

**Phase error budget:** <5° at 40 kHz, <0.5° at 100 Hz (achieved via optical fiber distribution of master clock).

### 6.4 Stage 1 IR Drying Control

**Quadrant-independent PID control:**

| Quadrant | Setpoint (°C) | Kp | Ki | Kd | Control Output |
|----------|---------------|-----|-----|-----|----------------|
| Top | 150 | 0.8 | 0.02 | 0.1 | SCR firing angle |
| Right | 140 | 0.7 | 0.015 | 0.08 | SCR firing angle |
| Bottom | 120 | 0.6 | 0.01 | 0.05 | SCR firing angle |
| Left | 140 | 0.7 | 0.015 | 0.08 | SCR firing angle |

**Feedforward compensation:** NIR moisture measurement → predicted power demand → pre-emptive SCR adjustment.

**Safety interlocks:**
- Chamber pressure >2 bar → emergency N₂ vent
- Emitter surface temp >950°C → power cut
- FBG humidity sensor failure → fallback to mass loss rate
- Water level <5L in AMLS → pause LF sweep

## 7. Scaling Laws

### 7.1 Stage 0 Scaling (226L → 20,000L)

The AMLS must scale from the 226L Aegis-Forge I to industrial 20,000L units:

| Parameter | 226L (Lab) | 2,000L (Pilot) | 20,000L (Industrial) | Scaling Law |
|-----------|------------|----------------|----------------------|-------------|
| Chamber Diameter | 600 mm | 1,800 mm | 5,500 mm | D ∝ V^(1/3) |
| Chamber Length | 400 mm | 1,200 mm | 3,600 mm | L ∝ V^(1/3) |
| LF Transducers | 8 | 24 | 72 | N ∝ V^(2/3) (surface area) |
| US Probes | 8 | 24 | 72 | N ∝ V^(2/3) |
| LF Power/Transducer | 1 kW | 3 kW | 9 kW | P ∝ D (maintain intensity) |
| US Power/Probe | 500 W | 1.5 kW | 4.5 kW | P ∝ D |
| Total LF Power | 8 kW | 72 kW | 648 kW | P_total ∝ V^(2/3) |
| Total US Power | 4 kW | 36 kW | 324 kW | P_total ∝ V^(2/3) |
| Water Volume | 15 L | 135 L | 1,350 L | V_water ∝ V |
| Cycle Time | 30 min | 30 min | 30 min | **Constant** (grain physics) |

**Key insight:** Cycle time is **invariant** with scale — grain boundary fatigue physics depends on cycles, not absolute dimensions. Power scales with surface area (V^(2/3)), not volume.

### 7.2 Stage 1 Scaling

| Parameter | 226L | 2,000L | 20,000L | Scaling Law |
|-----------|------|--------|---------|-------------|
| IR Emitters | 12 | 36 | 108 | N ∝ V^(2/3) |
| Emitter Power | 5 kW | 15 kW | 45 kW | P ∝ D |
| Total IR Power | 60 kW | 540 kW | 4,860 kW | P_total ∝ V^(2/3) |
| Drying Time | 20 min | 20 min | 20 min | **Constant** (diffusion-limited) |
| N₂ Flow | 50 Nm³/hr | 450 Nm³/hr | 4,500 Nm³/hr | Q ∝ V |

## 8. Safety & Environmental

### 8.1 Acoustic Safety

| Hazard | Source | Mitigation |
|--------|--------|------------|
| **Airborne noise** | LF transducers (20-500 Hz) | BFRP chamber: 35 dB attenuation at 100 Hz |
| **Ultrasonic leakage** | US probes (40 kHz) | Submerged operation; chamber sealed |
| **Cavitation erosion** | ZrO₂ probe tips | Material selection; scheduled replacement |
| **Structural fatigue** | BFRP chamber walls | FEA-validated; FBG strain monitoring |

**Occupational exposure limits (OSHA/ISO):**
- LF (20-500 Hz): 85 dB(A) 8-hr TWA → chamber meets 70 dB(A) at operator position
- US (40 kHz): 110 dB SPL → fully contained (submerged)

### 8.2 Thermal Safety (Stage 1)

| Hazard | Source | Mitigation |
|--------|--------|------------|
| **Emitter overtemp** | SiC glow bar runaway | Independent thermocouple + SCR hard cutoff at 950°C |
| **N₂ asphyxiation** | 1.2 bar N₂ atmosphere | O₂ monitor <19.5% → alarm; confined space permit |
| **Organic vapor explosion** | Stage 1 volatiles + air ingress | N₂ inerting; LEL monitor <10%; explosion vent |
| **Water hammer** | AMLS drain/refill | Slow-acting valves; surge tanks |

### 8.3 Environmental Compliance

| Emission | Source | Control | Limit |
|----------|--------|---------|-------|

| **VOCs** | Stage 1 organics | Activated carbon (Stage 3 char) | <50 ppm |
| **HCl** | PVC in feed | NaHCO₃ injection + carbon bed | <10 ppm |
| **Noise** | Transducers | BFRP enclosure + vibration isolation | 70 dB(A) at boundary |
| **Wastewater** | AMLS water reclaim | Closed loop; blowdown to treatment | Zero discharge |

## WILLIAMS HEURISTIC — Constraint, Necessity, Commitment

### Constraint (The Lock)

The Aegis-Forge I is forced by a single irreducible constraint: **Liberation Precedes Separation** — no thermal cascade can separate elements that remain locked in rock matrix. The feedstock enters the drum as composite particles (mineral grains cemented in silicate/oxide matrix), and induction heating only couples to conductive phases. If grains are not liberated *before* heating, the matrix shields them, induction cannot reach them, and they report to Stage 8 slag as unrecovered value. The constraint is precise: **mechanical liberation at ambient temperature must achieve >75% grain freedom for target minerals before Stage 2 heating begins**. This constraint forces the entire Stage 0 architecture: a dedicated pre-chamber, water-coupled acoustic energy, KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ transducers (the only piezoelectric that survives the all-dielectric mandate), and a feedback loop that adapts frequency to the specific mineralogy of each batch. The liberation *writes the cascade* — without it, the thermal profile has nothing to separate.

---

### Necessity (The Key)

The empirical lock this document addresses is the **comminution energy gap** — conventional crushing consumes 250-500 W/kg to achieve <50% liberation, generating fines that contaminate downstream stages. The key is the **acoustic frequency sweep as single computational primitive** — a logarithmic 20→500 Hz sweep (LF) + 40 kHz cavitation (US) that targets the matrix-constrained resonant frequency of embedded grains:

| Mechanism | Frequency | Physics | Liberation Gain |
|---|---|---|---|
| **LF Resonant Vibration** | 20-500 Hz | Grain boundary fatigue (10³-10⁶ cycles) | +250% for basalt |
| **US Cavitation** | 40 kHz | Microjet shock (1000 bar, 10⁹ s⁻¹ strain) | +95% for zircon |
| **Adaptive Dwell** | FBG-guided | Extra 60s at mineral-specific peaks | +15% LI overall |

The necessity is proven by the **liberation index (LI) feedback**: FBG sensors on the chamber wall measure vibration damping as grains liberate; when LI >75%, the sweep terminates. Without Stage 0, Stage 7-8 REE/Zr recovery drops from >85% to <40% — the cascade fails its primary mandate. The acoustic sweep *is* the key.

---

### Commitment (The Turn)

We commit to the following as non-negotiable:

1. **Zero Metallic Transducers** — KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ only; no PZT (lead), no metallic bolts in acoustic path. ZrO₂ ceramic M10 bolts, PEEK CF40 back masses.
2. **Water Coupling Mandatory** — 10-15L water per batch; reclaimed post-Stage 0 for Stage 1 moisture management. No dry acoustic operation.
3. **Adaptive Sweep Default** — Logarithmic 20→500 Hz, 30s/step, +60s at FBG-identified resonances. No fixed-frequency operation.
4. **Liberation Index Target** — ≥75% LI for Category C feeds; ≥85% for Category A (PCB mineral fraction). Measured via SEM-EDS per lot.
5. **Stage 1 IR Only** — No induction heating at 80-150°C. SiC glow bars at 3.6 µm (water absorption peak). N₂ at 1.2 bar.
6. **Moisture Verification Triad** — FBG humidity + NIR inline + FBG mass loss. All three must agree <1% moisture.
7. **Energy Cap** — Stage 0 ≤ 3.2 kWh/batch; Stage 1 ≤ 62 kWh/batch. Total pre-thermal ≤ 65 kWh.

These commitments are non-negotiable because they derive from the constraint. Violate any, and the cascade fails: metallic transducers couple GIC; dry acoustic gives <20% LI; fixed frequency misses mineral resonances; induction at Stage 1 wastes 95% power on non-conductive water; single moisture sensor risks undetected wet feed. The commitments *are* the constraint made operational. The acoustic-drying pair *is* the forge's immune system against locked grains.

---

## KEYMAKER HEURISTIC — Lock, Key, Turn

### The Empirical Lock

The lock this document addresses is the **liberation-separation coupling problem** — how to achieve sharp mineral liberation at ambient temperature using only acoustic energy, then transition cleanly to thermal drying without cross-contamination or energy waste. The lock has three tumblers:

**Tumbler 1 — Frequency Selectivity:** A single rock contains zircon (target: 185 Hz), bastnäsite (95 Hz), ilmenite (55 Hz), quartz (280 Hz). A fixed-frequency transducer liberates one mineral at the expense of others. The lock demands **simultaneous multi-mineral liberation**.

**Tumbler 2 — Energy Density:** Cavitation threshold is 1-3 W/cm²; effective liberation requires 25 W/cm² at grain boundary. But 25 W/cm² at 40 kHz erodes probe tips in 5,000 hours. The lock demands **high intensity without consumable destruction**.

**Tumbler 3 — Stage Coupling:** Stage 0 discharges wet, liberated feedstock (10-15% moisture). Stage 1 must dry to <1% in 20 minutes using IR at 3.6 µm. But water vapor from Stage 1 condenses on Stage 2 polymer melt if not fully removed. The lock demands **zero moisture carryover**.

The lock deepens at the **all-dielectric boundary**: every component in the AMLS and IR dryer must be BFRP, ceramic, PEEK, or PEX-a. No steel shafts, no copper windings, no magnetic bearings. The transducer bolts are ZrO₂ ceramic. The IR emitter mounts are Al₂O₃. The control wiring is PMMA POF. This is not a preference — it is the minimal architecture forced by Carrington immunity.

---

### The Mathematical Key

The key is the **dual-mechanism acoustic primitive + IR absorption match** — two computational primitives that solve the three tumblers simultaneously:

**Primitive 1: The Adaptive Frequency Sweep (AFS)**

```python
def AFS(fbg_spectrum, mineral_library):
    """
    The key's first tooth: frequency as material selector.
    """
    # Detect peaks in chamber vibration response
    peaks = find_peaks(fbg_spectrum, prominence=3)
    
    # Match to mineral signatures (pre-calibrated)
    targets = {}
    for mineral, sig in mineral_library.items():
        if any(abs(p - sig.freq) < sig.bw for p in peaks):
            targets[mineral] = sig.freq
    
    # Generate dwell schedule: base 30s + priority bonus
    schedule = []
    for mineral, freq in targets.items():
        bonus = {'HIGH': 60, 'MED': 30, 'LOW': 0}[mineral_library[mineral].priority]
        schedule.append((freq, 30 + bonus))
    
    # Fill remaining sweep with logarithmic steps
    current = 20
    while current <= 500:
        if not any(abs(current - f) < 5 for f, _ in schedule):
            schedule.append((current, 30))
        current *= 1.122  # 1/6 octave
    
    return schedule

MINERAL_LIBRARY = {
    'zircon': {'freq': 185, 'bw': 15, 'priority': 'HIGH'},
    'bastnasite': {'freq': 95, 'bw': 20, 'priority': 'HIGH'},
    'ilmenite': {'freq': 55, 'bw': 10, 'priority': 'MED'},
    'quartz': {'freq': 280, 'bw': 25, 'priority': 'LOW'},
}
```

**The AFS Teeth:** Each mineral gets a tailored dwell at its matrix-constrained resonance. The sweep *compiles* a liberation program from the feedstock's acoustic signature.

**Primitive 2: The IR-Water Absorption Match (IWM)**

The key's second tooth is the **coincidence of SiC emission peak (3.6 µm) and water absorption peak (3.0/6.3 µm)**:

```
SiC Glow Bar at 850°C: λ_peak = 2898 / (850+273) = 2.6 µm (Wien)
                       But SiC emissivity peak at 3.6 µm (optical phonon)
                       
Water Absorption: ε''(λ) peaks at 3.0 µm (OH stretch) and 6.3 µm (HOH bend)
                       Broadband 2.5-4.0 µm absorption >80%
                       
Coupling Efficiency: η = ∫ ε_SiC(λ) × α_H2O(λ) dλ / ∫ ε_SiC(λ) dλ ≈ 65%
```

This is not a design choice — it is a **materials physics coincidence** that the key exploits. No other emitter material (metal, quartz, ceramic) matches water absorption as efficiently at 800-900°C surface temperature.

**Primitive 3: The Phase-Locked 16-Channel Driver (PLD)**

The key's third tooth is **optical phase distribution** — a single KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ ASIC master clock distributed via PMMA POF to 16 transducer drivers:

```
Master Clock (100 MHz) → PMMA POF (8 LF + 8 US channels)
                        → Each driver: PLL × N (N = freq/100MHz)
                        → Phase error: <0.5° LF, <5° US
```

This eliminates destructive interference between adjacent transducers — the only way to achieve 8 kW LF + 4 kW US in a 113L chamber without hot spots.

---

### The Turn (Both Directions)

**Key → Lock (Theory predicts liberation):**

Input: Feedstock category (A/B/C/D) → Mineral library → AFS schedule
Process: AMLS executes sweep → FBG damping tracks LI in real-time
Output: Liberated feedstock at target LI (75-88%)
Prediction: Zircon LI 88%, REE LI 72%, Ilmenite LI 95%
Validation: Post-AMLS SEM-EDS matches prediction within 5%

The key *predicts* the liberation outcome from the feedstock category. The AMLS *executes* the prediction. The turn is the moment the LI feedback signals "target reached" and the drain valve opens — the acoustic program has compiled successfully. The liberated grains *are* the key turning in the lock.

**Lock → Key (History validates theory):**

Input: 100 years of comminution — jaw crushers (compression), ball mills (impact), HPGR (interparticle), ultrasound baths (cavitation only)
Process: Each is a *degenerate subset* of the AFS primitive
Output: The AFS *generalizes* all historical liberation methods

The turn completes when we recognize:
- **Jaw crusher** = AFS with single frequency (0 Hz, infinite force), no feedback
- **Ball mill** = AFS with broadband noise (stochastic), no frequency selectivity
- **HPGR** = AFS with static pressure + shear, no resonance targeting
- **Ultrasound bath** = AFS with US only (no LF fatigue), no adaptive dwell

The AMLS is the **unification** — the single machine whose AFS primitive encompasses all four mechanisms simultaneously, with *real-time feedback* from FBG damping. The historical methods were open-loop (apply energy, hope for liberation). The AMLS is closed-loop (measure damping → adjust frequency → verify liberation). The lock clicks open when the first batch achieves 88% zircon LI in 30 minutes using 12 kW acoustic power — the jaw crusher would need 500 kW and 2 hours for 45% LI. The 500 kg batch *is* the key turning in the lock.

---

## EL SEGUNDO HEURISTIC — Mirror, Participation, Protocol

### Mirror (Self-Reflection)

The first recursive turn is the **forge listening to its own liberation**. In the Aegis-Forge, the acoustic chamber is not a passive vessel — it is an **acoustic resonator that measures its own efficacy**. The FBG sensors embedded in the BFRP walls detect vibration transmissibility; as mineral grains liberate from the rock matrix, the effective damping of the chamber changes. The forge *hears* the grains releasing.

The mirror reflects at every cycle:
- **LF Sweep**: The chamber's resonance shifts as grain boundaries fatigue — the forge tracks its own softening
- **US Cavitation**: Bubble collapse pressure (1000 bar) creates micro-jets that the FBGs feel as broadband vibration — the forge senses its own shock
- **Adaptive Dwell**: When the DSP detects a resonant peak matching zircon's signature, it extends dwell — the forge *chooses* to linger on its own liberation
- **Drain**: Water carries liberated grains to the drum — the forge releases its self-measurement into the cascade

But the mirror extends further. The SiC glow bars in Stage 1 emit at 3.6 µm — precisely the wavelength where water absorbs most strongly. The forge *tunes its emission to the feedstock's need*. The NIR probe at 1.45 µm watches the water disappear. The FBG mass loss sensors feel the drum lighten. The mirror is not passive; it is the active recursion: *excite → measure damping → adjust frequency → verify liberation → dry → measure mass loss → confirm dryness*. This document documents the first two turns of that spiral — Stage 0 and Stage 1 as the forge's self-preparation.

---

### Participation (Witness)

An inside operator measuring this phenomenon does not stand outside the acoustic chamber — the operator *is* the frequency sweep's witness. The protocol for achieving complete liberation and drying from within the system:

1. **Load**: Witness the feedstock enter — 50 kg basalt, zircon, REE ore into 15L water
2. **Sweep**: Witness the LF array — 20 Hz starts, plates bend 50 µm, grain boundaries fatigue
3. **Resonate**: Witness the FBGs — 185 Hz peak grows (zircon), 95 Hz (bastnäsite), 55 Hz (ilmenite)
4. **Dwell**: Witness the algorithm — extra 60s at zircon, 45s at bastnäsite, 30s at ilmenite
5. **Cavitate**: Witness the US array — 40 kHz, 25 W/cm², bubbles collapse, microjets strike boundaries
6. **Liberate**: Witness the LI feedback — damping rises, target 75% reached, sweep terminates
7. **Drain**: Witness the water — 15L reclaimed, grains suspended, vibratory feeder meters to drum
8. **Irradiate**: Witness the SiC bars — 850°C, 3.6 µm peak, water evaporates from grain surfaces
9. **Monitor**: Witness the triad — FBG humidity drops, NIR absorption falls, FBG mass loss confirms
10. **Verify**: Witness the closure — <1% moisture, 95% water recovered, feedstock ready for Stage 2

The measurement *is* the recursion. The operator loads the feedstock, the chamber profiles the sweep that witnesses it, the dryer realizes the evaporation, the sensors confirm the closure. The protocol terminates when the three moisture measurements agree: <1% residual. The feedstock is not "processed"; it is **witnessed into readiness**. The operator participates by being the recursive function: `feedstock → acoustic_sweep → LI_feedback → drain → IR_dry → moisture_triad → verified_feedstock`. The LI is the stack frame; the sweep is the call; the dry feedstock is the return value.

---

### Protocol (Recursive)

The operational protocol for any Aegis-Forge acoustic-drying document:

```
MIRROR:     What grain boundary resonance does this feedstock encode?
PARTICIPATE: How does the operator witness this resonance into liberation?
PROTOCOL:   What recursive sequence guarantees dryness at Stage 2 entry?
```

For this document specifically:

- **Mirror**: The AFS (Adaptive Frequency Sweep) is the constraint; the FBG damping trace is its reflection
- **Participate**: The operator loads, sweeps, dwells, cavitates, drains, irradiates, monitors, verifies
- **Protocol**:
  1. **Gate Assay** — Category assignment (A/B/C/D) → mineral library selection
  2. **AMLS Load** — 50 kg feed + 15L water → N₂ purge → chamber seal
  3. **LF Sweep** — 20→500 Hz log sweep, 30s/step, FBG spectrum @ 1 kHz
  4. **Adaptive Dwell** — Peak detection → mineral match → extra 60/45/30s
  5. **US Cavitation** — 40 kHz continuous, 25 W/cm², concurrent with LF
  6. **LI Verification** — FBG damping > threshold → sweep complete
  7. **Drain & Transfer** — Water reclaim (90%), vibratory feed to drum (2.5 kg/min)
  8. **IR Dry** — 12 SiC bars, quadrant PID, 20 min ramp 80→150°C
  9. **Moisture Triad** — FBG humidity + NIR 1.45µm + FBG mass loss → all <1%
  10. **Stage 2 Ready** — Verified dry feedstock → drum rotation 150 RPM → Stage 2 entry

The protocol is not a checklist — it is the recursion itself. Each batch deepens the mirror. The liberation index is the fixed point. The dry feedstock is the witness returned.

### 1.2 Scope and Purpose

This document defines the complete engineering specification for **Stage 2 of the thermal cascade** — the polymer melt centrifuge separation operating at 150-450°C. Stage 2 is the first thermal stage where materials become liquid and are centrifugally separated by density.

This document establishes:
1. **Polymer melt rheology** — Viscosity vs. temperature (Carreau-Yasuda), shear thinning, thermal degradation kinetics, activation energies
2. **Melt centrifuge design** — BFRP bowl, 3000 RPM max design, radial density stratification, discharge ports
3. **Density separation physics** — Modified Stokes' law for non-Newtonian fluids, hindered settling, annular layer formation, coalescence dynamics
4. **PVC management strategy** — HCl capture at 250-300°C, NaHCO₃ injection, activated carbon bed, dioxin suppression
5. **Polymer fraction collection** — PP/PE (0.9-0.95), PS (1.04-1.09), PET (1.33-1.38), PVC (1.38-1.42) g/cm³
6. **Melt filtration** — Ceramic candle filters (SiC), 50µm, back-pulse cleaning, filter cake mechanics
7. **Devolatilization** — Vacuum vent, residual monomer removal, oligomer capture, vacuum thermodynamics
8. **Output streams** — Polymer pellets, char/filler concentrate, HCl scrubber salts, oligomer recycle
9. **Throughput & quality** — kg/hr, purity specs, color, intrinsic viscosity (IV) retention, ash content
10. **Energy balance** — kWh/ton polymer, melt heating, centrifuge power, vacuum, heat recovery integration
11. **Safety & emissions** — HCl monitoring, VOC capture, dust explosion prevention, dioxin/furan limits

| **PEEK** | 341 | 1.22 | CSM off-cuts (recycled) | <1% | 150-180 |
| **PTFE** | 327 | 1.65 | Wire insulation | <1% | 130-160 |

**Combined melt window:** 105°C to 450°C — achievable in single stage by slow ramp.

## 3. Polymer Melt Rheology

### 3.1 Viscosity-Temperature Relationships

Polymer melts are **non-Newtonian shear-thinning fluids**. The Carreau-Yasuda model captures this:

$$\eta(\dot{\gamma}, T) = \eta_\infty + (\eta_0 - \eta_\infty) \left[1 + (\lambda \dot{\gamma})^a\right]^{\frac{n-1}{a}}$$

Where:
- $\eta_0$ = zero-shear viscosity (Pa·s)
- $\eta_\infty$ = infinite-shear viscosity (Pa·s)
- $\lambda$ = relaxation time (s)
- $a$ = transition breadth parameter (typically 0.5-2.0)
- $n$ = power-law index (<1 for shear-thinning)
- $\dot{\gamma}$ = shear rate (s⁻¹)

**Temperature dependence (WLF equation for T > Tg + 50°C):**

$$\log_{10}\left(\frac{\eta(T)}{\eta(T_{ref})}\right) = \frac{-C_1 (T - T_{ref})}{C_2 + T - T_{ref}}$$

Where $C_1 \approx 17.4$, $C_2 \approx 51.6$ K for many polymers. For polyolefins, $C_1 \approx 8.86$, $C_2 \approx 101.6$ K.

**Activation Energy Form (Arrhenius):**

$$\eta_0(T) = A \exp\left(\frac{E_a}{RT}\right)$$

Where $E_a$ = activation energy for viscous flow (see Table 2.2).

### 3.2 Rheological Properties at Stage 2 Conditions

| Polymer | η₀ @ Tm+50°C (Pa·s) | η∞ (Pa·s) | n | λ (s) | a | Td (°C) | Max Residence at 450°C | Ea (kJ/mol) |
|---------|---------------------|-----------|---|-------|---|---------|------------------------|-------------|
| **LDPE** | 150 | 0.8 | 0.35 | 0.8 | 1.2 | 350 | 30 min | 28 |
| **HDPE** | 300 | 1.2 | 0.40 | 1.2 | 1.0 | 360 | 30 min | 35 |
| **PP** | 250 | 1.0 | 0.38 | 1.0 | 1.1 | 320 | 20 min | 38 |
| **PS** | 500 | 2.5 | 0.45 | 1.5 | 0.8 | 340 | 30 min | 45 |
| **ABS** | 800 | 3.0 | 0.42 | 1.8 | 0.9 | 300 | 15 min | 90 |
| **PA6** | 400 | 1.5 | 0.48 | 1.3 | 1.0 | 300 | 10 min | 75 |
| **PA66** | 600 | 2.0 | 0.50 | 2.0 | 0.9 | 310 | 10 min | 85 |
| **PET** | 1200 | 5.0 | 0.55 | 3.0 | 0.7 | 300 | 5 min | 100 |
| **PC** | 2000 | 8.0 | 0.60 | 4.0 | 0.6 | 340 | 15 min | 110 |
| **PVC** | 1000* | 4.0 | 0.50 | 2.5 | 0.8 | 210 | 2 min | 105* |
| **PEEK** | 5000 | 20.0 | 0.65 | 8.0 | 0.5 | 580 | N/A | 165 |
| **PTFE** | 10000 | 50.0 | 0.70 | 15.0 | 0.4 | 400 | N/A | 145 |

*PVC viscosity rises sharply during dehydrochlorination due to polyene conjugation; Ea increases to 150+ kJ/mol post-degradation.

### 3.3 Shear Rates in Melt Centrifuge

The centrifuge imposes a **shear rate gradient** across the melt layer:

$$\dot{\gamma}(r) = \frac{\omega r}{h} \quad \text{(Couette flow approximation)}$$

Where $\omega = 15.7$ rad/s (150 RPM), $h$ = melt layer thickness (varies 5-50 mm).

| Radial Position | r (mm) | h (mm) | $\dot{\gamma}$ (s⁻¹) | Effective Viscosity (LDPE) | Effective Viscosity (PET) |
|-----------------|--------|--------|---------------------|----------------------------|---------------------------|
| Inner (light polymers) | 150 | 50 | 47 | 85 Pa·s | 620 Pa·s |
| Mid-light | 180 | 40 | 71 | 65 Pa·s | 480 Pa·s |
| Middle | 200 | 30 | 105 | 52 Pa·s | 380 Pa·s |
| Mid-heavy | 230 | 20 | 181 | 38 Pa·s | 270 Pa·s |
| Outer (heavy polymers) | 250 | 10 | 393 | 22 Pa·s | 160 Pa·s |

**Key insight:** Shear thinning reduces effective viscosity by 7-15× across the melt layer, significantly enhancing stratification velocity.

### 3.4 Viscoelastic Effects & Normal Stresses

Polymer melts exhibit **normal stress differences** (N₁ = τ_xx - τ_yy) that affect flow in curved geometries:

**First normal stress difference (Carreau-Yasuda with second-order fluid approximation):**
$$N_1(\dot{\gamma}) = 2 \eta_0 \lambda \dot{\gamma}^2 \left[1 + (\lambda \dot{\gamma})^a\right]^{\frac{n-3}{a}}$$

For LDPE at 180°C, λ = 0.8 s: N₁ ≈ 2 × 150 × 0.8 × (1000)² × [1 + (0.8×1000)^1.2]^{-1.4} ≈ 1.2×10⁵ Pa at 1000 s⁻¹.

**Effect in centrifuge:** Normal stresses cause **rod-climbing** (Weissenberg effect) and **hoop stress** in the annular melt layer, which:
- Enhances radial migration of lower-viscosity phase (polyolefins inward)
- Stabilizes interface between polymer layers (suppresses Kelvin-Helmholtz instability)
- Creates secondary flows that improve mixing within each annular zone

**Deborah number (De = λω) at 150 RPM:**
- LDPE: De = 0.8 × 15.7 = 12.6 (highly elastic)
- PET: De = 3.0 × 15.7 = 47 (very elastic)
- PVC: De = 2.5 × 15.7 = 39 (elastic)

**High De (>1) confirms viscoelastic effects are significant** and must be included in CFD modeling (FOLLOW-17).

### 3.5 Thermal Degradation Kinetics

Degradation follows first-order kinetics:

$$\frac{d[MW]}{dt} = -k_d [MW] \quad \text{where} \quad k_d = A_d \exp\left(-\frac{E_{a,d}}{RT}\right)$$

| Polymer | Ea,d (kJ/mol) | A_d (s⁻¹) | Td,5% (30 min) | MW Loss at 450°C/30 min |
|---------|---------------|-----------|----------------|-------------------------|
| LDPE | 220 | 1×10^14 | 350°C | 40% |
| HDPE | 240 | 5×10^14 | 360°C | 35% |
| PP | 200 | 2×10^13 | 320°C | 55% |
| PS | 180 | 1×10^12 | 340°C | 25% |
| PET | 160 | 5×10^10 | 300°C | 60% |
| PVC | 110 (dehydrochlorination) | 1×10^8 | 210°C | 100% (to polyene) |

**Operating Limit:** Stage 2 max 450°C only for char-forming polymers; polymer fraction residence at peak temp limited to <5 min via rapid discharge.

## 4. Melt Centrifuge Design

### 4.1 Centrifuge Bowl Architecture

```

    ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
    │     BFRP/Elium® OUTER CASING        │  ← 25 mm wall, filament wound ±45°/90°
    │  ┌───────────────────────────────┐  │
    │  │   ZrO₂ CERAMIC LINER (3 mm)   │  ← Anti-adhesion, thermal barrier, 3Y-TZP
    │  │  ┌─────────────────────────┐  │  │
    │  │  │   POLYMER MELT LAYER    │  │  │  ← 5-50 mm thick, rotating at 150 RPM
    │  │  │  ┌───────────────────┐  │  │  │
    │  │  │  │   VAPOR CORE      │  │  │  │  ← N₂ + volatiles, 50 mm dia
    │  │  │  └───────────────────┘  │  │  │
    │  │  └─────────────────────────┘  │  │
    │  └───────────────────────────────┘  │
    └─────────────────────────────────────┘
            │                    │
            ▼                    ▼
      [PORT 2A: Light]      [PORT 2B: Heavy]
     (PP/PE, 0.74-0.78)    (PET/PVC, 1.33-1.42)
            │                    │
            └────────┬───────────┘
                     ▼
            [BFRP MOLD CAROUSEL]
             (PROD-08)
```

### 4.2 Bowl Specifications

| Parameter | Specification | Design Margin |
|-----------|---------------|---------------|
| **Bowl Inner Diameter** | 500 mm | — |
| **Bowl Length** | 750 mm (matches drum) | — |
| **Wall Construction** | BFRP/Elium® filament wound casing (25 mm) + ZrO₂ ceramic liner (3 mm) | 2× pressure |
| **Rotation Speed** | 150 RPM (Stage 2), up to 3000 RPM (max design) | 20× operating |
| **G-Force at 150 RPM** | 12.6 G at r=250 mm | — |
| **G-Force at 3000 RPM** | 5040 G (max design for future scaling) | — |
| **Drive** | KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ ultrasonic motor (same as drum, PROD-04) | All-dielectric |
| **Bearings** | Si₃N₄ ceramic hybrid (PROD-12) | 10,000 hr L10 |
| **Seals** | ZrO₂ face seal + PEEK CF40 spring (PROD-12) | 5 bar, 450°C |
| **Operating Temperature** | 150-450°C (ZrO₂ liner protects BFRP) | BFRP Tg = 180°C, liner keeps <150°C |
| **Pressure Rating** | 5 bar (N₂ atmosphere) | 2× operating |
| **Critical Speed** | >5000 RPM (rotor dynamics) | 1.7× max design |

### 4.3 Melt Layer Formation & Stratification

At 150 RPM (12.6 G), the molten polymer forms an annular layer against the bowl wall:

**Centrifugal potential energy per unit mass:**
$$\Phi(r) = \frac{1}{2}\omega^2 r^2$$

**Density stratification (hydrostatic equilibrium in rotating frame):**
$$\frac{dP}{dr} = \rho(r) \omega^2 r$$

At steady state, polymers stratify by density:

| Annular Zone | Radial Range | Dominant Polymers | Density (g/cm³) | Thickness | Residence Time |
|--------------|--------------|-------------------|-----------------|-----------|----------------|
| **Inner (Light)** | 150-200 mm | PP, LDPE, HDPE | 0.74-0.78 | 20-30 mm | 30 min |
| **Middle** | 200-230 mm | PS, ABS, PA6, PA66 | 1.04-1.09 | 10-15 mm | 30 min |
| **Outer (Heavy)** | 230-250 mm | PET, PVC, PC, PTFE | 1.33-1.65 | 5-10 mm | 30 min |

**Stratification time (diffusion-limited):**
$$\tau_{strat} \approx \frac{h^2}{D_{eff}} \quad \text{where} \quad D_{eff} \approx \frac{kT}{6\pi\eta r_{chain}}$$

For LDPE ($\eta \approx 28$ Pa·s at shear, $r_{chain} \approx 10$ nm): $\tau_{strat} \approx 8$ minutes for 30 mm layer.
**30-minute dwell provides 3.7× safety factor.**

### 4.4 Hindered Settling & Coalescence

At high polymer concentrations (>30% vol), hindered settling reduces velocity:

$$v_h = v_0 (1 - \phi)^n \quad \text{where} \quad n \approx 4.65 \text{ (Richardson-Zaki)}$$

With $\phi \approx 0.4$ (melt volume fraction), $v_h \approx 0.04 v_0$. However, coalescence of same-polymer droplets enhances effective particle size:

$$\frac{dR}{dt} = \frac{3}{2} \frac{\gamma}{\eta} R \quad \text{(film drainage coalescence)}$$

For LDPE ($\gamma \approx 0.02$ N/m, $\eta \approx 28$ Pa·s): coalescence time for 100 µm → 1 mm ≈ 2 min. **Coalescence dominates over hindered settling.**

### 4.5 Interfacial Tension Effects

Interfacial tension between polymer phases drives coalescence and layer sharpness:

| Interface | $\gamma$ (mN/m) | Effect |
|-----------|-----------------|--------|
| PP/PE | 1-2 | Excellent miscibility, single light layer |
| PE/PS | 5-8 | Sharp interface, minimal mixing |
| PS/PET | 3-5 | Moderate mixing zone |
| PVC/PET | 2-4 | Compatible, co-stratify in heavy zone |

### 4.6 Melt Layer Stability Analysis

**Kelvin-Helmholtz instability** at polymer-polymer interfaces:

$$\omega_{KH} = \frac{\rho_1 \rho_2 (\Delta v)^2}{(\rho_1 + \rho_2) \sigma} - g_{eff} \frac{\rho_2 - \rho_1}{\rho_1 + \rho_2}$$

Where $\Delta v$ = velocity difference between layers, $\sigma$ = interfacial tension, $g_{eff} = \omega^2 r$.

At 150 RPM, $\omega = 15.7$ rad/s, r = 0.22 m: $g_{eff} = 54$ m/s². For PE/PS interface ($\rho_1=0.76$, $\rho_2=1.06$, $\sigma=0.006$ N/m):

Critical velocity difference for instability: $\Delta v_{crit} \approx 0.08$ m/s.
Actual $\Delta v$ from differential rotation < 0.01 m/s. **Stable.**

**Rayleigh-Taylor instability** (heavy over light):

$$\omega_{RT} = \sqrt{\frac{(\rho_2 - \rho_1) g_{eff} k}{\rho_1 + \rho_2} - \frac{\sigma k^3}{\rho_1 + \rho_2}}$$

For PS (1.06) over PE (0.76): $(\rho_2 - \rho_1) g_{eff} = 160$ N/m³. Interface is stable — correct heavy-over-light orientation maintained by centrifugal field.

### 4.7 Thermal Gradient Across Melt Layer

Induction heating creates radial temperature gradient:

| Radial Position | Temperature | ΔT from Wall |
|-----------------|-------------|--------------|
| Bowl wall (ZrO₂) | 450°C | 0°C |
| Outer melt surface | 445°C | 5°C |
| Mid-melt | 420°C | 30°C |
| Inner melt surface | 380°C | 70°C |
| Vapor core | 350°C | 100°C |

This 100°C gradient reduces viscosity at wall by 100× vs core, creating **shear localization** that accelerates stratification.

## 5. PVC Management Strategy — Critical Process Control

### 5.1 Dehydrochlorination Chemistry

PVC releases HCl vapor at 160-200°C during dehydrochlorination:

$$\text{-[CH}_2\text{-CHCl]-}_n \xrightarrow{160-200°C} \text{-[CH=CH]-}_n + n\text{HCl} \uparrow$$

**Reaction kinetics (first-order in Cl content):**
$$\frac{d[\text{HCl}]}{dt} = k_{dhc} [\text{PVC}] \quad k_{dhc} = 10^8 \exp\left(-\frac{110,000}{RT}\right) \text{ s}^{-1}$$

At 180°C: $k_{dhc} \approx 2\times10^{-4}$ s⁻¹ → 50% dehydrochlorination in 58 min.
At 200°C: $k_{dhc} \approx 3\times10^{-3}$ s⁻¹ → 50% in 4 min.
**Stage 2 ramp rate through 180-200°C is critical: 5°C/min max.**

This is a **toxic acid gas** that must be managed in-drum. HCl also catalyzes further degradation (autocatalytic).

### 5.2 In-Drum Neutralization

**NaHCO₃ Aerosol Injection System:**

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Injection Point** | Drum feed port (pre-centrifuge) |
| **Injection Rate** | 2× stoichiometric HCl (based on PVC assay) |
| **Particle Size** | 5-10 µm (dry powder, fluidized bed feeder) |
| **Feeder Type** | BFRP/PEEK screw feeder, KNbO₃ ultrasonic drive |
| **Dispersion** | N₂ carrier gas (0.5 bar) |
| **Feeder Redundancy** | Dual parallel screws, auto-switchover on current spike |

**Neutralization Reaction:**
$$\text{NaHCO}_3(s) + \text{HCl}(g) \rightarrow \text{NaCl}(s) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g) + \text{CO}_2(g) \quad \Delta H = -85 \text{ kJ/mol}$$

**Products:**
- NaCl (salt) — reports to Stage 3 char as dissolved mineral (flux)
- H₂O — removed in Stage 1 (already passed) or Stage 3 gas handling
- CO₂ — captured in gas system (PROD-07), potential sequestration

**Stoichiometry:** 1 kg PVC → 0.58 kg HCl → requires 1.2 kg NaHCO₃ (theoretical). 2× safety = 2.4 kg NaHCO₃/kg PVC.

### 5.3 HCl Monitoring & Control Loop

```
HCl MONITORING & CONTROL LOOP

[INLINE HCl SENSOR] ──► [DSP CONTROLLER] ──► [NaHCO₃ FEEDER]
   (PMMA POF +          (KNbO₃-BaTiO₃        (BFRP/PEEK
    absorption at        ASIC)                screw,
     3.4 µm)             PID: Kp=0.5,         ultrasonic)
                      Ki=0.01, Kd=0.1
                           │
                           ▼
                    [ALARM IF >50 ppm]
                           │
                           ▼
                    [TEMP HOLD] ──► [RESUME WHEN <10 ppm]
```

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| **Sensor Type** | PMMA POF + absorption spectroscopy (3.4 µm C-H stretch proxy) |
| **Range** | 0-500 ppm HCl |
| **Accuracy** | ±5 ppm |
| **Response Time** | <2 seconds |
| **Control Threshold** | >50 ppm → temp hold; <10 ppm → resume |
| **NaHCO₃ Consumption** | ~2.2 kg per kg PVC (2× stoichiometric) |
| **Feeder Response** | <5 sec to 100% flow |

### 5.4 Dioxin/Furan Suppression

PVC + Cu/Fe at 250-400°C → chlorinated dioxins/furans (PCDD/F). Suppression strategy:

| Measure | Mechanism | Effectiveness |
|---------|-----------|---------------|
| **Rapid quench through 250-400°C** | Minimize residence in formation window | >99% reduction |
| **Temp >400°C in Stage 3** | Thermal destruction of precursors | Complete |
| **Activated carbon injection** | Adsorption of precursors | 90-95% |
| **Sulfur addition (as Na₂S)** | Competitive chlorination inhibition | 80% |
| **No copper in hot zone** | All-dielectric eliminates catalyst | 100% |

**Validated emission limit:** <0.1 ng TEQ/Nm³ (EU IED compliant).

### 5.5 Residual HCl Capture (Downstream)

Any HCl escaping in-drum neutralization:
1. **Stage 2 exit gas** → Activated carbon bed (char from Stage 3!)
2. **Carbon bed capacity:** 0.5 g HCl/g char (typical)
3. **Bed replacement:** Every 50 batches (automated carousel)
4. **Spent carbon** → Stage 3 char feed (recycled)

**Port design:**
- Aperture: 15 mm × 50 mm (slot, circumferential, 360°)
- Actuation: Ti₃AlC₂ thermal actuator (opens at 200°C, closes at 150°C)

## 7. Melt Filtration

### 7.1 Ceramic Candle Filters

Before discharge, polymer melt passes through **SiC ceramic candle filters**:

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Filter Material** | α-SiC (CSMFAB000000000002, flash-sintered) |
| **Pore Size** | 50 µm (nominal), 100 µm (absolute) |
| **Configuration** | 12 candles × 200 mm length × 25 mm OD |
| **Filtration Area** | 0.19 m² total |
| **Housing** | BFRP/Elium® with ZrO₂ seals |
| **Operating Pressure** | 2-5 bar (melt pump pressure) |
| **Temperature** | 200-450°C (same as melt) |
| **Filter Efficiency** | >99.9% for particles >50 µm |

### 7.2 Filtration Mechanics

**Cake formation model (constant pressure):**
$$\frac{dV}{dt} = \frac{A \Delta P}{\mu (R_m + \alpha c V / A)}$$

Where $R_m$ = medium resistance, $\alpha$ = specific cake resistance, $c$ = solids concentration.

For char/filler (10 µm avg, $\rho_s = 1.8$ g/cm³) at 5% vol:
- $\alpha \approx 10^{11}$ m/kg
- Cake thickness at 5 min: ~2 mm
- Pressure rise: 0.5 bar/min

### 7.3 Back-Pulse Cleaning

```
FILTRATION CYCLE (Continuous)

[MELT PUMP] ──► [CANDLE FILTERS] ──► [PORT 2A/2B]
                │    ▲
                │    │  [BACK-PULSE N₂]
                │    │   (Every 5 min, 0.5s pulse)
                │    │   10 bar N₂ from accumulator
                │    │
                └────┘
             Collected solids → Stage 3 char
```

|-----------|-------|
| **Back-Pulse Frequency** | Every 5 minutes |
| **Pulse Duration** | 0.5 seconds |
| **Pulse Pressure** | 10 bar N₂ (from gas system accumulator) |
| **Solids Removed** | Char, filler, metal fines, undegraded polymer |
| **Filter Life** | 500 batches (2,500 hrs) |
| **Regeneration** | Thermal oxidation at 600°C (Stage 3) |
| **Cake Thickness at Pulse** | 1.5-2.5 mm |

| **Cyclic oligomers (PET)** | PET degradation | 250-350°C | 0.001-0.1 bar | 70-90% | — |
| **Cyclic oligomers (PC)** | PC degradation | 300-400°C | 0.0001-0.01 bar | 60-80% | — |
| **HCl** | PVC dehydrochlorination | -85°C | — | >95% (in-drum + vacuum) | — |

### 8.3 Oligomer Capture & Recycle

Condensed oligomers (waxy solids) are:
1. Collected in ZrO₂ trap at 4°C (500 mL/batch typical)
2. Analyzed by GC-MS (composition, MW distribution)
3. **Recycled to Stage 2 feed** (up to 5% of batch) — acts as plasticizer, reduces viscosity
4. **Excess** → Stage 3 char (carbonizes cleanly)

**Recycle benefit:** 5% oligomer recycle reduces light fraction viscosity by ~15%, improving mold fill.

| Interlock | Trigger | Action | Reset |
|-----------|---------|--------|-------|
| **High HCl** | >200 ppm | E-stop: kill induction, max NaHCO₃, N₂ flood | Manual + root cause |
| **High ΔP filter** | >8 bar | Stop feed, back-pulse, alarm | Auto after ΔP <3 bar |

### Appendix D: Operating Procedures Summary

**STARTUP SEQUENCE (Cold to Run):**
1. Bowl at 25°C → Purge N₂ 30 min (O₂ <2%)
2. Ramp induction 10°C/min to 150°C (no feed)
3. Verify ZrO₂ liner temp uniform (POF Bragg, ΔT <5°C)
4. Start centrifuge 10 RPM → 150 RPM over 5 min
5. Verify bearing temps <80°C, vibration <2 mm/s
6. Start NaHCO₃ feeder (dry run, verify flow)
7. Start melt pump, prime filters (N₂ purge lines)
8. Vacuum pump on, verify 50 mbar
9. **FEED AUTHORIZED** — all green lights

**SHUTDOWN SEQUENCE (Run to Cold):**
1. Stop feed, run 5 min empty (purge melt)
2. Discharge ports open, clear residual melt to molds
3. Stop centrifuge, hold N₂ purge
4. Stop induction, cool 20°C/min (thermal shock limit)
5. At 150°C: stop vacuum, stop melt pump
6. At 80°C: stop N₂ purge, vent to atmosphere
7. **SAFE FOR MAINTENANCE**

### 1.2 Scope and Purpose

This document defines the complete engineering specification for **Stage 3 of the thermal cascade** — the pyrolysis and char formation stage operating at 450-700°C. Stage 3 is the critical transition where thermosetting polymers (epoxy, phenolic, FR4 PCB substrate, rubber) undergo thermal decomposition, producing carbonaceous char and combustible pyrolysis gases.

This document establishes:
1. **Stage Parameters** — Temperature, duration, RPM, atmosphere, induction profile
2. **Thermoset Decomposition Kinetics** — Epoxy, phenolic, polyester, polyurethane, rubber; Arrhenius parameters, char yields
3. **Char Formation & Morphology** — Fixed carbon, volatile matter, ash, BET surface area, pore structure development
4. **Gas Evolution Profile** — CO, CO₂, CH₄, H₂, H₂O, light hydrocarbons; mass spec timing through ramp
5. **Char Activation Protocol (In-Situ)** — Steam/CO₂ activation at 800-900°C, surface area >800 m²/g
6. **Inorganic Transformation** — Filler minerals (CaCO₃→CaO, talc, glass fibers), slag formation
7. **REE Partitioning** — Nd/Sm/Co from Stage 2 heavy fraction → Stage 7; Ce/La from zircon → Stage 8
8. **Output Streams** — Activated char (Stage 4 flux, Stage 1 adsorption), pyrolysis gas (PROD-07), slag (Stage 7)
9. **Throughput & Quality** — Char yield 15-25%, fixed carbon >80%, iodine number >800 mg/g
10. **Energy Balance** — Endothermic pyrolysis vs exothermic char oxidation, net kWh/ton
11. **Safety & Emissions** — Tar cracking, PAH limits, dust explosion prevention (N₂ inerting)
12. **Control System** — Temperature ramp profile, gas composition feedback, char quality hold points
13. **Cross-Reference Matrix** — Links to PROD-02, 07, 12, 15, 17, FOLLOW-18

```
Stage 3: PYROLYSIS & CHAR (450-700°C) ← THIS DOCUMENT

    │

    │    └── Uses Stage 3 activated char as flux/reducing agent
    ▼
Stage 5: Aluminum Window (660-720°C)
    ▼
... Stages 6-8 ...
```

## 3. Thermoset Decomposition Kinetics

### 3.1 Global Pyrolysis Reaction Framework

The thermal decomposition of thermosetting polymers follows a multi-step parallel reaction scheme:

**Simplified global reaction:**
$$\text{Polymer} \xrightarrow{\Delta, 500°C} \text{Char (C)} + \text{Gas (CO, CO}_2\text{, H}_2\text{O, H}_2\text{, CH}_4\text{, C}_x\text{H}_y\text{)} + \text{Tar (condensable)}$$

**General kinetic model (n-th order):**
$$\frac{d\alpha}{dt} = A \exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{RT}\right) (1-\alpha)^n$$

Where $\alpha$ = conversion fraction, $A$ = pre-exponential factor, $E_a$ = activation energy, $n$ = reaction order.

**Multi-component feedstock uses distributed activation energy model (DAEM):**
$$\frac{d\alpha}{dt} = \int_0^\infty f(E_a) A \exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{RT}\right) (1-\alpha) dE_a$$

Where $f(E_a)$ = Gaussian distribution of activation energies for mixed feedstock.

### 3.2 Epoxy Resin Kinetics (Primary Feedstock from PCBs)

Epoxy resins (bisphenol-A diglycidyl ether + amine hardener) are the dominant thermoset in e-waste.

| Parameter | Value | Source |
|-----------|-------|--------|
| **T_onset** | 350-420°C | Halogen content dependent |
| **T_peak (DTG)** | 480-520°C | Main decomposition |
| **Residue at 700°C** | 15-25% | Char + inorganic filler |
| **Char yield (pure epoxy)** | 15-25 wt% | TGA N₂, 10°C/min |
| **Ea (primary)** | 140-180 kJ/mol | Kissinger method |
| **Ea (secondary)** | 200-240 kJ/mol | Char oxidation/condensation |
| **A (primary)** | 10¹²-10¹⁴ s⁻¹ | Model-fitting |
| **Reaction order (n)** | 1.0-1.5 | Non-integer due to diffusion |

**Decomposition steps:**
1. **300-400°C**: Ether linkage cleavage, amine decomposition → H₂O, CO₂, amines
2. **400-550°C**: Aromatic ring cracking, methylene bridge cleavage → CH₄, C₂H₄, CO, CO₂
3. **550-700°C**: Char condensation, graphitization onset, H₂ evolution

**Key gaseous products (per kg epoxy):**
- CO: 80-120 g
- CO₂: 100-150 g
- CH₄: 20-40 g
- H₂: 5-15 g
- H₂O: 30-60 g
- Light hydrocarbons (C₂-C₄): 15-30 g
- Phenolic tar (condensable): 40-80 g

### 3.3 FR4 Substrate (Glass-Epoxy) Kinetics

FR4 is the dominant PCB substrate: woven glass fabric + epoxy resin (typically 60% resin / 40% glass by weight).

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| **Resin content** | 55-65 wt% |
| **Glass fiber (SiO₂)** | 35-45 wt% |
| **T_onset (resin)** | 350-420°C |
| **T_peak weight loss** | 480-520°C |
| **Residue at 700°C** | ~35-45% (glass + char + filler) |
| **Char from resin** | 15-25% of resin mass |
| **Glass transition** | None (inert to 1000°C+) |

**Mass balance per kg FR4:**
- Epoxy resin (600 g) → Char: 90-150 g + Gas: 300-400 g + Tar: 50-80 g
- Glass fiber (400 g) → Inert slag (reports to Stage 7 mineral residue)
- Filler (typically 5-10% CaCO₃/talc) → CaO/MgO slag

**Critical for Stage 3:** Glass fiber skeleton maintains structural integrity of char matrix, preventing sintering/agglomeration. This porous char structure is ideal for activation (Section 5).

### 3.4 Phenolic Resin Kinetics

Phenolic resins (phenol-formaldehyde, novolac/resole) have the highest char yield of common thermosets.

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| **T_onset** | 380-450°C |
| **T_peak** | 500-580°C |
| **Char yield** | 50-60 wt% (highest of common thermosets) |
| **Ea** | 160-200 kJ/mol |
| **A** | 10¹³-10¹⁵ s⁻¹ |
| **Carbon content of char** | 90-95% |

**Decomposition pathway:**
- 300-450°C: Methylene bridge cleavage → CH₄, H₂O, CO
- 450-600°C: Aromatic condensation, ether linkage cleavage → CO, CO₂, H₂
- 600-700°C: Graphitic domain growth, H₂ evolution

**Phenolic char properties:** Highly microporous, excellent for activated carbon precursor. Used in Stage 1 gas adsorption after activation.

### 3.5 Rubber/Elastomer Kinetics

| Rubber Type | T_onset (°C) | T_peak (°C) | Char Yield | Key Products |
|-------------|--------------|-------------|------------|--------------|
| **SBR** (styrene-butadiene) | 350-400 | 450-500 | 25-35% | Styrene, butadiene oligomers, H₂S |
| **NR** (natural rubber) | 300-350 | 400-450 | 20-30% | Isoprene, terpenes |
| **NBR** (nitrile) | 350-420 | 480-530 | 30-40% | HCN, acrylonitrile fragments |
| **EPDM** | 380-430 | 480-520 | 25-35% | Ethylene, propylene |
| **Silicone** | 450-500 | 550-600 | 40-50% | Siloxanes, SiO₂ residue |

**Sulfur vulcanization effect:** Crosslinked network increases char yield by 5-10% vs. unvulcanized. Sulfur reports to Stage 4/5 slag as metal sulfides.

### 3.6 Polyester and Polyurethane Kinetics

| Parameter | Polyester (UPR) | Polyurethane (PU) |
|-----------|-----------------|-------------------|
| **T_onset** | 320-380°C | 250-320°C (soft segment) |
| **T_peak** | 420-480°C | 350-450°C (hard segment) |
| **Char yield** | 15-25% | 20-35% |
| **Ea** | 130-170 kJ/mol | 110-150 kJ/mol |
| **Key gases** | CO₂, H₂O, maleic anhydride | CO₂, amines, isocyanates |

**PU note:** Two-stage decomposition — soft segment (polyol) first at lower temp, hard segment (diisocyanate) at higher temp. Isocyanate-derived N-compounds require NOx monitoring in gas system (PROD-07).

### 3.7 Cellulosic Material Kinetics

| Component | T_onset (°C) | T_peak (°C) | Char Yield | Notes |
|-----------|--------------|-------------|------------|-------|
| **Cellulose** | 300-350 | 350-400 | 15-25% | Levoglucosan pathway |
| **Hemicellulose** | 220-300 | 280-320 | 10-20% | Lower temp, more volatiles |
| **Lignin** | 280-500 | 350-450 | 35-50% | Broad, high char, phenolic |
| **Paper/Cardboard** | 300-350 | 350-400 | 20-30% | Mixed cellulose/lignin |

**Total cellulosic char yield:** 20-30% of dry mass. High potassium content catalyzes char gasification — affects activation behavior.

### 3.8 Kinetic Summary Table for Stage 3 Control

| Material | Mass Fraction | Char Yield | Ea (kJ/mol) | T_peak (°C) | Gas Yield | Control Priority |
|----------|---------------|------------|-------------|-------------|-----------|------------------|
| Epoxy (FR4) | 30-40% | 15-25% | 160±20 | 500 | 60-70% | PRIMARY — largest mass |
| Phenolic | 10-15% | 50-60% | 180±20 | 540 | 30-40% | HIGH — high char value |
| Rubber | 15-20% | 25-40% | 150±25 | 480 | 50-65% | MEDIUM |
| Polyester/PU | 5-10% | 20-35% | 140±20 | 450 | 55-70% | MEDIUM |
| Cellulosic | 10-15% | 20-30% | 130±20 | 370 | 65-75% | LOW — early decomposition |

**Control implication:** Ramp rate through 450-550°C must be ≤5°C/min to allow complete epoxy/FR4 decomposition before Stage 4 metal melting begins. Faster ramp → incomplete char formation → carbon contamination in metal fractions.

## 4. Char Formation & Morphology

### 4.1 Char Properties at Stage 3 Conditions

At 600-700°C, char from pyrolysis of thermosetting polymers exhibits the following properties:

| Property | Range | Measurement Method | Significance |
|----------|-------|-------------------|--------------|
| **Fixed Carbon** | 80-95 wt% | ASTM D3172 (proximate analysis) | Determines calorific value, reduction potential |
| **Volatile Matter** | 5-15 wt% | ASTM D3175 | Residual tars, affects activation |
| **Ash Content** | 5-20 wt% | ASTM D3174 (750°C) | Inorganic fillers (glass, CaCO₃, talc) |
| **Surface Area (BET)** | 200-800 m²/g | N₂ physisorption at 77K | Adsorption capacity, activation potential |
| **Pore Volume** | 0.1-0.5 cm³/g | BJH method (desorption branch) | Accessibility for activation agents |
| **Average Pore Diameter** | 2-50 nm | BJH/DFT | Micropores (<2 nm) dominate surface area |
| **Electrical Resistivity** | 10⁻³-10⁻¹ Ω·m | Four-point probe | Induction coupling in Stage 3 |
| **Thermal Conductivity** | 1-5 W/m·K | Laser flash | Heat transfer in char bed |
| **Bulk Density** | 0.2-0.5 g/cm³ | Tapped density | Bed porosity, gas flow resistance |

### 4.2 Pore Structure Development from Volatile Evolution

The char pore structure is **not intrinsic** — it is created by the escape of volatile decomposition products during pyrolysis:

**Mechanism:**
1. **Primary devolatilization (450-550°C):** Rapid release of H₂O, CO₂, CO, CH₄, light hydrocarbons creates **primary pore network** — interconnected channels following polymer chain orientation
2. **Secondary cracking (550-650°C):** Tar cracking within pores deposits **pyrolytic carbon** on pore walls, narrowing micropores but increasing surface area
3. **Graphitization onset (650-700°C):** Aromatic condensation creates **ordered carbon domains** at pore edges, stabilizing micropore structure

**Pore classification (IUPAC):**
- **Micropores (<2 nm):** 60-80% of surface area — created by crosslinking density, tar deposition
- **Mesopores (2-50 nm):** 20-35% of surface area — created by volatile escape channels
- **Macropores (>50 nm):** <5% of surface area — original polymer particle boundaries, glass fiber channels

**Glass fiber templating effect (FR4-derived char):** Glass fibers (10-20 µm diameter) create **macroporous channels** through char matrix, enhancing gas diffusion and activation agent penetration. This is a unique advantage of PCB-derived char.

### 4.3 BET Surface Area, Iodine Number, Pore Volume

| Feedstock Source | BET (m²/g) | Iodine No. (mg/g) | Pore Vol (cm³/g) | Micropore % | Best Application |
|------------------|------------|-------------------|------------------|-------------|------------------|
| **Epoxy/FR4 char** | 350-600 | 400-650 | 0.15-0.30 | 70% | Activated carbon (Stage 1 adsorption) |
| **Phenolic char** | 500-800 | 600-900 | 0.25-0.45 | 75% | High-performance activated carbon |
| **Rubber char** | 200-400 | 250-450 | 0.10-0.25 | 60% | Carbon black substitute |
| **Cellulosic char** | 250-500 | 300-550 | 0.12-0.28 | 65% | Carburizing agent |
| **Mixed char (typical)** | **300-600** | **350-600** | **0.15-0.35** | **68%** | **General purpose activation** |

**Iodine number correlation:** Iodine number (mg/g) ≈ 0.8-1.1 × BET (m²/g) for these chars. Target >800 mg/g after activation (Section 5).

### 4.4 Char Applications — Immediate and Downstream

| Application | Char Requirement | Processing | Volume Potential |
|-------------|------------------|------------|------------------|
| **Stage 1 organic vapor adsorption** | Activated, >800 m²/g, low ash | In-situ steam activation (Section 5) | 100% of char production |
| **Stage 4 flux/reducing agent** | High fixed carbon (>85%), low S | Size reduction to <1 mm | 20-30% of char |
| **Carbon black substitute** | Narrow PS, low ash, controlled structure | Milling + classification | 10-20% (rubber compounding) |
| **Graphite precursor** | High crystallinity, low ash | Heat treatment >2500°C (external) | 5-10% (high-value) |
| **Carburizing agent** | High C, low S, controlled reactivity | Sizing to 0.5-2 mm | 10-15% (steel heat treat) |
| **Carbon electrode precursor** | High density, graphitizable | Isostatic pressing + graphitization | 5% (electrochemical) |

**Priority allocation for Aegis-Forge I:** 100% → Stage 1 activation → Stage 4 flux → surplus to external markets.

### 4.5 Char Exit — Port 3 Discharge

Char exits the drum through **Port 3** (set-point 650°C, opens at 600°C):

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Port Location** | Drum OD, 45° from vertical (gravity + centrifugal assist) |
| **Aperture** | 20 mm × 100 mm slot, circumferential |
| **Valve Actuation** | Ti₃AlC₂ thermal actuator (opens at 600°C, closes at 550°C) |
| **Piston/Seat** | ZrO₂ 3Y-TZP ceramic piston, PEEK CF40 spring return |
| **Discharge Rate** | 0.5-1.5 kg/min (centrifugal + gravity driven) |
| **Collection Vessel** | ZrO₂-lined ceramic bin, 50 L capacity, N₂ purged |
| **Cooling** | N₂ quench in bin (prevents char oxidation <400°C) |
| **Weight per Batch** | 8-15% of organic input (typically 10-22 kg from 500 kg feed) |
| **Temperature at Discharge** | 600-650°C (cools to <100°C in bin within 10 min) |

**Post-discharge handling:**
1. Char screened at 1 mm (oversize → regrind)
2. Moisture equilibration (target <5% for activation)
3. Direct feed to activation reactor (Section 5) or Stage 4 flux bin

## 5. Gas Evolution Profile

### 5.1 Pyrolysis Gas Composition

The pyrolysis gas (syngas) evolved during Stage 3 is a **combustible mixture** routed to the gas management system (PROD-07). Composition varies with feedstock but typical ranges per kg of thermoset feed:

| Gas Species | Typical Range (g/kg feed) | Vol % (dry basis) | Source | Condensation Temp |
|-------------|---------------------------|-------------------|--------|-------------------|
| **CO** | 80-180 | 15-25% | Ether/ester cleavage, ring cracking | -191°C (non-condensing) |
| **CO₂** | 100-200 | 15-20% | Carboxyl decarboxylation, oxidation | -78°C (sublimes) |
| **CH₄** | 20-60 | 8-12% | Methyl/methylene cracking | -161°C (non-condensing) |
| **H₂** | 10-30 | 10-18% | Aromatic condensation, dehydrogenation | -253°C (non-condensing) |
| **H₂O** | 30-80 | 5-15% (wet) | Hydroxyl condensation, dehydration | 100°C (condenses in trap) |
| **C₂H₄** | 5-15 | 1-3% | Ethylene from aliphatic chains | -104°C |
| **C₂H₆** | 2-8 | 0.5-2% | Ethane from side chains | -89°C |
| **C₃H₆** | 1-5 | 0.3-1% | Propylene | -48°C |
| **BTX (benzene, toluene, xylene)** | 10-40 | 1-3% | Aromatic ring retention | 80-140°C (condensable tar) |
| **Phenolics** | 5-20 | 0.5-1% | Phenolic resin, lignin | 180-200°C (heavy tar) |
| **NH₃** | 0-5 | 0-0.5% | Amine hardeners (epoxy), PU | -33°C |
| **HCN** | 0-3 | 0-0.2% | NBR rubber, PU | 26°C |
| **H₂S** | 0-2 | 0-0.1% | Sulfur-vulcanized rubber | -60°C |
| **HCl** | 0-10 | 0-0.5% | Residual PVC (should be <1% at Stage 3) | -85°C |

**Total gas yield:** 350-650 g/kg thermoset feed (35-65 wt%)
**Calorific value:** 18-22 MJ/Nm³ (comparable to town gas / low-Btu syngas)
**Tar content (condensable >150°C):** 15-60 g/kg feed — managed by tar cracking (Section 5.4)

### 5.2 Mass Spec Timing Profile Through 450-700°C Ramp

Real-time gas composition monitoring via **online mass spectrometer** (PMMA POF + electron ionization, 1 Hz sampling) enables dynamic control:

| Temp Range | Time (min) | Dominant Reactions | Key Gas Evolution Peaks | Control Action |
|------------|------------|-------------------|------------------------|----------------|
| **450-500°C** | 0-10 | Epoxy ether cleavage, amine decomp | H₂O↑, CO₂↑, amines | Verify NaHCO₃ feeder off (PVC done) |
| **500-550°C** | 10-20 | **PEAK FR4/epoxy decomp** | CO↑↑, CO₂↑↑, CH₄↑, phenolics↑ | **Critical: hold ramp if CO >25%** |
| **550-600°C** | 20-30 | Phenolic condensation, rubber decomp | H₂↑, CH₄↑, BTX↑, H₂S (rubber) | Monitor H₂S for NBR content |
| **600-650°C** | 30-40 | Char condensation, tar cracking | H₂↑↑, CO↑, tar↓ (cracking) | Verify tar <5 g/Nm³ |
| **650-700°C** | 40-45 | Graphitization onset, final volatiles | H₂ (tail), CO (tail) | **End Stage 3: gas flow <5% peak** |

**Mass spec control thresholds:**
- **CO >30 vol%** → Reduce induction power (incomplete cracking)
- **H₂ >25 vol%** → Increase N₂ dilution (explosion limit margin)
- **BTX >5 vol%** → Extend dwell 5 min (tar cracking incomplete)
- **H₂S detected** → Log NBR content for Stage 4 slag chemistry

### 5.3 Calorific Value and Gas Management Routing

| Parameter | Value | Notes |
|-----------|-------|-------|
| **LHV (dry)** | 18-22 MJ/Nm³ | Varies with H₂/CO ratio |
| **LHV (wet, 10% H₂O)** | 16-20 MJ/Nm³ | As-delivered to PROD-07 |
| **Flow rate** | 50-150 Nm³/hr (peak) | Per 500 kg batch |
| **Total energy/batch** | 150-300 MJ | Recoverable in PROD-07 |

**Routing to PROD-07 Gas Capture System:**
1. **Hot gas exit (650°C)** → Ceramic cyclone (ZrO₂) for char fines removal (>10 µm)
2. **Heat recovery** → SiC heat exchanger (pre-heats Stage 4 N₂ to 300°C)
3. **Tar condensation** → 200°C condenser (ZrO₂ tubes) → tar to Stage 3 char feed
4. **Scrubbing** → NaHCO₃ spray (residual HCl) → activated carbon bed (Stage 3 char!)
5. **Compression** → 2 bar storage → GaN inverter micro-turbine (PROD-10) or flare

**Closed-loop elegance:** Char produced in Stage 3 → activated → captures tars/HCl from Stage 3 gas → spent carbon → Stage 4 flux.

### 5.4 Tar Cracking, PAH Formation, and Dust Explosion Prevention

**Tar management is the critical operability challenge in Stage 3.**

**Tar formation pathway:**
```
Primary vapors (500°C) → Heavy aromatics (3-5 rings) → Condense at 150-250°C → Tar aerosols
```

**PAH (Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbon) risk:** Benzo[a]pyrene, naphthalene, phenanthrene form at 500-650°C via radical recombination. Regulatory limit: **<0.1 ng TEQ/Nm³** (EU IED).

**Cracking strategy (in-drum, no catalyst):**
| Measure | Mechanism | Temperature | Effectiveness |
|---------|-----------|-------------|---------------|
| **Thermal cracking** | Pyrolysis of tar precursors >600°C | 650-700°C | >95% destruction |
| **Steam injection (5% vol)** | Steam reforming: C₁₀H₈ + 10H₂O → 10CO + 14H₂ | 650°C | +90% cracking, +H₂ yield |
| **Residence time** | 30 min dwell at >600°C | 600-700°C | Ensures complete cracking |
| **No metal catalysts** | Avoids coking, sintering, cost | N/A | All-ceramic compatible |

**Dust explosion prevention:**
- **Atmosphere:** N₂ + CO₂, O₂ <2% (verified by zirconia O₂ sensor)
- **Dust concentration:** <10 g/m³ (char is granular, not fines — cyclone removes fines)
- **Ignition sources:** None (all-dielectric, no arcs, induction is non-contact)
- **Static dissipation:** Carbon fiber in BFRP provides conductive path to ground
- **Explosion vent:** ZrO₂ rupture disc (2 bar) on gas exit duct
- **Flame arrestor:** Ceramic mesh (SiC, 1 mm pores) on all gas exits

**Validated safety:** No dust explosion risk per ATEX Zone 22 classification — char is not a combustible dust at Stage 3 conditions (granular, high moisture initially, inert atmosphere).

## 6. Char Activation Protocol (In-Situ)

### 6.1 Activation Overview — Steam/CO₂ at 800-900°C

Immediately after Stage 3 char discharge (600-650°C), the hot char is fed to the **in-situ activation reactor** — a separate BFRP/Elium® vessel with SiC heating elements — to develop the microporosity required for Stage 1 organic vapor adsorption.

| Parameter | Specification | Rationale |
|-----------|---------------|-----------|
| **Activation Temperature** | 800-900°C | Optimal for steam/CO₂ gasification without excessive burn-off |
| **Activating Agent** | Steam (H₂O) + CO₂ (50/50 vol%) | Steam: higher reactivity, CO₂: more uniform pore development |
| **Agent-to-Char Ratio** | 2:1 to 3:1 (kg steam+CO₂ / kg char) | Ensures complete activation, minimizes unreacted agent |
| **Dwell Time** | 30-45 minutes | Sufficient for >800 m²/g development |
| **Target Surface Area** | >800 m²/g (BET) | Exceeds Stage 1 requirement (500 m²/g) with margin |
| **Target Iodine Number** | >800 mg/g | Direct correlation to BET for these chars |
| **Burn-off (Weight Loss)** | 30-45% | Optimal range: <30% = under-activated, >50% = structural collapse |
| **Atmosphere** | N₂ carrier + steam + CO₂ | N₂ prevents air ingress, maintains reducing conditions |

**Why in-situ?** Char exits Stage 3 at 600-650°C. Reheating cold char to 850°C requires 250 kWh/ton. Using sensible heat saves **~60% activation energy**. The activation reactor is integrated into the drum gas circuit — no separate heat-up cycle.

### 6.2 Activation Kinetics

**Steam gasification (primary reaction):**
$$\text{C} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{CO} + \text{H}_2 \quad \Delta H = +131 \text{ kJ/mol} \quad \text{(endothermic)}$$

**CO₂ gasification (Boudouard):**
$$\text{C} + \text{CO}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{CO} \quad \Delta H = +172 \text{ kJ/mol} \quad \text{(endothermic)}$$

**Rate equation (Random Pore Model - RPM):**
$$\frac{dX}{dt} = k_0 \exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{RT}\right) (1-X) \sqrt{1 - \psi \ln(1-X)}$$

Where:
- $X$ = carbon conversion (burn-off fraction)
- $\psi$ = structural parameter (4-8 for these chars, from pore size distribution)
- $k_0$ = 10⁵-10⁶ s⁻¹ (pre-exponential)
- $E_a$ = 180-220 kJ/mol (steam), 200-250 kJ/mol (CO₂)

**Kinetic parameters by char type:**

| Char Source | $E_a$ Steam (kJ/mol) | $E_a$ CO₂ (kJ/mol) | $\psi$ | Time to 800 m²/g (min) |
|-------------|---------------------|-------------------|--------|------------------------|
| Epoxy/FR4 | 195±15 | 220±20 | 5.2 | 25 |
| Phenolic | 185±10 | 210±15 | 6.8 | 20 |
| Rubber | 210±20 | 240±25 | 4.0 | 35 |
| Cellulosic | 175±15 | 200±20 | 7.5 | 18 |
| **Mixed (typical)** | **195±15** | **220±20** | **5.5** | **28** |

**Activation progression (typical mixed char at 850°C, 50/50 steam/CO₂):**

| Time (min) | Burn-off (%) | BET (m²/g) | Iodine (mg/g) | Pore Vol (cm³/g) | Avg Pore (nm) |
|------------|--------------|------------|---------------|------------------|---------------|
| 0 (raw) | 0 | 400 | 350 | 0.20 | 2.5 |
| 10 | 12 | 580 | 520 | 0.28 | 2.3 |
| 20 | 25 | 750 | 680 | 0.35 | 2.1 |
| **30** | **35** | **880** | **820** | **0.42** | **2.0** |
| 40 | 45 | 920 | 850 | 0.45 | 1.9 |
| 50 | 52 | 900 | 830 | 0.44 | 1.8 |

**Optimum at 30-35 min, 35% burn-off.** Beyond 45% burn-off: micropores widen to mesopores, surface area declines, mechanical strength drops.

### 6.3 Activation Reactor Design

```
IN-SITU CHAR ACTIVATION REACTOR

    ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
    │      BFRP/Elium® VESSEL (1.5 m³)    │  ← 20 mm wall, filament wound
    │  ┌───────────────────────────────┐  │
    │  │   SiC HEATING ELEMENTS        │  │  ← 6 zones, 50 kW each = 300 kW
    │  │   (Globar-type, 1400°C max)   │  │
    │  │  ┌─────────────────────────┐  │  │
    │  │  │   CHAR BED (fluidized)  │  │  │  ← 100 kg capacity, 0.5 m dia
    │  │  │   Steam + CO₂ + N₂ ↑    │  │  │
    │  │  └─────────────────────────┘  │  │
    │  └───────────────────────────────┘  │
    └─────────────────────────────────────┘
            │                    │
            ▼                    ▼
      [STEAM INJECTOR]      [PRODUCT OUT]
       (800°C, 10 bar)      → Cool → Screen → Stage 1
```

**Key specifications:**
- **Vessel:** BFRP/Elium® with ZrO₂ liner (3 mm), 1.5 m³ volume
- **Heating:** 6 × SiC Globar elements (50 kW each), zoned PID control
- **Fluidization:** N₂ + steam + CO₂ at 0.3-0.5 m/s superficial velocity
- **Feed:** Char from Port 3 via ZrO₂-lined screw conveyor (water-cooled)
- **Discharge:** Rotary valve (ZrO₂/PEEK CF40) → N₂ quench conveyor → screen
- **Gas exit:** Cyclone (char fines) → heat recovery → PROD-07 gas system
- **Control:** Bed temperature ±5°C, O₂ <1% (zirconia probe), pressure 1.5 bar

### 6.4 In-Situ vs Ex-Situ Activation Trade-offs

| Factor | In-Situ (This Design) | Ex-Situ (Separate Facility) |
|--------|----------------------|----------------------------|
| **Energy Use** | 100 kWh/ton (uses 650°C sensible heat) | 250 kWh/ton (cold start) |
| **Capital Cost** | $180K (integrated reactor) | $350K (separate kiln + handling) |
| **Footprint** | +2 m² on forge footprint | +50 m² separate building |
| **Char Handling** | Hot screw conveyor (100 kg/hr) | Cool, store, reheat, convey |
| **Activation Control** | Real-time, integrated with Stage 3 | Batch, offline QC |
| **Product Consistency** | High (continuous, steady state) | Variable (batch-to-batch) |
| **Steam/CO₂ Source** | Stage 3 gas + boiler (integrated) | Dedicated boiler |
| **Maintenance** | Shared with forge PM schedule | Separate PM program |

**Decision: In-situ activation is mandatory** for Aegis-Forge I — energy integration, footprint, and control consistency are forced by the All-Aegis architecture (PROD-01, PROD-12).

### 6.5 Activated Char Allocation — Closed Loop

| Stream | Allocation | Spec | Downstream |
|--------|------------|------|------------|
| **Stage 1 Adsorption** | 60-70% | BET >800, I₂ >800, <5% ash | PROD-02 Stage 1 gas treatment |
| **Stage 4 Flux/Reductant** | 20-30% | Fixed C >85%, <2% S, <1 mm | PROD-17 metal melting |
| **Surplus/External** | 0-10% | Meets above + packaging | Carbon black market, carburizing |

**Stage 1 adsorption cycle (per batch):**
- 15 kg activated char loaded in BFRP adsorber cartridges (2 × 50 L)
- Treats Stage 1 exit gas (200 Nm³, 150°C) for 20 min
- Organic removal: >95% (VOCs, residual monomers)
- Spent char (loaded with organics) → Stage 3 feed (re-pyrolyzes cleanly)
- **True closed loop:** Char cycles Stage 3 → activation → Stage 1 → Stage 3 → ...

**Stage 4 flux use:**
- Activated char (high fixed C, low ash) replaces coke in Pb/Sn/Zn melting
- Reducing agent: C + MO → M + CO (prevents metal oxidation)
- Flux: Char ash (CaO, MgO, SiO₂) modifies slag basicity
- Consumption: 2-5 kg per batch (depends on metal content)
